standard.summary: Machine learning enables unbinned, highly-differential cross section measurements. A recent idea uses generative models to morph a starting simulation into unfolded data; this approach can be extended using morphing techniques such as Schrödinger Bridges and Direct Diffusion, ensuring the models learn correct conditional probabilities and reaching accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art conditional generative unfolding methods. Related work introduces unfolding approaches like SBUnfold, where a generative model maps one set of events into another without requiring a known probability density, combining strengths of discriminative and generative models.

citations.claim: Machine learning enables unbinned, highly-differential cross section measurements. A recent idea uses generative models to morph a starting simulation into the unfolded data. We show how to extend two morphing techniques, Schrödinger Bridges and Direct Diffusion, in order to ensure that the models learn the correct conditional probabilities, bringing distribution mapping to a similar level of accuracy as state-of-the-art conditional generative unfolding methods.

SBUnfold is an unfolding approach that combines the strengths of both discriminative and generative models. Its key feature is that its generative model maps one set of events into another without having to go through a known probability density, and it achieves excellent performance on a synthetic Z+jets dataset.

balanced.summary: Machine learning enables unbinned, highly-differential cross section measurements. A recent idea uses generative models to morph a starting simulation into the unfolded data, and extensions of morphing techniques such as Schr\"odinger Bridges and Direct Diffusion ensure that the models learn correct conditional probabilities, reaching accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art conditional generative unfolding (doc1). Other generative approaches, like SBUnfold, combine strengths of discriminative and generative models by mapping one set of events into another without requiring a known probability density (doc2). A broad evaluation of ML-based unfolding methods shows that all tested techniques accurately reproduce particle-level spectra across complex observables, offering a toolkit for new measurements (doc4). Recent extensions address variable-dimensional full-event unfolding, such as a variational latent diffusion modification demonstrated in semi-leptonic top quark pair production at the LHC (doc5), and direct generation of full detector-level events from partons using transformers, score-based models, and normalizing flows (doc7).

citations.claim: Machine learning enables unbinned, highly-differential cross section measurements; a recent idea uses generative models to morph a starting simulation into the unfolded data. The authors extend two morphing techniques, Schr\"odinger Bridges and Direct Diffusion, to ensure the models learn correct conditional probabilities, bringing distribution mapping to similar accuracy as state-of-the-art conditional generative unfolding.

SBUnfold uses Schr\"odinger Bridges and diffusion models to combine the strengths of discriminative and generative models, mapping one set of events into another without going through a known probability density as in normalizing flows and standard diffusion models.

The landscape of ML-based unfolding includes known, upgraded, and new methods; evaluations on two datasets show all techniques accurately reproduce particle-level spectra across complex observables, providing an exciting toolkit for new measurements with unprecedented detail.

A novel modification to the variational latent diffusion model (VLD) approach allows unfolding of high- and variable-dimensional feature spaces, enabling full-event unfolding in collider data, demonstrated in semi-leptonic top quark pair production at the LHC.

PIPPIN generates full events at detector-level from parton-level information using transformers, score-based models, and normalizing flows, tackling multiplicity variations between parton and reconstructed object spaces and achieving accurate results for fast detector simulation.

standard.summary: Mitigating explicit and implicit biases in LLMs is a critical focus in NLP, but many current methodologies evaluate scenarios in isolation rather than considering broader context and the spectrum of potential biases (doc_2). The STOP dataset addresses this by introducing 450 offensive progressions with 2,700 unique sentences of varying severity across 9 demographics and 46 sub-demographics, revealing that even the best models detect bias inconsistently, with success rates ranging from 19.3% to 69.8% (doc_2). Aligning models with human judgments on STOP can improve answer rates on sensitive tasks such as BBQ, StereoSet, and CrowS-Pairs by up to 191% (doc_2). Comprehensive reviews categorize biases as intrinsic and extrinsic, and mitigation strategies as pre-model, intra-model, and post-model (doc_5). More advanced approaches like MOMA use multi-agent causal interventions to reduce bias scores by up to 87.7% while maintaining downstream accuracy (doc_7). Another approach, BiasGPT, creates multiple customized model instances reflecting different demographic biases and merges their perspectives to capture a broader spectrum of human experiences (doc_4).

citations.claim: Mitigating explicit and implicit biases in LLMs is a critical focus in NLP, but many current methodologies evaluate scenarios in isolation without considering broader context or the spectrum of potential biases within each situation.

The STOP dataset includes 450 offensive progressions containing 2,700 unique sentences of varying severity across 9 demographics and 46 sub-demographics, and evaluation shows even the best models detect bias inconsistently, with success rates ranging from 19.3% to 69.8%.
Aligning models with human judgments on STOP can improve model answer rates on sensitive tasks such as BBQ, StereoSet, and CrowS-Pairs by up to 191%.

A comprehensive review categorizes biases as intrinsic and extrinsic, analyzes bias evaluation methods (data-level, model-level, output-level), and mitigation strategies (pre-model, intra-model, post-model).

The MOMA multi-objective multi-agent framework reduces bias scores by up to 87.7% with only marginal performance degradation (up to 6.8% on BBQ) and enhances the multi-objective metric icat on StereoSet by up to 58.1%.

BiasGPT develops multiple customised GPT instances, each reflecting biases in demographic characteristics like gender, age, and race, which collaborate to merge diverse perspectives into an integrated response.

balanced.summary: Mitigating explicit and implicit biases in large language models (LLMs) is a critical focus in natural language processing, yet many current methodologies evaluate scenarios in isolation rather than considering broader context and the full spectrum of potential biases. The STOP dataset addresses this gap by testing offensive progressions across escalating severity and diverse demographics, revealing that even top models detect bias inconsistently and that aligning models with human judgments on such progressions can improve performance on other sensitive-task benchmarks. Other work categorizes biases as intrinsic or extrinsic and reviews data-level, model-level, and output-level evaluation methods, alongside pre-model, intra-model, and post-model mitigation strategies. A multi-objective, multi-agent framework has been shown to reduce social bias substantially while largely maintaining downstream accuracy. Additionally, prompt-engineering sensitivity and consistency metrics help expose failures in model behavior, and configuring multiple model instances with different demographic biases can generate more diverse and representative outputs. Together, these studies underscore the need to move beyond isolated bias tests toward context-aware, multi-dimensional evaluation and mitigation.

citations.claim: Current methodologies for mitigating explicit and implicit biases in LLMs often evaluate scenarios in isolation without considering broader context or the spectrum of biases; the STOP dataset addresses this with 450 offensive progressions covering 9 demographics and 46 sub-demographics, and shows model success rates for bias detection range from 19.3% to 69.8%.

Bias in LLMs can be categorized as intrinsic or extrinsic, and evaluation methods include data-level, model-level, and output-level approaches, with mitigation strategies categorized as pre-model, intra-model, and post-model techniques.

The multi-objective multi-agent framework (MOMA) reduces bias scores by up to 87.7% while causing only marginal performance degradation of up to 6.8% on the BBQ dataset, significantly enhancing the icat metric on StereoSet by up to 58.1%.

Sensitivity and consistency metrics, which are complementary to task performance, measure how LLM predictions vary across prompt rephrasings and can guide prompt engineering to balance robustness with performance.

A framework called BiasGPT configures multiple customized GPT instances, each reflecting biases in specific demographic characteristics such as gender, age, and race, to merge diverse perspectives into more inclusive AI dialogue.

standard.summary: 360-degree VR videos immerse viewers in a spherical environment, allowing them to explore and interact with the virtual world from all angles, offering unparalleled levels of immersion. However, this format also presents challenges such as the lack of effective attention guidance, limited spatial resolution, and accessibility barriers for some users, which are addressed in the literature.

citations.claim: Within the expansive domain of virtual reality (VR), 360° VR videos immerse viewers in a spherical environment, allowing them to explore and interact with the virtual world from all angles. While this video representation offers unparalleled levels of immersion, it often lacks effective methods to guide viewers' attention toward specific elements within the virtual environment.

Omnidirectional Videos (or 360° videos) are widely used in Virtual Reality (VR) to facilitate immersive and interactive viewing experiences. However, the limited spatial resolution in 360° videos does not allow for each degree of view to be represented with adequate pixels, limiting the visual quality offered in the immersive experience.
360° videos enable users to freely choose their viewing paths, but blind and low vision (BLV) users are often excluded from this interactive experience.

balanced.summary: 360-degree VR videos place viewers in spherical environments enabling free exploration and interaction, yet realizing their immersive potential faces gaps in attention guidance, resolution, content manipulation, orientation, accessibility, and interactive generation. Methods span script-based object focusing (doc1), deep-learning super-resolution (doc2), depth-adaptive stereo composition (doc3), depth-aware orientation estimation (doc4), branching narratives for blind and low vision users (doc5), game-engine virtual fieldwork (doc6), real-time 3D Gaussian avatars (doc7), VR tennis broadcasting with embedded visualizations (doc8), text-driven panorama generation (doc9), and fully navigable 3D scene generation (doc10). These works extend 360 video from passive viewing to guided, accessible, and interactive immersive experiences.

citations.claim: 360-degree VR videos immerse viewers in a spherical environment, allowing them to explore and interact with the virtual world from all angles, though they often lack effective methods to guide viewers' attention toward specific elements.

Omnidirectional 360 videos are widely used in VR to facilitate immersive and interactive viewing, but limited spatial resolution constrains visual quality, motivating deep-learning super-resolution approaches such as the proposed S3PO model.

360-degree images and videos are an economic and popular way to provide VR experiences using real-world content, and the proposed per-view projection method preserves geometry and removes ghost artifacts in stereo panorama composition.
Depth-aware orientation estimation supports spatial coherence and perceptual stability in immersive visual content such as VR and AR applications.

Blind and low vision users are often excluded from the interactive experience of 360-degree videos; Branch Explorer transforms them into branching narratives to support accessible interactive viewing.

Virtual fieldwork software in a game engine enables scientists to apply field skills to virtual outcrop representations, such as those on the seafloor, using large immersive environments and VR headsets.

VRGaussianAvatar integrates real-time full-body 3D Gaussian Splatting avatars into VR using only head-mounted display tracking signals, sustaining interactive performance and improving perceived appearance, embodiment, and plausibility.

VR tennis broadcasting can be enhanced through embedded visualizations and adaptive camera motions, improving viewer comprehension, narrative engagement, and immersion compared to traditional VR broadcasting.

Text-driven 360-degree panorama generation enables synthesis of panoramic images directly from textual descriptions, simplifying immersive visual content creation and extending to 3D scenes and panoramic video.
WorldExplorer generates fully navigable 3D scenes with consistent visual quality across a wide range of viewpoints, enabling realistic and unrestricted exploration in virtual environments.

standard.summary: Recent years have seen neural networks applied to phase retrieval in imaging, achieving superior accuracy and speed over traditional techniques, especially in the presence of noise in interferometric contexts. A 3D-2D Phase Retrieval U-Net (PRUNe) was introduced for noisy interferometric imaging, taking noisy and randomly phase-shifted interferograms as input and outputting a 2D phase image; it outperformed a state-of-the-art singular value decomposition algorithm, achieving 2.5–4 times lower mean squared error at multiple signal-to-noise ratios for both low and high signal intensities. Additionally, a Neural Architecture Search generated Phase Retrieval Net (NAS-PRNet) achieved high-fidelity phase retrieval in real time, with a PSNR of 36.7 dB and SSIM of 86.6%, and a 15x speedup over a recent Mamba-UNet. Deep-learning methods also provide robust phase retrieval for imperfect diffraction patterns from X-ray free-electron lasers, significantly reducing data processing time for real-time reconstruction. Further work compares data-driven and physics-driven deep learning strategies, highlighting their effectiveness and trade-offs.

citations.claim: In recent years, neural networks have been used to solve phase retrieval problems in imaging with superior accuracy and speed than traditional techniques, especially in the presence of noise.
We introduce a 3D-2D Phase Retrieval U-Net (PRUNe) that takes noisy and randomly phase-shifted interferograms as inputs, and outputs a single 2D phase image.

PRUNe reconstructions consistently show more accurate and smooth reconstructions, with a x2.5 - 4 lower mean squared error at multiple signal-to-noise ratios for interferograms with low (< 1 photon/pixel) and high (~100 photons/pixel) signal intensity.

NAS-PRNet has achieved high-fidelity phase retrieval by achieving a peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) of 36.7 dB and a Structural SIMilarity (SSIM) of 86.6% as tested on interferograms of biological cells.
NAS-PRNet achieves phase retrieval in only 31 ms, representing 15x speedup over the most recent Mamba-UNet with only a slightly lower phase retrieval accuracy.
This method provides robust phase retrieval for simulated data and performs well on weak-signal single-pulse diffraction data from X-ray free-electron lasers.
the method significantly reduces data processing time, facilitating real-time image reconstructions that are crucial for high-repetition-rate data acquisition.
In recent years, deep learning has been proven to be highly effective in addressing phase recovery problems.
we comprehensively compare these two deep learning phase recovery strategies in terms of time consumption, accuracy, generalization ability, ill-posedness adaptability, and prior capacity.

balanced.summary: In recent years, neural networks have been applied to phase retrieval in imaging and have shown superior accuracy and speed compared with traditional techniques, especially under noise and in interferometric contexts. A 3D-2D Phase Retrieval U-Net (PRUNe) for noisy, randomly phase-shifted interferograms consistently outperformed a singular value decomposition algorithm, with 2.5-4x lower mean squared error across signal-to-noise ratios and low-to-high photon intensities. In off-axis quantitative phase imaging, an automatically searched NAS-PRNet achieved high-fidelity phase retrieval in 31 ms, a 15x speedup over Mamba-UNet with only slightly lower accuracy. Deep learning also enables real-time phase retrieval from imperfect X-ray free-electron laser diffraction data. Different deep learning strategies exist: data-driven supervised, physics-driven self-supervised, and co-driven approaches, each with trade-offs; self-supervised physics-informed GANs can retrieve phase and absorption from a single X-ray hologram without paired or simulated training data, and self-supervised learning can avoid ground-truth requirements by exploiting translation invariance. Nonetheless, theoretical worst-case robustness bounds show that for highly localized measurements, accurate high-resolution recovery may require extremely many measurements regardless of the algorithm; and in some interferometric settings, intensity-only multifrequency measurements can recover images without phase reconstruction at all.

citations.claim: PRUNe, a 3D-2D Phase Retrieval U-Net, takes noisy and randomly phase-shifted interferograms and outputs a 2D phase image; its reconstructions have 2.5-4x lower mean squared error than a state-of-the-art SVD algorithm at multiple SNRs for low and high photon intensities.

NAS-PRNet, an encoder-decoder neural network found by neural architecture search, achieves phase retrieval in 31 ms (15x faster than Mamba-UNet) with a PSNR of 36.7 dB and SSIM of 86.6% on interferograms of biological cells.

A new deep-learning-based phase retrieval method provides robust phase retrieval for imperfect diffraction patterns and weak-signal single-pulse data from X-ray free-electron lasers, significantly reducing data processing time for real-time reconstruction.

Deep learning phase recovery strategies include data-driven supervised learning, physics-driven self-supervised learning, and co-driven approaches, which differ in time consumption, accuracy, generalization, ill-posedness adaptability, and prior capacity.
A self-supervised physics-informed generative adversarial network reconstructs both phase and absorbance from a single X-ray hologram without paired, unpaired, or simulated training data.
A self-supervised method solves nonlinear phase retrieval without ground truth by exploiting the natural invariance of images to translations.

Lower Lipschitz bounds imply that robust recovery from highly localized measurements in ptychographic/Fourier ptychographic imaging may require an extremely large number of measurements in the presence of worst-case noise, independent of the reconstruction algorithm.

With sufficient source location and frequency diversity, interferometric imaging can recover all multifrequency interferometric data from intensity-only measurements without phase reconstruction, with no loss of resolution in homogeneous media.

standard.summary: A method for machine learning and serving of discrete field theories in physics is developed. The learning algorithm trains a discrete field theory from observational data on a spacetime lattice, and the serving algorithm uses the learned discrete field theory to predict new field observations for new boundary and initial conditions. The serving algorithm is a structure-preserving geometric algorithm proven superior to conventional discretization-based algorithms. Its effectiveness is demonstrated on nonlinear oscillations and the Kepler problem, where it learns planetary orbit data and predicts other orbits, including parabolic and hyperbolic escaping orbits, without learning Newton's laws. The algorithms also apply when special relativity and general relativity effects are important.

citations.claim: A method for machine learning and serving of discrete field theories in physics is developed, with a learning algorithm that trains a discrete field theory from a set of observational data on a spacetime lattice.
The serving algorithm uses the learned discrete field theory to predict new observations of the field for new boundary and initial conditions.

The serving algorithm of discrete field theories belongs to structure-preserving geometric algorithms, which have been proven superior to conventional algorithms based on discretization of differential equations.

The method's effectiveness is demonstrated using nonlinear oscillations and the Kepler problem, where the serving algorithm correctly predicts other planetary orbits, including parabolic and hyperbolic escaping orbits, without learning Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation.
The proposed algorithms are also applicable when effects of special relativity and general relativity are important.

balanced.summary: The core method is presented in [doc_1]: it develops algorithms for machine learning and serving of discrete field theories in physics. The learning algorithm trains a discrete field theory from observational data on a spacetime lattice, and the serving algorithm uses the learned theory to predict new field observations for new boundary and initial conditions. This discrete-theory approach avoids difficulties of learning continuous theories with AI and uses structure-preserving geometric algorithms, demonstrated on nonlinear oscillations and the Kepler problem, where planetary orbits are learned from data similar to Kepler's and other orbits are predicted without Newton's laws. This method fits within the wider scientific machine learning and physics-enhanced ML landscape described in the other documents: [doc_2] explains combining physics-based and data-driven models; [doc_4] outlines physics-guided, physics-encoded, and physics-informed approaches motivated by limited data and explainability; [doc_8] proposes projecting model outputs onto physical manifolds to enforce physical consistency.

citations.claim: A method for machine learning and serving of discrete field theories is developed: the learning algorithm trains a discrete field theory from a set of observational data on a spacetime lattice, and the serving algorithm uses the learned discrete field theory to predict new observations for new boundary and initial conditions.

Learning discrete field theories overcomes the difficulties associated with learning continuous theories by artificial intelligence, and the serving algorithm belongs to structure-preserving geometric algorithms, which are superior to conventional algorithms based on discretization of differential equations.

The algorithms are demonstrated on nonlinear oscillations and the Kepler problem; the learning algorithm learns a discrete field theory from planetary orbit data similar to Kepler's data, and the serving algorithm predicts other orbits, including parabolic and hyperbolic escaping orbits, without learning Newton's laws.

Scientific Machine Learning combines physics-based and data-driven models: physics-based models rely on physical understanding and numerical approximation, while data-driven models extract input-output relations, and SciML injects physics and mathematical knowledge into ML algorithms.

Physics-Enhanced Machine Learning is motivated by limited informative data, avoiding accurate-but-wrong predictions, handling uncertainties, and providing explainable inferences, with approaches grouped as physics-guided, physics-encoded, and physics-informed.

Physics-consistent machine learning directly enforces compliance with physical principles by projecting model outputs onto the manifold defined by those laws, ensuring predictions inherently adhere to chosen physical constraints and improving reliability and interpretability.

standard.summary: The paper directly addresses the development of a robotic rehabilitation system for the upper limbs using collaborative end-effector solutions. It highlights that commercial collaborative robots offer significant advantages for this task because they are optimized from an engineering perspective and ensure safe physical interaction with humans.

citations.claim: In this paper, we address the development of a robotic rehabilitation system for the upper limbs based on collaborative end-effector solutions. The use of commercial collaborative robots offers significant advantages for this task, as they are optimized from an engineering perspective and ensure safe physical interaction with humans.

balanced.summary: The paper that directly addresses the development of robotic rehabilitation for upper limbs using collaborative end-effector solutions with commercial robots is doc_1, which highlights the engineering optimization and safe interaction of cobots but also notes limitations such as limited size range and industrial-oriented control modes. To optimize task performance, it proposes an optimization-based design method and an admittance-type Virtual Fixture control architecture that supports Programming by Demonstration and both passive and active modes. The broader literature provides context on upper-limb rehabilitation and collaborative assistive robotics: doc_2 reviews assistive devices and notes that few are commercially available; doc_3 advocates robot-mediated physical human-human interaction; doc_5 discusses ethical responsibility in AI-based exoskeletons; doc_6 presents a five-bar end-effector for finger rehabilitation; doc_7 uses adaptive collaborative robotics to mitigate compensatory movements; doc_8 integrates AR with Programming by Demonstration; doc_9 presents a laser-guided interface for people with upper-limb impairments; and doc_10 explores AI-enhanced shared control. Collectively, these works illustrate diverse collaborative, end-effector, and optimization-focused strategies in the field.

citations.claim: This paper addresses the development of an upper-limb rehabilitation system using collaborative end-effector solutions with commercial robots, proposing an optimization-based design method and an admittance-type Virtual Fixture control architecture to optimize task performance.
A systematic review of upper-limb assistive devices shows a diversity of technologies and applications, but few devices are commercially available, limiting their real impact.
The paper advocates robot-mediated physical human-human interaction, integrating therapist expertise with robotic strength, accuracy, and repeatability.
Ethical concerns in AI-based exoskeletons, including responsibility distribution among exoskeleton, patient, and therapist, need to be integrated into the development process.
A five-bar mechanism end-effector for finger rehabilitation executes natural flexion-extension movement, with position control using fifth-order polynomials.
An adaptive collaborative robotics framework uses a personalised mobility model and constrained optimisation to mitigate compensatory movements in upper-limb prosthesis users.
RAMPA integrates AR and ML to enable Programming by Demonstration on industrial robotic arms, addressing safety and programming barriers.
A laser-guided interface with visual servoing and neural-network perception allows people with upper-limb impairments to control a robotic manipulator via head movements.
AI-enhanced shared control for assistive robotic arms aims to reduce mental load while keeping the human in the loop.

standard.summary: The most directly relevant document is [doc_1], which addresses applications in nuclear physics and structural dynamics involving matrices with uncertainty that depend on parameters omega, and focuses on efficiently computing the minimal eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix pencil (A,B) with B positive definite. It proposes a projection-based small parametrized eigenvalue problem using multiple eigenvectors and derivatives to approximate the minimal eigenvalue. Additional documents provide related context: [doc_8] discusses eigenvalue solvers for nuclear reactor modeling, [doc_3] addresses model-form uncertainty in computational mechanics and structural dynamics, and [doc_5] and [doc_7] describe eigenvalue slicing techniques for large sparse problems.

citations.claim: In applications of linear algebra including nuclear physics and structural dynamics, there is a need to deal with uncertainty in matrices that depend on a set of parameters omega, and the interest is in the minimal eigenvalue of a matrix pencil (A,B) with A,B symmetric and B positive definite.

The paper proposes constructing a small parametrized eigenvalue problem by projection, using multiple eigenvectors and derivatives of eigenvectors, so that its minimal eigenvalue has small error relative to the large problem, avoiding the non-smoothness issues of global polynomial approximations.

The paper describes eigenvalue solvers for modeling nuclear reactors, including a multigroup Krylov solver, Rayleigh Quotient Iteration eigenvalue solver, and multigrid preconditioner, which together enable efficient large-scale reactor calculations.
The paper proposes a probabilistic model of subspaces based on probabilistic PCA to characterize model-form uncertainty in computational mechanics and structural dynamics.

EVSL (EigenValues Slicing Library) is a software package for solving large sparse real symmetric standard and generalized eigenvalue problems by dividing the spectrum into subintervals and using polynomial or rational filtering with Krylov methods.

Localized spectrum slicing constructs a set of sparse vectors spanned approximately by eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues near a target mu, leading to sparse projected matrices that can solve interior eigenvalue problems efficiently.

balanced.summary: The motivating eigenvalue problem in applications such as nuclear physics and structural dynamics is the minimal eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix pencil (A(ω),B(ω)) with B positive definite, where the matrices depend on parameters ω and may be uncertain. The main approach proposed for this problem uses a small projected eigenvalue problem constructed with multiple eigenvectors and their derivatives, enabling fast evaluation of the minimal eigenvalue as a function of ω and computation of statistical moments without suffering from non-smoothness. Related techniques include spectrum slicing for large sparse symmetric generalized eigenproblems, specialized nuclear reactor eigenvalue solvers, stochastic subspace methods for model-form uncertainty in structural dynamics, and rank-completing perturbations for singular pencils, along with randomized methods for rank-deficient systems that arise in eigenvector computations.

citations.claim: Applications in nuclear physics and structural dynamics require dealing with uncertainty in matrices; the paper focuses on matrices depending on parameters ω and computes the minimal eigenvalue of a symmetric pencil (A,B) with B positive definite, using a small projected eigenvalue problem built from multiple eigenvectors and derivatives to approximate the minimal eigenvalue and its statistical moments.

EVSL solves large sparse real symmetric standard and generalized eigenvalue problems by spectrum slicing, using polynomial and rational filtering coupled with Krylov subspace methods and subspace iteration.

In nuclear reactor modeling, Denovo accelerates eigenvalue calculations with a multigroup Krylov solver, Rayleigh Quotient Iteration, and a multigrid-in-energy preconditioner, converging faster than power iteration for large reactors.
A stochastic subspace method based on probabilistic PCA characterizes model-form uncertainty in projection-based reduced-order models, applicable to computational mechanics and structural dynamics.
Singular generalized eigenvalue problems can be solved by a rank-completing perturbation of the original pencil, offering a fast and robust alternative to staircase methods.
Randomized methods for consistent rank-deficient linear systems can compute eigenvectors corresponding to a known eigenvalue by using a random rank-k perturbation to obtain a nonsingular matrix.

standard.summary: Outliers can contaminate the measurement process of many nonlinear systems, with causes including sensor errors, model uncertainties, change in ambient environment, data loss, or malicious cyber attacks; when the extended Kalman filter (EKF) is used, these outliers can seriously reduce estimation accuracy. To address this, a robust EKF approach using an innovation saturation mechanism is proposed, where an adaptive saturation bound prevents outlier-corrupted innovations from damaging state estimation, and the approach is proven to yield bounded-error estimation under bounded outlier disturbances. The method is demonstrated in a mobile robot localization simulation and shows improved robustness against outliers of various magnitudes, types, and durations compared to existing methods.

citations.claim: Outliers can contaminate the measurement process of many nonlinear systems, and can be caused by sensor errors, model uncertainties, change in ambient environment, data loss or malicious cyber attacks; when the extended Kalman filter is applied, outliers can seriously reduce estimation accuracy.

The paper proposes an innovation saturation mechanism to modify the EKF, featuring adaptive adjustment of the saturation bound, and proves it can generate bounded-error estimation in the presence of bounded outlier disturbances.

An application study on mobile robot localization shows the proposed robust EKF approaches effectively reject outliers of various magnitudes, types and durations, at significant computational efficiency and without requiring measurement redundancy.

balanced.summary: Measurement outliers in nonlinear systems can arise from sensor errors, model uncertainties, environmental changes, data loss, and malicious cyber attacks; when the extended Kalman filter (EKF) is used, such outliers can seriously reduce state-estimation accuracy. A robust EKF design uses an innovation saturation mechanism with adaptively adjusted saturation bounds to prevent outlier-corrupted innovations from damaging the estimate, yielding bounded-error estimation under bounded outlier disturbances [doc_1]. For malicious sensor attacks, resilient state estimation can be achieved by designing individual high-gain observers for each redundant sensor output and solving a nonlinear error-correcting problem to detect attacks and estimate the state [doc_2]. In discrete-time nonlinear systems under sensor false-data injection and measurement noise, a bank of input-to-state stable observers can be used to detect and isolate attacked sensors by checking consistency with attack-free trajectories [doc_3]. More broadly, anomaly detection in cyber-physical systems spans data-driven, model-driven, hybrid, and system-oriented approaches, each with strengths and weaknesses [doc_6]. Adaptive anomaly detection is a promising direction for evolving attacks, though most reviewed works focus on only one aspect of adaptation rather than jointly addressing data processing and model adaptation [doc_9]. Security metrics for networked control systems quantify the potential impact of stealthy sensor attacks and can be used to redesign controllers and monitors to minimize that impact while preserving attack-free performance [doc_8]. In addition, statistical investigation of the Shapley value for anomaly localization shows that a single fixed-term test can achieve the same probability of error as the full Shapley-value test for independent observation cases [doc_10]. Finally, integrated cyber-physical risk assessment can identify worst-case attacks, showing that a strategic attacker can accelerate physical-system failure by almost 19% while remaining undetected compared with a random attacker [doc_4].

citations.claim: Outliers can contaminate the measurement process of many nonlinear systems, caused by sensor errors, model uncertainties, ambient environment changes, data loss, or malicious cyber attacks, and they can seriously reduce the accuracy of the extended Kalman filter; the paper proposes an innovation saturation mechanism with adaptive saturation bound to build robustness.

For uniformly observable nonlinear systems with redundant sensors under possibly unbounded sensor attacks, individual high-gain observers are designed per measurement output, and a nonlinear error-correcting problem exploiting redundancy enables attack detection and resilient state estimation.

For discrete-time nonlinear systems under potentially unbounded sensor attacks and measurement noise, a bank of input-to-state stable observers can be used to detect and isolate sensor attacks by checking consistency with attack-free trajectories.

An optimization-based cyber-physical risk assessment framework models worst-case attacks that maximize physical impact, avoid detection, and comply with constraints; results show a worst-case strategic attacker causes almost 19% further acceleration in failure time while remaining undetected compared to a random attacker.

A comprehensive review of anomaly detection in cyber-physical systems categorizes techniques into data-driven, model-driven, hybrid data-model, and system-oriented approaches, highlighting strengths and weaknesses of each.

For a class of perturbed linear time-invariant systems under stealthy sensor attacks, security metrics quantify the potential attack impact and synthesis tools redesign controllers and monitors to minimize that impact while guaranteeing attack-free performance.

A systematic literature review of adaptive anomaly detection in cyber-physical systems finds that reviewed works focused on a single aspect of adaptation, either data processing or model adaptation, but rarely both at the same time.

A statistical investigation of using the Shapley value for anomaly localization in sensor data systems finds that a single fixed-term test achieves the same probability of error as the full Shapley-value test for all independent observation cases.

standard.summary: High-fidelity 3D assets with materials composed of fibers (including hair), complex layered material shaders, or fine scattering geometry are ubiquitous in high-end realistic rendering, but remain computationally expensive. doc_1 proposes a neural relightable asset representation that precomputes shading and scattering, allowing existing renderers to use a single neural architecture. Related work addresses material modeling and synthesis: doc_4 introduces a large public PBR material dataset, doc_6 synthesizes real-world measured BRDFs via hyperdiffusion, and doc_5 assigns PBR materials to 3D objects from images. For geometry and scattering, doc_3 reconstructs strand-level hair, doc_8 represents heterogeneous subsurface scattering with a neural BSSRDF, and doc_2 demonstrates a web-based physically based path tracer using OpenPBR for high-fidelity rendering. doc_7 preserves hairstyle details in animatable avatars. Together these documents present strategies for handling complex materials, fibers, hair, and scattering in realistic rendering pipelines.

citations.claim: High-fidelity 3D assets with materials composed of fibers (including hair), complex layered material shaders, or fine scattering geometry are ubiquitous in high-end realistic rendering applications.
The authors design a neural representation for 3D assets with complex shading that supports full relightability and full integration into existing renderers, precomputing all shading and scattering.
MatSynth is a dataset of 4,000+ CC0 ultra-high resolution PBR materials, larger, more diverse, and higher resolution than previously publicly available.

M^3ashy enables high-quality reconstruction of complex real-world materials by leveraging neural fields as a compact continuous representation of BRDFs and allows flexible multi-modal material synthesis.
MatCLIP extracts shape- and lighting-insensitive descriptors of PBR materials to assign plausible textures to 3D objects based on images, achieving top-1 accuracy of 76.6%.
GroomCap reconstructs faithful and high-fidelity hair geometry without relying on external data priors, using a neural implicit hair volume and Gaussian-based optimization.

The neural BSSRDF represents the appearance of heterogeneous translucent objects, captures all-frequency relighting, and can be integrated into existing rendering frameworks while achieving interactive frame rates.
This work presents a web-based, open-source path tracer for rendering physically-based 3D scenes using WebGPU and OpenPBR, achieving near real-time path tracing in web browsers.
SOAP generates rigged, topology-consistent avatars from any portrait and preserves details like braided hair or accessories.

balanced.summary: The documents describe multiple approaches for creating, capturing, and rendering high-fidelity 3D assets with complex material appearances, including hair fibers, layered shaders, and subsurface scattering. RNA precomputes shading for such assets to simplify rendering; a WebGPU path tracer brings physically-based materials to the browser; GroomCap captures high-fidelity hair geometry; MatSynth provides a large PBR material dataset; MatCLIP assigns PBR materials to 3D models; M^3ashy synthesizes measured BRDFs; SOAP generates animatable avatars preserving hairstyles; and a neural BSSRDF represents heterogeneous translucent objects. Collectively, these works address the ubiquity and computational expense of complex materials in realistic rendering.

citations.claim: High-fidelity 3D assets with materials composed of fibers (including hair), complex layered material shaders, or fine scattering geometry are ubiquitous in high-end realistic rendering applications, and rendering them is computationally expensive due to heavy shaders and long scattering paths.
A web-based, open-source path tracer using WebGPU and the OpenPBR surface shading model can render high-fidelity physically-based 3D scenes directly in web browsers.
GroomCap reconstructs high-fidelity hair geometry from multi-view input using a neural implicit hair volume, without relying on external data priors.
MatSynth provides a dataset of 4,000+ CC0 ultra-high resolution PBR materials, which are crucial for virtual relightable assets.
MatCLIP extracts shape- and lighting-insensitive descriptors of PBR materials to assign realistic materials to 3D models from images.
M^3ashy uses a multi-modal conditional hyperdiffusion model to synthesize real-world measured BRDFs, leveraging neural fields as a compact continuous representation.
SOAP generates rigged, topology-consistent avatars from any portrait while preserving details like braided hair or accessories.
A neural BSSRDF representation can represent and render the appearance of heterogeneous translucent objects with subsurface scattering, accounting for geometry and heterogeneities.

standard.summary: The study introduces ArthroPhase, the first arthroscopy dataset for surgical phase recognition in ACL reconstruction, comprising the ACL27 dataset of 27 labeled ACL surgery videos, and develops a novel transformer-based model that integrates spatio-temporal features via ResNet-50 and transformer layers, including a Surgical Progress Index (SPI). It achieved 72.91% accuracy on ACL27 and 92.4% accuracy on Cholec80, establishing a benchmark for arthroscopic phase recognition.

citations.claim: This study aims to advance surgical phase recognition in arthroscopic procedures, specifically Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) reconstruction, by introducing the first arthroscopy dataset and developing a novel transformer-based model.
The ACL27 dataset comprises 27 videos of ACL surgeries, each labeled with surgical phases.
The proposed model achieved an overall accuracy of 72.91% on the ACL27 dataset and 92.4% accuracy on the Cholec80 dataset, with a Surgical Progress Index output error of 10.6% and 9.86% respectively.

balanced.summary: The study described in the query is directly presented in doc_1, which introduces the first arthroscopy dataset (ACL27) for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction and develops a novel transformer-based model for surgical phase recognition. This model integrates spatio-temporal features and a Surgical Progress Index (SPI), achieving 72.91% accuracy on ACL27 and 92.4% on Cholec80, demonstrating effectiveness and generalizability. The broader context of surgical phase recognition is supported by doc_3, which shows that temporal context improves phase classification for both surgeons and AI models, and by doc_9, which provides a benchmark for phase recognition and instrument tasks in endoscopic video, emphasizing the importance of procedural context. Other documents are less directly relevant to the query, focusing on implant design (doc_2), knee osteoarthritis imaging (docs_4,5,6), pain estimation (doc_7), and shoulder lesion diagnosis (doc_8).

citations.claim: Introduced the first arthroscopy dataset (ACL27) for ACL reconstruction and a novel transformer-based model for surgical phase recognition, achieving 72.91% accuracy on ACL27 and 92.4% on Cholec80, with a Surgical Progress Index (SPI).
Temporal context improves surgical phase classification accuracy for both surgeons and AI models, as shown in a comparative analysis on robot-assisted partial nephrectomy.

A multi-center dataset and challenge (PhaKIR 2024) support surgical phase recognition with instrument keypoint estimation and instance segmentation, highlighting the role of procedural context and temporal information.
A fully automated workflow for patient-specific knee implants was developed, but it focuses on implant design rather than phase recognition.

Deep learning models using Swin Transformer detect Bankart lesions in shoulder MRI, but this is not about arthroscopic surgical phase recognition.

standard.summary: Multi-parameter Tikhonov regularization uses multiple penalties and is useful when the sought-after solution exhibits several distinct features at once. Research studies parameter choice rules, including the discrepancy principle and balancing principle, for selecting vector-valued regularization parameters, with theoretical justifications and numerical demonstrations. An augmented approach revisits the balancing principle and derives a new 'balanced discrepancy principle', also providing error estimates and algorithms.

citations.claim: Multi-parameter Tikhonov regularization with multiple penalties is useful when the sought-for solution exhibits several distinct features simultaneously, and the discrepancy principle and balancing principle are studied for choosing the regularization parameter.

Multi-parameter regularization with multiple penalties promotes simultaneously distinct features of sought-for objects, and the balancing principle is revisited from an augmented viewpoint to derive a new parameter choice strategy called the balanced discrepancy principle.

balanced.summary: Multi-parameter Tikhonov regularization with multiple penalties is studied for inverse problems where the sought-for solution exhibits several distinct features simultaneously; parameter choice rules include the discrepancy principle and the balancing principle, with theoretical results on consistency, convergence rates, and a posteriori error estimates. Extensions and related approaches include an augmented balanced discrepancy principle, elastic-net regularization with simultaneous l1/l2 penalties, discrepancy-based joint selection of regularization and discretization levels, Morozov's discrepancy principle in Bregman iterated variational regularization, discrepancy-based parameter choice in Arnoldi-Tikhonov methods, heuristic parameter choice rules for weakly bounded noise, and nonlinear constrained Tikhonov regularization with a priori and a posteriori choices.

citations.claim: Multi-parameter Tikhonov regularization with multiple penalties is studied; such models are useful when the sought-for solution exhibits several distinct features simultaneously, and discrepancy and balancing principles are analyzed.

Multi-parameter regularization with multiple penalties promotes simultaneously distinct features, and a balanced discrepancy principle is derived from an augmented Tikhonov viewpoint, with a priori and a posteriori error estimates.
Elastic-net regularization enforces simultaneously l1 and l2 penalties, and convergence rates for both a priori and a posteriori parameter choice rules are established.

A nonlinear constrained Tikhonov regularization approach uses a second-order sufficient optimality condition as a nonlinearity condition and derives convergence rates for a priori and a posteriori choice rules, including the discrepancy principle and balancing principle.

A discrepancy-based choice for the regularization parameter and discretization level is proposed using a relaxed version of Morozov's discrepancy principle, proving existence and regularizing properties.
Morozov's discrepancy principle is used for a deterministic choice of the regularization parameter in Bregman iterated variational regularization with TV penalization.
A new strategy for setting the Tikhonov regularization parameter in the Arnoldi-Tikhonov method is based on the discrepancy principle, without initial knowledge of the noise norm.

Heuristic parameter choice rules such as quasi-optimality, heuristic discrepancy, and Hanke-Raus rules are analyzed for Tikhonov regularization with weakly bounded noise and unknown noise level, with convergence and convergence rates proved under certain noise conditions.

For Tikhonov regularization with a general convex penalty on a Banach space, error bounds for a Bregman distance split into a smoothness-dependent term and a noise-dependent term, resembling standard quadratic Tikhonov regularization in Hilbert spaces.

standard.summary: Accurate and rapid state-of-health (SOH) monitoring is essential for lithium-ion battery-powered portable mobile devices because it indicates the available energy information, especially under variable working conditions. However, conventional SOH monitoring may be computationally heavy and thus unsuitable for portable devices. Recent methods address this need through lightweight transfer learning, discharge-pulse equivalent-circuit analysis, physics-informed neural networks, graph-convolutional networks on partial discharge curves, Gaussian process field-data monitoring, and dedicated pulse-test datasets for diagnostics.

citations.claim: Accurate and rapid state-of-health (SOH) monitoring plays an important role in indicating energy information for lithium-ion battery-powered portable mobile devices, and traditional TL-based SOH monitoring is infeasible in portable devices because substantial computational resources are consumed during the TL stage.

The parameters of an equivalent electrical model describing voltage evolution during a discharge pulse at the end of the charge phase are used to estimate SOH, achieving a mean absolute error of around 1% in the worst case.

A parameterized physics-informed neural network identifies internal battery parameters in about 30 seconds, achieving a 47x speedup over the finite volume method, and improves SOH estimation accuracy by at least 60.61% compared to models without parameter incorporation.

The proposed GCN-based approach systematically selects discharge voltage segments using the Matrix Profile anomaly detection algorithm and achieves precise SOH estimation with a root mean squared error of less than 1%.
Gaussian process resistance models on lithium iron phosphate battery field data enable probabilistic fault detection rules and advanced online monitoring of battery systems.
The PulseBat Dataset contains pulse test experiments on 464 retired lithium-ion batteries and can be used for critical diagnostics tasks such as state-of-health estimation.

balanced.summary: Accurate and rapid state-of-health (SOH) monitoring is critical for lithium-ion battery-powered portable mobile devices because it indicates energy information and supports safe operation under variable conditions (doc_3). However, traditional monitoring methods face challenges such as computational cost, limited data, and the need for rapid assessments. Recent approaches address these by using discharge-pulse analysis (doc_1, doc_7), lightweight transfer learning (doc_3), physics-informed neural networks (doc_8), graph neural networks (doc_9), Gaussian process models (doc_6, doc_10), and physics-informed frameworks (doc_4). These methods enable real-time monitoring with high accuracy, e.g., RMSE below 1% (doc_9), MAE around 1% (doc_1), and substantial speedups (doc_8), while also supporting field-data analysis and second-life battery diagnostics.

citations.claim: Accurate and rapid SOH monitoring plays an important role in indicating energy information for lithium-ion battery-powered portable mobile devices; a lightweight TL-based approach with CITL is proposed to reduce computational burden.
Real-time SoH monitoring remains a major challenge; a discharge-pulse-based method using equivalent electrical model parameters estimates SoH with MAE around 1% and can be integrated into BMS.

A parameterized physics-informed neural network identifies internal battery parameters in about 30 seconds (47x speedup) and improves SOH estimation accuracy by at least 60.61% compared to models without parameter incorporation.
A graph neural network approach using systematically selected discharge voltage segments achieves precise SOH estimation with RMSE less than 1%.
Gaussian process resistance models on field data enable online health monitoring and fault analysis, processing over a million data points for battery systems.
PulseBat dataset provides multidimensional rapid pulse test data from 464 retired lithium-ion batteries, supporting diagnostics such as SOC and SOH estimation.
A Gaussian Process-based ageing model can learn from real operation data; a model trained on only 18 cells achieves 0.53% MAE in capacity curve prediction.
A transferable physics-informed framework enables online degradation diagnosis, knee-onset detection, and advanced BMS functions such as second-life repurposing.

standard.summary: Adverse drug reactions significantly affect patient outcomes and healthcare costs in cancer therapy, and artificial intelligence that predicts them in real time could revolutionize oncology treatment; a systematic review and meta-analysis found pooled sensitivity of 0.82, specificity of 0.84, and AUC of 0.83 for AI-based ADR prediction models in cancer patients. Causal machine learning also supports personalized prediction of treatment efficacy and toxicity using clinical and real-world data, but interpretability and clinical integration remain important challenges.

citations.claim: Adverse drug reactions considerably impact patient outcomes and healthcare costs in cancer therapy. Using artificial intelligence to predict adverse drug reactions in real time could revolutionize oncology treatment.
The pooled results were 0.82 (95% CI:0.69, 0.9), 0.84 (95% CI:0.75, 0.9), and 0.83 (95% CI:0.77, 0.87) for sensitivity, specificity, and AUC, respectively, of ADR predictive models.

Causal machine learning (ML) offers flexible, data-driven methods for predicting treatment outcomes including efficacy and toxicity, thereby supporting the assessment and safety of drugs. A key benefit of causal ML is that it allows for estimating individualized treatment effects, so that clinical decision-making can be personalized to individual patient profiles.
However, the interpretability of results by doctors is rarely considered which is a factor that needs to be improved.

We posit that the prevailing technology-centric approaches underpin this challenge, rendering such systems fundamentally incompatible with clinical practice, specifically diagnostic reasoning and decision making.

balanced.summary: AI models for predicting adverse drug reactions in cancer patients show promising pooled performance, with sensitivity 0.82, specificity 0.84, and AUC 0.83, though biomarker integration and standardized multicenter studies remain needed (doc_1). Complementary work demonstrates that hybrid ML/LLM systems can predict pain episodes with high accuracy (doc_4), causal ML can estimate individualized treatment effects and toxicity (doc_5), and explainable AI (XAI) methods improve interpretability, which is critical but often neglected for clinical adoption (doc_3, doc_8, doc_9). However, translational gaps persist: many models are not designed to support clinical reasoning (doc_10), and applications like EHR classification require human oversight before clinical use (doc_7). AI/ML also offers opportunities for recurrence prediction and personalized care, but real-time ADR prediction must be paired with interpretable, clinically integrated approaches to revolutionize oncology treatment.

citations.claim: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies involving 93,248 oncology patients found pooled sensitivity 0.82, specificity 0.84, and AUC 0.83 for AI models predicting adverse drug reactions such as cardiotoxicity, neutropenia, nephrotoxicity, and hepatotoxicity.

A hybrid machine learning and large language model pipeline predicted breakthrough pain episodes in lung cancer inpatients with accuracy 0.876 (48h) and 0.917 (72h), with sensitivity improvements of 10.6% and 10.7% from LLM augmentation.

Causal machine learning enables estimation of individualized treatment effects for efficacy and toxicity, supporting drug safety assessment and personalized clinical decision-making using clinical trial and real-world data.
Despite advances in machine learning and deep neural networks for cancer research, the interpretability of results by doctors is rarely considered, which is a factor that needs improvement.

Explainable AI (XAI) methods make AI decisions transparent and interpretable, improving decision-making for healthcare professionals, but ongoing challenges require continued development across diverse medical datasets.

XAI techniques such as SHAP, LIME, and Grad-CAM integrated with machine learning and deep learning models can lead to more accurate breast cancer diagnoses and personalized treatment plans, fostering trust among medical professionals.

The limited clinical impact of AI is largely due to technology-centric approaches; data-driven support tools should be designed as sociotechnical systems that complement doctors' cognitive and epistemic activities to bridge the translational gap.

Large language models and BioBERT can classify cancer diagnoses from structured and unstructured EHR data, with GPT-4o achieving 81.9% accuracy on free-text diagnoses, but reliable clinical applications require standardized documentation and human oversight.

AI and ML models may increase the accuracy and reliability of cancer recurrence prediction, enabling personalized medicine and proactive patient management through analysis of large volumes of genetic, clinical, and treatment data.

standard.summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have blurred the boundary of high-quality text generation between humans and machines, which is favorable for generative text steganography. However, current advanced steganographic mapping is not suitable for LLMs because most users are restricted to black-box APIs or user interfaces, lacking access to training vocabulary and sampling probabilities. To address this, methods such as LLM-Stega construct keyword sets and encrypted steganographic mappings with reject-sampling optimization to enable covert communication through LLM interfaces. Other approaches, like Innamark, hide information in text by substituting whitespace characters without changing semantics, while multimodal AI chains can embed messages beyond spatial and temporal domains in audiovisual media.

citations.claim: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have blurred the boundary of high-quality text generation between humans and machines, which is favorable for generative text steganography.

Current advanced steganographic mapping is not suitable for LLMs since most users are restricted to accessing only the black-box API or user interface of the LLMs, thereby lacking access to the training vocabulary and its sampling probabilities.

LLM-Stega constructs a keyword set and designs a new encrypted steganographic mapping to embed secret messages, with an optimization mechanism based on reject sampling to guarantee accurate extraction and rich semantics.
Large language models (LLMs) have gained significant popularity; differentiating between a text written by a human and one generated by an LLM has become almost impossible.

A chain of multimodal artificial intelligence deconstructs audiovisual content into a cover text, embeds a message within the linguistic domain by biasing the word sampling process of a language generation model, and reconstructs the audiovisual content.

balanced.summary: Recent advances in LLMs have blurred the boundary between human and machine text generation, making generative text steganography more favorable. Current advanced steganographic approaches include LLM-Stega, a black-box method operating through LLM user interfaces with a keyword set and reject-sampling optimization [doc_1]; a multimodal chain that hides messages beyond spatial and temporal domains by biasing word sampling [doc_3]; Innamark, which preserves semantics by substituting Unicode whitespace characters [doc_7]; and fine-tuned LLMs as hidden-message carriers, though vulnerable to extraction attacks and protected by UTFC [doc_10]. The field also sees deep-learning steganalysis [doc_2], rising synthetic content and model-collapse risks [doc_6], imperfect LLM-text detectors [doc_8], latent-space vulnerabilities for jailbreaks/data extraction [doc_9], reversible sentence embeddings via memory tokens [doc_5], and foveation-based capacity gains in visual steganography [doc_4].

citations.claim: Recent advances in large language models have blurred the boundary of high-quality text generation between humans and machines, which is favorable for generative text steganography, and current advanced steganographic mapping is not suitable for LLMs because most users only have black-box API or user interface access.

LLM-Stega is a black-box generative text steganographic method based on user interfaces of LLMs, constructing a keyword set, designing encrypted steganographic mapping, and using a reject-sampling optimization mechanism to ensure accurate extraction and rich semantics.

A chain of multimodal AI can deconstruct audiovisual content into cover text, embed a message in the linguistic domain by biasing word sampling, and reconstruct audiovisual content by synchronizing auditory and visual modalities with the stego text.

Innamark is an information-hiding method that conceals any byte-encoded sequence in pure, unformatted text by substituting conventional whitespace characters with visually similar Unicode whitespace characters, preserving semantics and enabling configurable compression, encryption, hashing, and error correction.

Simple fine-tuning can embed hidden text into LLMs, which is revealed only when triggered by a specific query, enabling LLM fingerprinting and steganography; however, this is vulnerable to extraction attacks such as Unconditional Token Forcing, and Unconditional Token Forcing Confusion provides a defense.

With the evolution of generative linguistic steganography, conventional steganalysis falls short in robustly quantifying alterations, so the research paradigm has pivoted toward deep-learning-based linguistic steganalysis.

A large share of newly published webpages and the active web corpus is now AI-generated, and recursive training on synthetic content risks eroding linguistic and semantic diversity, producing model collapse.

Four cutting-edge LLM-generated text detectors show suboptimal performance compared to an ad-hoc detector that identifies abrupt writing style changes around the time of LLM proliferation, indicating the need for specialized detectors.

Exploiting latent space discontinuities, an architectural vulnerability related to sparsity of training data, can craft universal jailbreaks and data extraction attacks that generalize across various LLMs and image generation models.

LLMs can generate reversible sentence embeddings using a special memory token, allowing exact reconstruction of the original text without modifying model weights, across datasets, sequence lengths, and model scales.
Using efficient latent representations and foveated rendering, steganography models can improve capacity limits from 100 to 500 bits while achieving better accuracy and comparable visual quality.

standard.summary: The quality control of printed circuit boards (PCBs) is emphasized as paramount in advancing electronic device technology. Machine learning methodologies, particularly deep learning-based object detection and ensemble learning, are widely used to improve defect detection efficiency and accuracy. [doc_1] presents an ensemble learning framework combining EfficientDet, MobileNet SSDv2, Faster RCNN, and YOLOv5 for PCB defect detection, achieving 95% accuracy. Similar YOLO-based approaches with ConSinGAN data augmentation achieve high accuracy for other electronic components and metal sheets (e.g., 95.50% for DIP components in [doc_2], 91.3% for metal sheets in [doc_4]). Other advanced methods include explicit dual distribution learning for surface defects [doc_5], quantile online learning for semiconductor failure analysis [doc_7], and vision transformers for SEM image defect classification [doc_10]. A comprehensive survey categorizes ML techniques for material defect detection into unsupervised, supervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement, and generative learning [doc_6]. Together, these documents demonstrate that ML-driven defect detection is central to modern quality control in electronics manufacturing.

citations.claim: The quality control of printed circuit boards (PCBs) is paramount in advancing electronic device technology; an ensemble learning framework achieves 95% accuracy in detecting diverse PCB defects.
An automated defect detection system for dual in-line package (DIP) components using YOLOv7 with ConSinGAN achieves 95.50% accuracy and 285 ms detection time.
A YOLO-based model (YOLOv9 with ConSinGAN) for metal sheet defect detection achieves 91.3% accuracy and 146 ms detection time.
ExDD explicitly models dual feature distributions and achieves 94.2% I-AUROC and 97.7% P-AUROC on KSDD2 for surface defect detection.

Machine learning has emerged as the core technology and prominent research direction for material defect detection, with techniques categorized into unsupervised, supervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement, and generative learning.
A quantile online learning method for semiconductor failure analysis achieved 86.66% overall accuracy and outperformed existing methods.
Vision transformer-based automatic defect classification of SEM images achieved over 90% classification accuracy with fewer than 15 images per defect class.

balanced.summary: Quality control of printed circuit boards (PCBs) is critical in advancing electronic device technology, and numerous machine learning methodologies have been used to improve defect detection efficiency and accuracy. One comprehensive framework integrates four distinct PCB defect detection models (EfficientDet, MobileNet SSDv2, Faster RCNN, and YOLOv5) into an ensemble learning strategy, achieving 95% accuracy in detecting diverse PCB defects. For mass-produced electronic components such as DIPs, YOLO-based automated systems combined with ConSinGAN data augmentation yield high performance, with YOLOv7 reaching 95.50% accuracy and a detection time of 285 ms, surpassing threshold-based approaches. Similar YOLO-based approaches for metal sheets show that YOLOv9 with ConSinGAN achieves 91.3% accuracy and 146 ms detection time, integrated into an AOI/SCADA system. A comprehensive survey categorizes ML techniques for material defect detection into unsupervised, supervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement learning, and generative learning, providing a foundation for future research. In surface defect detection, the ExDD framework explicitly models dual feature distributions and uses latent diffusion with domain-specific textual conditioning to generate synthetic defects, achieving 94.2% I-AUROC and 97.7% P-AUROC on KSDD2. In semiconductor failure analysis, a quantile online learning method achieves an overall accuracy of 86.66% and improves accuracy by 15.50% over the second-best method on a GAA-FET dislocation defect dataset. Additionally, vision transformers with transfer learning and semi-supervised learning achieve classification accuracies over 90% for SEM image defect classification on 300mm wafers with fewer than 15 images per defect class, demonstrating the potential for efficient in-house classification tools.

citations.claim: An ensemble learning framework integrating EfficientDet, MobileNet SSDv2, Faster RCNN, and YOLOv5 achieves 95% accuracy in PCB defect detection.
YOLOv7 with ConSinGAN data augmentation achieves 95.50% accuracy and 285 ms detection time for DIP component defect detection, outperforming threshold-based approaches.
YOLOv9 with ConSinGAN achieves 91.3% accuracy and 146 ms detection time for metal sheet defect detection, and is integrated into an AOI/SCADA system.
The survey categorizes ML techniques for material defect detection into unsupervised, supervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement learning, and generative learning.
ExDD uses explicit dual distribution learning and diffusion-based synthetic defect generation to achieve 94.2% I-AUROC and 97.7% P-AUROC on KSDD2.
Quantile online learning for semiconductor failure analysis achieves 86.66% overall accuracy and improves accuracy by 15.50% on the GAA-FET dislocation defect dataset.
Vision transformers with transfer learning and semi-supervised learning achieve over 90% classification accuracy on SEM wafer defect images with fewer than 15 images per defect class.

standard.summary: The paper introducing Denoising Diffusion Anomaly Detection (DDAD) notes that traditional reconstruction-based methods have struggled to achieve competitive performance in anomaly detection. DDAD proposes a novel denoising process for image reconstruction conditioned on a target image, where the target image is set as the input image to guide denoising toward defectless reconstruction while preserving nominal patterns. Anomalies are localized via pixel-wise and feature-wise comparison of input and reconstructed image, and a domain adaptation method fine-tunes the feature extractor using nearly identical generated examples. DDAD achieves state-of-the-art image-level AUROC of 99.8% on MVTec and 98.9% on VisA benchmarks.

citations.claim: Traditional reconstruction-based methods have struggled to achieve competitive performance in anomaly detection. In this paper, we introduce Denoising Diffusion Anomaly Detection (DDAD), a novel denoising process for image reconstruction conditioned on a target image.

balanced.summary: Traditional reconstruction-based methods have struggled to achieve competitive performance in anomaly detection. The paper introduces Denoising Diffusion Anomaly Detection (DDAD), a novel denoising process for image reconstruction conditioned on a target image, which ensures coherent restoration closely resembling the target. Setting the target as the input image guides the denoising process toward defectless reconstruction while maintaining nominal patterns, with anomalies localized via pixel-wise and feature-wise comparison. DDAD achieves state-of-the-art results on MVTec and VisA benchmarks. Related work highlights reconstruction-based challenges such as computational cost, pattern mismatch, and noise-level selection, and explores conditioning strategies for medical and industrial anomaly detection, as well as diffusion-based denoising frameworks for tabular data.

citations.claim: Traditional reconstruction-based methods have struggled to achieve competitive performance in anomaly detection; we introduce Denoising Diffusion Anomaly Detection (DDAD), a novel denoising process for image reconstruction conditioned on a target image.

DDAD employs conditioning where the target image is set as the input image to guide the denoising process, leading to a defectless reconstruction while maintaining nominal patterns; anomalies are localized via pixel-wise and feature-wise comparison.
DDAD achieves state-of-the-art results of 99.8% and 98.9% image-level AUROC on MVTec and VisA benchmarks, respectively.

Reconstruction-based approaches present three major challenges: computationally expensive iterative sampling, reconstructed image may correspond to a different normal pattern, and choosing an appropriate intermediate noise level is challenging.
RADAR overcomes limitations of reconstruction-based anomaly detection by directly producing anomaly maps from the diffusion model, improving both detection accuracy and computational efficiency.

We propose conditioning the denoising process of diffusion models with additional information derived from a latent representation of the input image, allowing accurate and local adaptation to the input intensity distribution while avoiding replication of unhealthy structures.
The conditioning approach improves Dice score by 11.9%, 20.0%, and 44.6% for BraTS, ATLAS, and MSLUB datasets, respectively, while maintaining competitive performance on WMH.

This review explores anomaly localization in medical images using denoising diffusion models, discusses supervision schemes, and highlights open challenges including detection bias, domain shift, computational cost, and model interpretability.

We propose an unsupervised anomaly detection framework based on a diffusion model incorporating synthetic anomaly (Synomaly) noise and a multi-stage diffusion process, trained purely on healthy images without needing anomalous samples or pixel-level annotations.

Reconstruction-based methods in industrial anomaly detection face difficulty controlling generalization boundary: overly strong generalization can reconstruct abnormal regions, while poor generalization fails to reconstruct high-frequency normal components; we propose EdgRec reconstructing RGB images from gray value edges.

We propose the Diffusion-Scheduled Denoising Autoencoder (DDAE), integrating diffusion-based noise scheduling and contrastive learning into the encoding process to improve anomaly detection in tabular data.

standard.summary: Multi-object tracking (MOT) is a critical computer vision task, with applications ranging from surveillance systems to autonomous driving; however, threats to MOT algorithms have not been widely studied, and incorrect association between tracked objects and their assigned IDs can lead to severe consequences such as wrong trajectory predictions [doc_4]. MOT algorithms are commonly categorized into two-stage and single-stage approaches, where two-stage methods are simpler to implement, whereas single-stage methods can yield better results in occluded situations at the cost of more training data [doc_7]. Other works target weaknesses in tracking-by-detection MOT, such as ghost tracks and Kalman-filter state-estimation drift [doc_8], or propose learning data association from only bounding-box coordinates [doc_9]. Sensor-fusion and geometric approaches also advance MOT, e.g., radar-camera fusion with online calibration [doc_6] and camera-angle-aware pseudo-3D tracking for occlusion and depth accuracy [doc_5]. UAV-focused MOT uses global-local detection and spatio-temporal feature fusion to improve trajectory continuity [doc_10]. For evaluation, GOSPA and T-GOSPA quasi-metrics include costs for localisation error, false/missed objects, and track switching [doc_1].

citations.claim: MOT is critical in computer vision with applications from surveillance to autonomous driving; threats have not been widely studied, and incorrect ID association can cause severe consequences.
MOT algorithms are categorized as two-stage and single-stage; two-stage are simpler to adapt, while single-stage can yield better results in occluded situations at the cost of more training data.
RobMOT addresses tracking-by-detection limitations by reducing ghost tracks and Kalman-filter drift, improving MOTA and HOTA.
TWiX learns data association using only bounding-box coordinates, without IoU, motion priors, or camera compensation.
A radar-camera fused MOT framework uses online calibration and common features for autonomous association.
CAMOT estimates camera angle to address occlusion and inaccurate depth estimation, enabling pseudo-3D MOT.
GL-DT uses spatio-temporal feature fusion and global-local collaborative detection to improve small-target detection and trajectory continuity for UAV MOT.
GOSPA and T-GOSPA quasi-metrics measure MOT performance with costs for localisation, false/missed objects, and track switching.

balanced.summary: Multi-object tracking (MOT) is a critical computer vision task with applications ranging from surveillance systems to autonomous driving; however, threats to MOT algorithms have not been widely studied, and incorrect association between tracked objects and their assigned IDs can lead to severe consequences such as wrong trajectory predictions (doc_4). Work in this area spans evaluation metrics, with GOSPA and T-GOSPA quasi-metrics proposed to measure MOT performance by penalizing localization error, false objects, and missed objects (doc_1); overviews of extended object tracking and its applications to sensors such as cameras, radar, lidar, and RGB-D (doc_2); model-based approaches using the Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture filter and standard point-object model, which revealed mismatches on the MOT-17 dataset (doc_3); and camera angle-aware tracking to address occlusion and depth estimation errors, achieving state-of-the-art results on MOT17 and MOT20 (doc_5). Other works improve MOT via radar-camera fusion with online calibration (doc_6), compare single-stage and two-stage 3D tracking for greenhouse robotics (doc_7), enhance robustness by reducing ghost tracks and state-estimation drift in LiDAR-based 3D tracking (doc_8), learn data association using only bounding-box coordinates (doc_9), and address small-target tracking and trajectory continuity for multi-UAV scenarios (doc_10).

citations.claim: Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) is a critical task in computer vision, with applications ranging from surveillance systems to autonomous driving; however, threats to MOT algorithms have yet been widely studied, and incorrect association between tracked objects and their assigned IDs can lead to severe consequences such as wrong trajectory predictions.
GOSPA and T-GOSPA quasi-metrics are introduced for evaluating multi-object tracking algorithms, including costs for localization error, false objects, and missed objects.
