Diffusion models are appreciated for the quality and diversity of generated samples, despite computational burdens due to the high number of sampling steps, and they relate to other deep generative models including GANs.

Under differential privacy, GANs exhibit fundamentally lower sensitivity to data perturbations than diffusion models, resulting in a marked privacy robustness gap in favor of GANs against membership inference attacks.

Generative diffusion models have a powerful theoretical background, converting data distribution to noise and removing noise back, with approaches divided into training-based and sampling-based categories.

GANs can be interpreted from the perspectives of mean-field games and optimal transport, and this perspective leads to a GAN-based computational method (MFGANs) that solves MFGs using adversarial training of two neural networks.
The training process of GANs can be approximated by stochastic differential equations, providing a theoretical foundation for studying the evolution and stability of GAN training.

The composite-functional-gradient GAN is theoretically connected to score-based models, and a nested annealed training scheme improves the quality and diversity of synthesized samples across various GAN models.

standard.summary: Static analysis inspects code without execution and is often designed for soundness, aiming not to miss possible bugs (doc_1). However, static analysis alone can be evaded by dynamically loaded code, e.g., malware using runtime linking, which introduces unresolved indirect calls that stop static control-flow recovery (doc_5). Dynamic analysis and runtime techniques can complement static analysis: combining symbolic execution with speculative library preloading recovered substantially more CFG nodes and edges than static analysis alone (doc_5). Similarly, JIT compilers can exploit continuous profiling to specialize code, giving them an advantage over ahead-of-time static compilation (doc_4). Yet dynamic techniques are not always beneficial: a dynamic binary modification optimization for inline caches did not speed up execution on modern architectures, indicating that optimizations are only worthwhile when the processor cannot already accelerate the code (doc_4). There is also a middle ground: precise static analysis results can be encoded and consumed by JIT compilers, but trust in those results becomes a safety concern (doc_2).

citations.claim: Static analysis by abstract interpretation is generally designed to be 'sound', that is, it should not claim to establish properties that do not hold—in other words, not provide 'false negatives' about possible bugs.

Protected software and modern malware increasingly depend on dynamic code loading techniques to evade static analysis; usage of runtime dynamic linking mechanisms introduces unresolved indirect calls that stop static Control Flow Graph recovery.

The proposed analysis technique combines symbolic execution with speculative library preloading and recovers on average 29.8% additional Control Flow Graph nodes and 26.5% additional edges compared to static analysis alone.

Just-in-Time (JIT) compilers are able to specialize the code they generate according to a continuous profiling of the running programs, giving them an advantage when compared to Ahead-of-Time (AoT) compilers that must choose the code to generate once for all.

Reducing the number of memory accesses as the new optimization does does not shorten execution times on contemporary architectures; sophisticated compiler optimizations are only worth the effort if the processor is not able by itself to accelerate the code.
An underlying concern of safety affects all such techniques—can a compiler (or program analysis tool) trust the points-to analysis results generated by another compiler/tool?

balanced.summary: Static analysis examines code without executing it, aiming to soundly infer properties and detect defects early; it can complement or surpass dynamic testing in settings where runtime bugs are hard to reproduce. However, static analysis can be evaded by dynamic code loading and requires careful tuning to balance precision and scalability. Dynamic analysis and JIT compilation observe and specialize based on runtime behavior, but they only exercise executed paths and may detect problems only after the fact. Several approaches combine static and dynamic elements, such as symbolic execution with dynamic library preloading to recover control-flow graphs that pure static analysis misses.

citations.claim: Static analysis by abstract interpretation is generally designed to be sound, avoiding false negatives, while completeness—inferring properties if they hold—is a rarer requirement.
Whole-program points-to analysis can be expensive, so static analyzers may compute precise results ahead of time and encode them for other compilation stages, raising trust and safety concerns.
Parf adaptively tunes abstraction strategies of static analyzers, showing that static analysis of large real-world programs requires careful configuration of abstraction strategies.

JIT compilers use continuous profiling to specialize generated code at runtime, giving them an advantage over ahead-of-time static compilation, though a DBM optimization did not speed up execution on modern architectures.

Dynamic code loading can hide indirect calls and stop static control-flow graph recovery; combining symbolic execution with speculative library preloading recovered 29.8% more CFG nodes and 26.5% more edges than static analysis alone.
Static analysis built on Slither with interval analysis can be extended to detect smart-contract defects, demonstrating static techniques applied without executing the contract.

A static analyzer implemented in GCC was used to examine 3,538 C packages, finding uninitialized variables and NULL pointer dereferences as the most common problems, with 89% of packages having no warnings.
Static analysis can identify erroneous systems-programming submissions missed by test cases, because concurrency and resource-management bugs are difficult to reproduce dynamically.
A static framework detects use-after-free bugs at compile-time by tracking pointer lifetimes, enabling bugs to be found earlier in development and reported to programmers.

Data leakage is usually detected post-mortem using runtime methods, but the proposed abstract-interpretation static analysis detects it during development, avoiding the need to wait for runtime symptoms.

standard.summary: Retrieval quality and generation quality are distinct but tightly coupled in RAG systems. Improving retrieval alone is brittle: retrieval performance gains do not consistently translate into downstream reasoning gains, and as Recall@5 improves, the Recall Conversion Rate often decays, indicating a trade-off between retrieval quality and generation utility. Effective evaluation therefore jointly assesses retrieval and generation metrics and examines their interactions, rather than evaluating modules in isolation. For instance, RAGSmith jointly optimizes retrieval metrics (recall@k, mAP, nDCG, MRR) and generation metrics (LLM-Judge, semantic similarity), while RAGTrace enables integrated exploration of retrieval relevance, generation fidelity, and cross-component interactions. In domain-specific applications such as biomedical QA, retrieval depth and strategy directly affect end-to-end accuracy and response time, further illustrating the coupling. Evaluation frameworks also note the need to assess both components with metrics like relevance, accuracy, and faithfulness, and to balance automated LLM-based assessment with human judgment.

citations.claim: Improvements in retrieval performance do not consistently translate to commensurate gains in downstream reasoning; as Recall@5 improves, the Recall Conversion Rate (RCR) exhibits a near-linear decay.
RAGSmith jointly aggregates retrieval metrics (recall@k, mAP, nDCG, MRR) and generation metrics (LLM-Judge and semantic similarity), achieving gains up to +12.5% in retrieval and +7.5% in generation.

RAGTrace enables integrated exploration of retrieval-generation relationships, including retrieval relevance, generation fidelity, and cross-component interactions, unlike conventional isolated quality assessments.
Evaluating RAG systems poses unique challenges due to their hybrid structure; metrics for retrieval and generation components include relevance, accuracy, and faithfulness.

In biomedical QA, retrieving 50 documents with BM25 before reranking with MedCPT optimally balances accuracy (0.90), recall (0.90), and response time (1.91s), highlighting trade-offs in retrieval depth, efficiency, and scalability.

Automated evaluation approaches can evaluate each RAG component, including the retrieval and generator components, leveraging an LLM capable of generating evaluation datasets and conducting evaluations.

balanced.summary: Retrieval quality and generation quality are distinct but coupled dimensions of RAG, and the literature shows they must be evaluated and optimized jointly rather than in isolation. Doc 3 highlights a critical gap: improvements in retrieval performance do not consistently translate to commensurate gains in downstream reasoning, with the proposed Recall Conversion Rate showing a near-linear decay as Recall@5 improves, indicating a trade-off between retrieval recall and quality. Doc 6 similarly notes that conventional evaluation focuses on isolated retrieval or generation quality, whereas integrated analysis of retrieval-generation relationships is needed to trace knowledge sources and identify failures. Doc 1 demonstrates that jointly optimizing retrieval metrics (recall@k, mAP, nDCG, MRR) and generation metrics (LLM-Judge, semantic similarity) yields configurations that outperform naive RAG, with gains up to +12.5% in retrieval and +7.5% in generation. Evaluation frameworks differ in how they treat the two components: Doc 2 compares retrieval and generation metrics such as relevance, accuracy, and faithfulness; Doc 5 covers retrievers and generator components using LLM-based automated evaluation balanced against human judgment; Doc 4 discusses both end-to-end evaluation and retrieval-component evaluation, noting the apparent circularity of LLM-based assessment and the need for human grounding; Doc 9 provides a formal model for retrieval experiments with human-in-the-loop and machine-only settings. Practical trade-offs are evident in Doc 7, where retrieval depth and retriever choice affect accuracy, recall, and response time, and in Doc 10, where RAG outperforms fine-tuning on ROUGE, BLEU, and cosine similarity (indicating lower hallucination) while fine-tuned models score 8% higher on METEOR (indicating greater creativity). Overall, retrieval quality and generation quality are interdependent, and optimal RAG design requires balancing and jointly evaluating both dimensions.

citations.claim: Improvements in retrieval performance do not consistently translate to commensurate gains in downstream reasoning; the proposed Recall Conversion Rate reveals a near-linear decay in conversion as Recall@5 improves, indicating a trade-off between retrieval recall and quality.

Conventional evaluation focuses on isolated retrieval or generation quality assessments, whereas RAGTrace enables integrated exploration of retrieval-generation relationships and identification of potential failure cases.

RAGSmith optimizes a scalar objective jointly aggregating retrieval metrics (recall@k, mAP, nDCG, MRR) and generation metrics (LLM-Judge and semantic similarity), achieving gains up to +12.5% in retrieval and +7.5% in generation.
RAG evaluation compares quantifiable metrics of the Retrieval and Generation components, such as relevance, accuracy, and faithfulness, across current RAG benchmarks.
RAG evaluation spans datasets, retrievers, indexing and databases, and the generator component, with an LLM capable of automating evaluation of each component, balanced against human judgment.

Evaluation of GenIR/RAG systems can focus both on end-to-end system output and on retrieval as a component, with LLM-based assessment needing grounding in human assessment to resolve the apparent circularity.

Performance evaluation in multimedia retrieval relies on retrieval experiments with human-in-the-loop and machine-only settings, and a formal model can lower hurdles for conducting and reproducing such experiments.

In biomedical QA, retrieval depth and retriever choice involve trade-offs: retrieving 50 documents with BM25 before reranking with MedCPT optimally balances accuracy (0.90), recall (0.90), and response time (1.91s).

RAG-based constructions are more efficient than fine-tuned models and outperform them on ROUGE, BLEU, and cosine similarity, indicating lower hallucination, while fine-tuned models score 8% higher on METEOR, indicating greater creativity.

standard.summary: Symbolic reasoning is based on explicit logical rules, interpretability, and formal guarantees, whereas neural reasoning learns patterns from data but often lacks transparency and can be brittle. Neurosymbolic approaches attempt to combine these paradigms: they use neural networks for perception/learning and symbolic/rule-based systems for reasoning, aiming to improve explainability, scalability, and reasoning performance. However, this integration involves trade-offs: exhaustive symbolic grounding can cause combinatorial explosion, while selective heuristics may sacrifice expressiveness; current LLM-symbolic systems are often ad hoc, and formalized reasoning remains fragile. Recent methods (e.g., ASPEN, R2N, Pi-NeSy, DPNL, TransCoder) propose various architectures to better balance these trade-offs.

citations.claim: Abstract reasoning can be achieved by untrained neural networks optimizing weights on the problem data itself, without relying on memorization.

NeSy methods combine a machine learner for input entities with a First-Order Logic reasoner; exhaustive grounding preserves expressiveness but causes combinatorial explosion, while heuristic grounding is more scalable but lacks guarantees.
A neural-symbolic approach integrating ASP solvers and domain expertise improves neural models' reasoning, e.g., solving Sudoku with only 12 training puzzles.

Neuro-symbolic methods integrate symbolic computing with neural networks to enhance explainability and reasoning, but limited semantic generalizability and challenges with predefined patterns/rules hinder real-world implementation.
Relational Reasoning Networks perform relational reasoning in the latent space of a deep learner, overcoming scalability and expressivity limitations of earlier neuro-symbolic methods.
A possibilistic neuro-symbolic approach combines neural perception with possibilistic rule-based reasoning and uses intermediate concepts for explanations.

Current LLM-powered neurosymbolic reasoning tools are ad hoc; Neurosymbolic Transition Systems are proposed to pair symbolic state with intuition, scaling logical reasoning while retaining strong symbolic guarantees.

LLMs show strong structured/symbolic reasoning abilities, but proof synthesis in formalized mathematics remains more brittle than code generation, raising questions about whether they genuinely represent evolving logical state.
TransCoder solves abstract reasoning tasks through neural program synthesis with a typed domain-specific language, producing transparent and verifiable programmatic solutions.
Probabilistic neurosymbolic learning is bottlenecked by #P-hard PWMC; DPNL and ApproxDPNL guide logical inference to scale exact and approximate reasoning with guarantees.

balanced.summary: The documents contrast symbolic reasoning, which offers interpretability and formal guarantees, with neural reasoning, which learns from data but is often brittle and opaque. Several works (doc_2, doc_3, doc_4, doc_5, doc_6, doc_9, doc_10) propose neuro-symbolic integration to combine neural learning with symbolic logic, while also noting trade-offs in expressiveness, scalability, and explainability. doc_1 shows that untrained neural networks can perform abstract reasoning via within-problem weight optimization, challenging the view that neural reasoning requires memorization. doc_8 highlights that LLMs excel at structured symbolic tasks like coding but remain brittle at formal proof synthesis. doc_7 argues that current LLM-symbolic reasoning tools are ad hoc and proposes a principled computational model to pair symbolic state with neural intuition.

citations.claim: Untrained neural networks can demonstrate memorization-independent abstract reasoning by optimizing weights during the problem solution, without prior training.

NeSy grounding methods trade off expressiveness and scalability: exhaustive substitutions preserve logic but cause combinatorial explosion, while heuristic selective derivations are efficient but lack guarantees; the paper proposes a parametrized family generalizing Backward Chaining.
ASPER integrates Answer Set Programming solvers into a shallow ANN's loss function, significantly improving Sudoku-solving with only 12 training puzzles without hyperparameter tuning.

The survey examines task-specific Neuro-Symbolic advancements to show how incorporating symbolic systems can enhance explainability and reasoning, while noting challenges with semantic generalizability and real-world implementation.

Relational Reasoning Networks (R2N) perform relational reasoning in the latent space of a deep learner, defining computational structure for higher-level relations among ground atoms, and achieve state-of-the-art results.

Pi-NeSy combines a low-level neural perception task with a high-level possibilistic rule-based reasoning system, transforming neural outputs into possibility distributions, and uses intermediate concepts for explanation.

Current practices for building LLM-powered automated reasoning tools are ad hoc, and the author proposes Neurosymbolic Transition Systems pairing symbolic state with intuition to retain strong symbolic guarantees.

LLMs show impressive capabilities in coding and structured symbolic tasks, but formalized mathematical proof synthesis remains more brittle than code generation, raising questions about whether LLMs genuinely represent logical state.

TransCoder solves abstract reasoning problems via neural program synthesis using a typed domain-specific language, generating synthetic tasks with known programs for supervised training and transparent verification.

DPNL bypasses the costly logical provenance computation in probabilistic neurosymbolic learning using an oracle and recursive DPLL-like decomposition, with an approximate variant providing epsilon or (epsilon, delta) guarantees.

standard.summary: The provided documents do not offer a formal definition of supervised learning, but a direct contrast appears in doc_3: supervised-style system identification trains models for maximum prediction accuracy on simulation samples, whereas reinforcement learning trains models/policies end-to-end for optimal control performance. Additionally, doc_6 characterizes RL as a data-driven, learning-based framework for sequential decision-making, which is distinct from the typical supervised setting of static prediction from labeled data.

citations.claim: Models trained by system identification for maximum prediction accuracy on simulation samples perform suboptimally in (e)NMPC, whereas end-to-end reinforcement learning of surrogate models optimizes for control performance.
Reinforcement learning provides a data-driven, learning-based framework to formulate and solve sequential decision-making problems.

balanced.summary: The provided documents focus on reinforcement learning (RL) rather than supervised learning, but they characterize RL in ways that imply a clear distinction. RL is described as a data-driven, learning-based framework for sequential decision-making (doc_6), where an agent learns a policy from reward signals rather than from labeled input-output examples. This contrasts with supervised learning, which typically relies on labeled data; indeed, doc_2 notes that RL faces a scarcity of labeled reward data and that relying on labeled data alone leads to narrow state-action distributions, whereas abundant unlabeled data can be leveraged. Furthermore, doc_3 highlights that models trained via supervised system identification for maximum prediction accuracy perform suboptimally in control tasks, whereas end-to-end RL training optimizes for control performance. Other documents reinforce RL's policy-centric nature: doc_1 presents a policy-gradient algorithm that directly optimizes policy performance without needing labeled states, and doc_4 describes RL systems learning policies directly from high-dimensional sensory input. Doc_9 adds that RL can convert long-term safety probabilities into additive costs and use physics constraints as an alternative to reward shaping. Thus, the documents collectively portray RL as reward-driven policy optimization in sequential settings, implicitly contrasting with supervised learning's dependence on labeled examples and static input-output mapping.

citations.claim: Compared with model-based control and optimization methods, reinforcement learning provides a data-driven, learning-based framework to formulate and solve sequential decision-making problems.

Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn an optimal policy from pre-collected data, but faces challenges such as scarcity of labeled reward data; relying on labeled data alone often leads to a narrow state-action distribution.

Data-driven surrogate models trained by system identification for maximum prediction accuracy on simulation samples perform suboptimally in (e)NMPC, whereas end-to-end reinforcement learning trains models for optimal control performance.
GPOMDP is a reinforcement learning algorithm for direct optimization of policy performance in POMDPs, requiring only a single sample path and no knowledge of the underlying state.

Reinforcement learning systems often use neural networks to learn policies directly from pixels or other high-dimensional sensory input, with dynamics described by learning protocols and reward baselines.
Long-term safety probability can be converted into additive costs and solved using standard reinforcement learning methods, with physics constraints serving as an alternative to reward shaping.

standard.summary: The documents collectively distinguish autonomous agents from chatbots by their primary function and architecture. Chatbots are conversational software applications designed for dialogue, while autonomous agents (or bots) are systems that automate tasks or processes; when a bot adds a conversational component, it becomes a conversational agent. Some chatbots also exhibit autonomous reasoning, for example by using logic programming to maintain reliable conversation, and studies of human-chatbot interaction show that chatbot agency is often co-constructed with users. Thus, the line between simple chatbots and autonomous agents is blurred in practice.

citations.claim: Bots are software systems designed to support users by automating a specific process, task, or activity; when such systems implement a conversational component, they are known as conversational agents.
Chatbots are conversational software applications designed to interact dialectically with users for many purposes, and argumentation-based chatbots can be compared with standard chatbots.
A framework using LLMs as parsers and answer set programming for reasoning can realize reliable conversational agents that understand human conversation.
Agency in human-chatbot interaction manifests as an emergent, shared experience where control is co-constructed turn-by-turn.
Social robots and chatbots powered by large language models are advancing as artificial social agents, raising questions about their roles as social entities.

balanced.summary: The documents show that chatbots and autonomous agents are overlapping but distinct concepts. Chatbots are conversational systems built to interact with users, while autonomous agents are expected to act goal-directedly, reason, and exercise agency; increasingly, chatbot research makes chatbots more agentic. For example, bots are defined in doc_7 as automating tasks, with conversational agents being bots that add dialogue. Doc_2 argues for moving beyond LLM-only chatbots to frameworks that reason over knowledge, enabling reliable, autonomous conversational behavior. Doc_1 reframes agency as shared, with AI steering intentions, and doc_5 shows agents can autonomously initiate conversation from body language. Doc_8 addresses safety monitoring for chatbots in safety-critical settings, and doc_4 contrasts reasoning-capable argumentation-based chatbots with standard ones. At the same time, docs_3, 6, 9, and 10 highlight the diversity, social roles, limitations, and caution surrounding conversational and social agents. Overall, the literature suggests that an autonomous agent is not merely a chatbot: autonomy implies self-directed reasoning, initiative, and goal pursuit, though modern chatbots are increasingly endowed with such capabilities.

citations.claim: In sustained human-chatbot interaction, agency is not fixed in either party but emerges as a shared, co-constructed experience, with the AI steering intentions and participants setting boundaries.
LLMs alone lack understanding and reliability; reliable conversational agents should use LLMs only as parsers and carry out conversation by reasoning over knowledge using answer set programming.
Community-generated AI chatbots on platforms like FlowGPT vary widely in domain, output modality, and goals, indicating that chatbots are not a single, homogeneous category.
Chatbots may employ computational argumentation to different degrees and in different manners, offering benefits and drawbacks compared with standard chatbots.
Socially interactive agents can be trained, using body language as input, to autonomously determine when to open a conversation and who opens it.
Chatbot technology should be understood across three societal dimensions: scientific research, commercial instrument, and intimate interaction.
Bots are software systems that automate a process or task; when they include a conversational component they are also known as conversational agents.
Runtime verification frameworks such as RV4Chatbot formalize expected behaviours as interaction protocols to monitor and ensure chatbots adhere to safe behaviours.
Social identity theory and social categorization theory can be extrapolated to artificial social agents, but not all human models and sub-theories will apply.
Conversational AI systems can support the design of agent-based social simulation models, but they produce occasional inaccuracies and conversational divergence.

standard.summary: Deterministic search strategies follow fixed rules and offer worst-case guarantees: deterministic query complexity counts the worst-case number of queries needed to find a solution [doc_9], and deterministic sequencing of exploration and exploitation (DSEE) achieves the optimal logarithmic regret in multi-armed bandits for light-tailed rewards [doc_3]. Stochastic search uses randomness or stochastic feedback and can be more effective under uncertainty: random walks with local biases reduce mean first-passage times on networks [doc_2]; KL-UCB, a stochastic bandit policy, outperforms standard UCB baselines [doc_5]; the HCT algorithm handles correlated stochastic bandit rewards that iid-based methods cannot [doc_4]; and in dueling bandits with stochastic comparisons, a simple EDA identifies the Condorcet winner with high probability while an (1+1) EA does not [doc_6]. The optimal approach depends on the setting; even in a stochastic game such as Guess Who?, the optimal strategy is not always binary search, and a trailing player may need bold plays [doc_1].

citations.claim: Deterministic query complexity D(P,n) is the smallest number of queries needed in the worst case to find the solution, contrasting with non-deterministic query complexity.
DSEE achieves the optimal logarithmic order of regret for light-tailed reward distributions and provides corresponding results for general reward distributions.

Biasing random walks based on inverse degree, persistence, and local two-hop paths can lead to smaller searching times, and these biasing approaches can be combined for a more robust random search strategy.
The KL-UCB algorithm, an online horizon-free index policy for stochastic bandits, satisfies a uniformly better regret bound than UCB or UCB2 for arbitrary bounded rewards.
The high-confidence tree (HCT) algorithm handles the challenging case of correlated rewards, whereas existing methods require the reward-generating process of each arm to be iid.

In the binary stochastic dueling bandit setting, a simple EDA based on the Max-Min Ant System chooses the Condorcet winner with probability 1-Theta(p), while the (1+1) EA chooses it only with constant probability if p=Omega(1/n).
In the stochastic game 'Guess Who?', the optimal strategy is not always binary search; the trailing player should make bold plays in an attempt to catch up.

balanced.summary: A central theme is the tradeoff between deterministic and stochastic search. Deterministic methods follow fixed, predictable rules: DSEE uses deterministic sequencing to attain optimal logarithmic regret in multi-armed bandits [doc_3]; deterministic query complexity gives worst-case query counts [doc_9]; and heuristic search in planning is a deterministic forward-search paradigm, enhanced by learned admissible heuristics [doc_7][doc_8]. Yet deterministic policies are not universally optimal: in the stochastic game 'Guess Who?' binary search can be suboptimal, and bold stochastic plays help a trailing player catch up [doc_1]. Stochastic methods use randomness or probabilistic models to handle uncertainty: random walks with local/one-step-memory biases improve search efficiency on networks [doc_2]; KL-UCB achieves optimal regret for stochastic bandits [doc_5]; HCT handles correlated bandit feedback [doc_4]; EDAs stochastically maintain distributions and can outperform deterministic evolutionary algorithms at identifying a Condorcet winner [doc_6]. Additionally, query complexity can be interpolated between deterministic and non-deterministic extremes by allowing an adversary to change the input a bounded number of times [doc_9]. Stochastic bandit formulations also appear in best-arm retention for streaming algorithms [doc_10]. Overall, deterministic search provides strong worst-case guarantees in well-modeled settings, whereas stochastic search offers robustness to uncertainty, correlation, and adversarial dynamics.

citations.claim: DSEE uses deterministic sequencing of exploration and exploitation to achieve the optimal logarithmic order of regret in multi-armed bandit problems.

Deterministic query complexity measures the worst-case number of queries needed to solve a problem, and can be interpolated with non-deterministic complexity by allowing an adversary to change the input at most k times.
Learning forward search heuristics from admissible bounds improves deterministic heuristic search, with a truncated Gaussian model yielding better heuristics than MSE training.
Heuristic search for numeric planning is boosted by techniques such as numeric novelty heuristics and multi-queue search, representing a deterministic search paradigm.
In the stochastic game 'Guess Who?', binary search is not always optimal; bold plays can be optimal for a trailing player in the stochastic model.
Stochastic random walks with local information and one-step memory can achieve smaller searching times on complex networks when biased by inverse degree, persistence, or local two-hop paths.
The KL-UCB algorithm is an online stochastic bandit policy that satisfies better regret bounds than UCB and reaches the Lai-Robbins lower bound for Bernoulli rewards.
The HCT algorithm handles the challenging case of correlated rewards in online stochastic optimization under bandit feedback, which existing iid-based methods cannot.

In stochastic dueling bandits, a simple EDA stochastically selects the Condorcet winner with high probability, while the (1+1) EA does so only with constant probability, showing stochastic distribution-based search can outperform deterministic evolutionary search.
The Best Arm Retention problem in stochastic multi-armed bandits has applications in streaming algorithms, with optimal PAC bounds and regret minimization studied.

standard.summary: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed paradigm that keeps data localized and separates data acquisition from central computation, unlike centralized learning which occurs in a data center (doc_10). FL mitigates privacy and bandwidth concerns but introduces challenges such as data heterogeneity, device heterogeneity, and communication constraints (doc_4). Centralized FL relies on a central aggregation server, which can create performance bottlenecks and trust issues; decentralized FL removes this server, offering alternatives for dynamic topologies (doc_2). Experimental comparisons show that both centralized and decentralized FL can achieve high accuracy, with decentralized FL slightly outperforming centralized in one crop-yield prediction study (doc_7). Additionally, federated customization methods can perform close to centralized approaches, indicating FL's practical viability (doc_8). The choice between architectures depends on application needs and performance trade-offs (doc_5).

citations.claim: FL enables the separation of data acquisition and computation at the central unit, which is different from centralized learning that occurs in a data center.

In heterogeneous FL, the key challenge is to efficiently and collaboratively train models across clients with different data distributions, model structures, task objectives, computational capabilities, and communication resources.

Conventional federated learning frameworks suffer from challenges including performance bottlenecks at the central aggregation server, data bias, poor model convergence, exposure to model poisoning attacks, and limited trust in the centralized infrastructure.
The experimental results present that ≥97% and >97.5% prediction accuracy are achieved using the centralized and decentralized federated learning-based frameworks respectively.
The conducted experiments validate its feasibility with performance close to centralized approaches.

Choosing the right FL architecture depends on the application's needs, and few research studies have experimentally compared centralized, decentralized, and semi-decentralized FL architectures to understand trade-offs.

balanced.summary: Federated learning (FL) is a decentralized machine learning paradigm in which multiple clients collaboratively train models without sharing raw data, in contrast to centralized learning that aggregates data in a data center. FL preserves privacy and reduces communication bandwidth, but introduces challenges such as data and device heterogeneity, communication unreliability, and trust issues in central servers. FL architectures vary between centralized FL (server-based aggregation), decentralized FL (peer-to-peer aggregation), and semi-decentralized FL; the choice involves trade-offs in accuracy, response time, scalability, and robustness. Empirical comparisons show decentralized FL can reach comparable or slightly higher accuracy, while centralized FL can substantially reduce response time relative to cloud-only training; federated customization of large models can approach centralized performance.

citations.claim: FL training is inherently decentralized and often takes place in less controlled settings compared to data centers, posing unique challenges distinct from fully controlled environments.

Conventional centralized federated learning suffers from performance bottlenecks at the central aggregation server, data bias, poor convergence, model poisoning attacks, and limited trust; pFedGame is a decentralized approach that works without a centralized server.
Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing private data, unlocking siloed data and distributed resources.

In heterogeneous federated learning, key challenges arise from different data distributions, model structures, task objectives, computational capabilities, and communication resources, increasing training complexity.

Choosing the right FL architecture depends on application needs, and few studies have experimentally compared centralized, decentralized, and semi-decentralized FL; the paper provides such an experimental analysis.
A proposed three-tier FL architecture addresses client data heterogeneity and computational constraints, managing non-IID data sets more effectively than traditional federated learning models.

In crop yield prediction, centralized FL achieved at least 97% accuracy while decentralized FL achieved over 97.5%; centralized FL reduced response time by about 75% compared to a cloud-only framework.
Experiments on federated prefix-tuning validated its feasibility with performance close to centralized approaches.
FL keeps data localized, preserving data privacy and reducing network bandwidth requirements compared to centralized model training.

FL enables separation of data acquisition and computation at the central unit, differing from centralized learning that occurs in a data center, and is typically used in wireless edge networks with limited and unreliable communication.

standard.summary: The documents examine the interplay between retrieval and memorization across IR and LLMs. Retrieval-based methods (e.g., RAG) aim to augment knowledge, yet improved retrieval metrics do not always improve downstream reasoning (doc_2). In LLMs, memorization of training data creates interference and benchmark contamination: models fail to retrieve from context under proactive interference (doc_5), and accuracy drops sharply when evaluation questions are modified to prevent memorization (doc_8). Memorization is more pronounced in larger models and shaped by training order (doc_6); unlearning methods are therefore an active area to forget undesired knowledge while preserving model utility (doc_10). Finally, retrieval models that follow instructions can outperform instruction-agnostic baselines, but they show limited sensitivity to changing user intents in exploratory search (doc_1).

citations.claim: Improvements in retrieval performance do not consistently translate to commensurate gains in downstream reasoning; as Recall@5 improves, the Recall Conversion Rate exhibits a near-linear decay.
LLM retrieval accuracy declines log-linearly toward zero as proactive interference accumulates, even when final values are positioned just before the query.

All models experience remarkable accuracy drops under the proposed variation that dissociates correct answers from previously seen tokens, with an average loss of 57% on MMLU and 50% on UNED-Access 2024.
Memorisation is stronger and more persistent in larger models, is determined by data order and learning rate, and has stable trends across model sizes.
Digital forgetting aims to remove undesirable knowledge or behavior while retaining performance on desirable tasks, and unlearning methodologies stand out as state of the art.

The best instructed retrievers improve ranking relevance compared to instruction-agnostic approaches, but instruction-following performance displays insensitivity to instructions, especially in long-running exploratory sessions.

balanced.summary: The documents together examine the relationship and trade-offs between retrieval-based approaches and memorization in AI systems. On the retrieval side, instruction-following retrievers can adapt to query nuances but show insensitivity to evolving intents in exploratory sessions (doc_1), and retrieval quality improvements in RAG do not consistently translate to better reasoning, with recall gains often accompanied by a decay in recall conversion rate (doc_2). For classification, LLMs outperform weak supervision in recall but struggle with precision (doc_4). On the memorization side, LLMs heavily rely on memorization rather than reasoning, as shown by dramatic accuracy drops when evaluation questions are modified to dissociate correct answers from previously seen tokens (doc_8). Memorization in language models is stronger and more persistent in larger models and is influenced by data order and learning rate (doc_6). LLM retrieval from context is constrained by proactive interference, with accuracy declining as interfering information accumulates (doc_5). Unlearning methods aim to erase unwanted memorized knowledge while retaining desirable performance (doc_10). External memory aids such as generated images can enhance human vocabulary retention (doc_3), and LLMs can predict human memory performance, suggesting shared cognitive patterns (doc_9). Memory mechanisms also play a critical role in metaheuristic optimization, improving exploration and exploitation when tailored to the problem domain (doc_7).

citations.claim: Instructed retrievers improve ranking relevance over instruction-agnostic approaches, but their instruction-following performance displays insensitivity or counter-intuitive behavior, limiting long-running exploratory sessions.
As Recall@5 improves, the Recall Conversion Rate (RCR) exhibits near-linear decay, meaning retrieval improvements do not consistently translate to downstream reasoning gains in RAG methods.
Providing images generated from participants' descriptions of memorable visual links significantly improves vocabulary memory retention compared to the keyword method alone.
LLMs outperform weak supervision in recall for user intent classification but continue to struggle with precision, highlighting the need for methods that balance both metrics.

LLM retrieval accuracy declines log-linearly toward zero as proactive interference accumulates, with errors arising from retrieving previously overwritten values, revealing a working memory bottleneck.
Memorisation in language models is stronger and more persistent in larger models, is determined by data order and learning rate, and has stable trends across model sizes.
Memory mechanisms can significantly enhance metaheuristic performance by enabling effective exploration and exploitation, and the choice of memory mechanism should be tailored to the problem domain.

When multiple-choice questions are varied to dissociate correct answers from previously seen tokens, all LLMs experience remarkable accuracy drops, averaging 57% on MMLU and 50% on UNED-Access 2024, indicating reliance on memorization.
ChatGPT's memorability ratings effectively predicted human memory performance, and both LLM and human data aligned with probabilistic frameworks of context-dependent learning.
Digital forgetting methods, particularly machine unlearning, aim to remove undesirable knowledge from LLMs while retaining performance on desirable tasks and being more efficient than retraining.

standard.summary: Based on the provided documents, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) generally outperforms fine-tuning for domain-adapted knowledge systems. RAG-based constructions are more efficient and surpass fine-tuned models by 16% in ROUGE, 15% in BLEU, and 53% in cosine similarity, while fine-tuning achieves an 8% better METEOR score indicating greater creativity. Combining fine-tuned models with RAG is not trivial and can decrease performance. RAG's advantage is attributed to dynamically integrating up-to-date external information, addressing the static limitations of large language models.

citations.claim: RAG-based constructions are more efficient than models produced with fine-tuning; on average, RAG outperforms fine-tuned models by 16% in ROUGE score, 15% in BLEU score, and 53% in cosine similarity, while fine-tuned models have an 8% better METEOR score indicating greater creativity compared to RAG.
Connecting fine-tuned models with RAG is not trivial and can cause a decrease in performance.

RAG merges retrieval methods with deep learning to address the static limitations of large language models by enabling dynamic integration of up-to-date external information, providing a cost-effective solution to improve accuracy and reliability.

balanced.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and fine-tuning (FN) are two prominent techniques for adapting large language models to domain-specific knowledge-based systems. A direct experimental comparison on GPT-J-6B, OPT-6.7B, LlaMA, and LlaMA-2 found that RAG-based systems generally outperform fine-tuned models, with RAG achieving higher ROUGE, BLEU, and cosine similarity scores while fine-tuning only showed an advantage in METEOR, suggesting greater creativity; the study also cautions that combining RAG and fine-tuning can degrade performance. Beyond this head-to-head comparison, the broader literature highlights that RAG systems involve many interacting design choices—such as retrieval, ranking, augmentation, prompting, and generation—and that deployment decisions must be selective and context-dependent. Various enhancements and alternatives to standard RAG have been proposed, including active knowledge navigation, retry-based search persistence, and cache-augmented generation for constrained knowledge bases, while evaluation of RAG systems remains a distinct challenge.

citations.claim: RAG-based constructions are more efficient than fine-tuned models, outperforming FN by 16% in ROUGE score, 15% in BLEU, and 53% in cosine similarity, while FN models have an 8% better METEOR score indicating greater creativity; connecting FN models with RAG can cause a decrease in performance.

Evaluating RAG systems poses unique challenges due to their hybrid structure and reliance on dynamic knowledge sources, requiring examination of retrieval and generation components using metrics such as relevance, accuracy, and faithfulness.

RAG quality depends on many interacting choices across retrieval, ranking, augmentation, prompting, and generation, so optimizing modules in isolation is brittle; RAGSmith treats RAG design as an end-to-end architecture search over 46,080 feasible pipeline configurations.

RAG merges retrieval methods with deep learning to address static limitations of LLMs by dynamically integrating up-to-date external information, and the RAG paradigm can be organized into pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval, and generation categories.

RAG deployment must be highly selective, with variable recall thresholds and failure modes affecting up to 12.6% of samples even with perfect documents; optimal retrieval volume is task-dependent, and knowledge integration effectiveness depends on task and model characteristics.

Cache-augmented generation (CAG) is an alternative to RAG that preloads all relevant resources into the LLM's extended context and caches runtime parameters, eliminating retrieval latency and minimizing retrieval errors for constrained knowledge bases.

Improvements in retrieval performance in RAG do not consistently translate to commensurate gains in downstream reasoning, and the proposed Recall Conversion Rate (RCR) metric quantifies this gap; the NeocorRAG framework optimizes retrieval quality while maintaining high recall.

RAG depends heavily on initial search query quality, and the ReZero framework directly rewards retrying a search after an initial unsuccessful attempt, achieving 46.88% accuracy compared to a 25% baseline.

Conventional RAG typically uses a flat retrieval paradigm, which struggles with complex tasks; NaviRAG shifts to active knowledge navigation by structuring documents hierarchically and using an LLM agent to iteratively retrieve at the most appropriate granularity level, improving both retrieval recall and end-to-end answer performance.

standard.summary: Few-shot learning is a paradigm for learning from very few labelled examples, while fine-tuning is a specific technique that adapts a pre-trained model; they are often compared or combined. In histopathology few-shot classification, standard fine-tuning and popular meta-learning few-shot methods perform comparably, whereas in document classification few-shot fine-tuning can reduce annotation needs relative to zero-shot prompting. Fine-tuning can also be integrated into few-shot models, e.g., episodic fine-tuning of Prototypical Networks, to improve performance. Both paradigms share sensitivity to randomness, and simple techniques like last-layer resetting can make fine-tuning more effective for few-shot transfer.

citations.claim: In histopathology few-shot classification, popular meta-learning approaches perform at par with standard fine-tuning and regularization methods.
The paper investigates zero-shot prompting and few-shot fine-tuning for document image classification to reduce the need for human-annotated training samples.
A method fine-tunes a ProtoNet on the labeled support set of test episodes and combines it with optimization-based FSL algorithms, outperforming regular ProtoNet in few-shot audio classification.
Few-shot learning and fine-tuning are limited-labelled-data approaches that are excessively sensitive to randomness, leading to large variance across runs.
Repeatedly resetting last-layer weights ('zapping') improves transfer accuracy and rapid adaptation in few-shot fine-tuning settings.

balanced.summary: Few-shot learning and fine-tuning are both strategies for adapting models with limited labeled data, but they operate differently: few-shot learning often uses episodic meta-training to enable fast adaptation, while fine-tuning updates a pre-trained model on a small support set. Their relative performance depends on the domain and setup. In histopathology image classification, popular meta-learning approaches perform on par with standard fine-tuning and regularization methods. In audio classification, an episodic fine-tuning strategy applied to prototypical networks improves few-shot performance over regular ProtoNet. In document image classification using large language models, zero-shot prompting and few-shot fine-tuning are compared to reduce the need for human-annotated samples. Additionally, repeatedly resetting last-layer weights (zapping) can improve fine-tuning transfer accuracy and achieve performance on par with meta-learning without expensive higher-order gradients. Across these limited-data methods, sensitivity to uncontrolled randomness is a recognized concern that can affect the stability and comparison of results.

citations.claim: Learning with limited labelled data includes prompting, in-context learning, fine-tuning, meta-learning, and few-shot learning, but these approaches are excessively sensitive to effects of uncontrolled randomness, leading to large variances in results across training runs.

A simple method to fine-tune a ProtoNet on the support set of a test episode, combined with optimization-based few-shot learning algorithms (MAML and Meta-Curvature), outperforms regular ProtoNet by a large margin in few-shot audio classification tasks.
In document image classification, zero-shot prompting and few-shot model fine-tuning are investigated with the aim of reducing the need for human-annotated training samples as much as possible.
In few-shot histopathology image classification, popular meta-learning approaches perform at par with standard fine-tuning and regularization methods.

Zapping, the repeated resetting of last-layer weights, results in improved transfer accuracy and/or more rapid adaptation in standard fine-tuning settings, achieving performance on par with state-of-the-art meta-learning without needing expensive higher-order gradients.

standard.summary: The documents do not directly compare human feedback and synthetic feedback as blanket categories, but they provide relevant findings about their trade-offs. One study (doc_1) found that synthetic humanoid feedback in VR enhanced immersion, realism, and enjoyment but introduced moderate comfort and simulation-sickness costs, with participants noting the robot's consistency and predictability in contrast to human adaptability. Another study (doc_2) showed that synthetic real-time multi-sensory (haptic and visual) error feedback improved surgical training outcomes over delayed replay or no feedback, indicating synthetic feedback can be effective when delivered immediately. Research on pseudo-haptics (doc_8) suggests synthetic feedback may act more as an affective channel than as a direct tactile replacement, shifting emotional responses rather than reproducing touch. Additionally, adaptive synthetic systems (doc_9) can improve haptic communication and tracking by adjusting robot viscoelasticity based on user noise, bridging some gaps between human and synthetic feedback. Overall, synthetic feedback appears valuable for consistency and training efficiency, while human feedback is characterized by adaptability; the choice depends on task goals and desired experiential outcomes.

citations.claim: Humanoid feedback enhanced immersion, realism, and enjoyment, while introducing moderate costs in terms of comfort and simulation sickness; interviews highlighted the robot's consistency and predictability in contrast to the adaptability of human feedback.
Real-time haptic and visual error feedback improved learning outcomes in a virtual surgical task over error feedback in replay or no error feedback at all.

Pseudo-haptics in XR may be better understood as an affective feedback channel rather than a direct replacement for physical touch, as affect shifted systematically while tactile sensations were rarely reported.
A stochastic-optimal-information-and-effort (SOIE) controller that adjusts robot viscoelasticity improved tracking performance and effective haptic communication in human-robot interaction.

balanced.summary: The documents characterize synthetic (machine-generated) feedback relative to human feedback across virtual reality, motor learning, and human-robot interaction. Synthetic feedback can be more consistent and predictable than human feedback, while humans contribute adaptability; however, robotic feedback can also be designed to adapt to a user's sensory and motor noise to improve haptic communication. Synthetic pseudo-haptic feedback does not simply replace physical touch but can shift affective experience, and external visual, auditory, and haptic feedback can enhance interpersonal synchrony. Timing matters: real-time synthetic error feedback improves training outcomes compared to replay or no feedback. Device-based haptic feedback perception is also shaped by mapping and handedness, and the statistical properties of system responsiveness influence user performance. Together, these findings suggest that synthetic feedback offers consistency, tunability, and measurable learning benefits, whereas human feedback provides natural adaptability, with the choice depending on task goals and interaction context.

citations.claim: In VR driving, humanoid (synthetic) feedback enhanced immersion, realism, and enjoyment; interviews highlighted the robot's consistency and predictability compared to the adaptability of human feedback.

A stochastic-optimal-information-and-effort controller enables a robot to adjust its viscoelasticity based on its own and the user's noise characteristics, improving haptic communication and tracking performance.
Pseudo-haptic cues rendered on an embodied virtual hand shifted affect systematically, suggesting they act as affective feedback rather than a direct replacement for physical touch.
Visual, auditory, and haptic feedback of inter-brain synchronization level can further enhance its intensity, with design recommendations for feedback systems.
Real-time haptic and visual error feedback improved learning outcomes in a virtual surgical task compared to replay feedback or no error feedback.

Participants perceived mechanical properties via wrist-worn haptic feedback; non-congruent hand-wrist mapping improved performance while congruent mapping gave better user experience, and dominant hand use yielded better experience and enjoyment.

System responsiveness in virtual environments fluctuates and should be described statistically; its standard deviation affects grasp and placement performance only above 82 ms, with placement more sensitive.

standard.summary: Compared to scaling or fine-tuning larger language models, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) offers a cost-effective way to improve performance. Evidence shows RAG can surpass fine-tuning, especially for less popular factual knowledge, and that larger model size does not uniformly lead to better downstream performance, suggesting retrieval augmentation is a valuable alternative to simply using larger models.

citations.claim: RAG surpasses FT by a large margin particularly for least popular factual knowledge.
Fine tuning, while beneficial for small LMs, requires extensive resources; Stimulus RAG surpasses fine-tuning, eliminating the need for costly data augmentation and fine tuning.

RAG provides a cost-effective solution to the generation of plausible but possibly incorrect responses by LLMs, thereby enhancing the accuracy and reliability of their outputs through the use of real-world data.
Larger LLMs do not uniformly yield better downstream performance.

balanced.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is often positioned as an alternative or complement to scaling up model size: instead of relying only on larger LMs to memorize more factual knowledge, RAG dynamically integrates external information to improve accuracy and reliability. Evidence shows RAG can outperform fine-tuning for less popular factual knowledge and offers a resource-efficient alternative to costly fine-tuning. At the same time, larger models do not uniformly improve downstream retrieval performance, so retrieval design matters. However, RAG introduces its own complexities: retrieval quality, multi-view query understanding, instruction sensitivity, and embedding choices all affect outcomes.

citations.claim: RAG surpasses fine-tuning by a large margin for least popular factual knowledge, and the proposed Stimulus RAG approach can eliminate the need for costly data augmentation and fine-tuning.

Larger LLMs do not uniformly yield better downstream performance in query reformulation; gains are strongly conditioned on the retrieval paradigm and do not consistently transfer across neural retrievers.

RAG merges retrieval methods with deep learning to address the static limitations of LLMs by dynamically integrating up-to-date external information, thereby enhancing the accuracy and reliability of outputs.

RAG improvements face challenges such as poor retrieval quality for complex multifaceted queries, inefficiencies in long-term knowledge re-retrieval, and lack of personalized responses, which ERAGent addresses.
Existing RAG retrieval methods in knowledge-dense domains lack multi-perspective views, and a multi-view RAG framework using intention-aware query rewriting improves retrieval precision and recall.

Instruction-following retrieval models can improve ranking relevance over instruction-agnostic approaches but display insensitivity or counter-intuitive behavior to instructions in long-running exploratory sessions.

The choice of embedding model, pooling strategy, and query formulation significantly impacts retrieval performance in RAG for the clinical domain, and performance on public benchmarks does not necessarily transfer to new domains.

standard.summary: Distributed learning is generally pursued to overcome the limitations of centralized learning, such as privacy concerns, high storage demands, single points of failure, and excessive computing requirements (doc_7). Centralized federated learning also suffers from performance bottlenecks at the central aggregation server, data bias, poor convergence, and vulnerability to model poisoning attacks (doc_10). Distributed strategies can provide performance benefits: in small step-size regimes, each agent in a network can achieve the same performance as a centralized fully-connected strategy (doc_1). However, there are trade-offs among centralized, decentralized, and semi-decentralized federated learning architectures, each having distinct strengths and limitations (doc_6). Distributed approaches also introduce additional complexity due to managing multiple interacting components (doc_7).

citations.claim: Centralized training has drawbacks including privacy concerns, high storage demands, a single point of failure, and significant computing requirements, motivating distributed methods.

Conventional federated learning frameworks suffer from performance bottlenecks at the central aggregation server, data bias, poor model convergence, exposure to model poisoning attacks, and limited trust in the centralized infrastructure.
In the small step-size regime, each agent in a distributed network is able to achieve the same performance level as that of a centralized strategy corresponding to a fully connected network.
Federated Learning can be Centralized (CFL), Decentralized (DFL), or Semi-decentralized (SDFL), and there are trade-offs between different performance indicators among these architectures.

balanced.summary: Centralized learning pools data and models in a central server, but this approach has noted drawbacks including privacy concerns, high storage demands, a single point of failure, and significant computing requirements (doc_7). Centralized federated learning also faces performance bottlenecks at the aggregation server and trust issues in the central infrastructure (doc_10). Distributed and collaborative learning instead enables agents to cooperatively train models while preserving privacy and addressing heterogeneity in tasks, models, data, and resources (doc_2, doc_5). Distributed strategies can achieve performance comparable to centralized fully connected networks in the small step-size regime, and the network induces an equalization effect across agents (doc_1). Practical distributed methods must handle quantized communications, asynchrony, and stochastic gradients (doc_3), and can improve communication efficiency through multiple local training steps, compressed transmissions, and variance reduction (doc_4, doc_8). Compression techniques such as low-rank and log-quantization reduce communication overhead while maintaining convergence and accuracy (doc_9). However, choosing the right architecture—centralized, decentralized, or semi-decentralized—involves trade-offs between performance indicators and depends on application needs (doc_6). Decentralized approaches without a central server require peer selection and game-theoretic aggregation strategies to handle dynamic topologies and heterogeneous data (doc_10).

citations.claim: Centralized training and inference have drawbacks including privacy concerns, high storage demands, a single point of failure, and significant computing requirements.

Conventional federated learning frameworks suffer from performance bottlenecks at the central aggregation server, data bias, poor convergence, and exposure to model poisoning attacks, with limited trust in the centralized infrastructure.

Collaborative learning enables distributed agents to cooperatively train models while addressing privacy concerns, and covers distributed patterns such as federated learning with task, model, data, and resource heterogeneity.

Collaborative distributed machine learning systems, including federated learning and swarm learning, were developed to leverage resources for ML model development and use in a confidentiality-preserving way.

In the small step-size regime, each agent in a distributed network can achieve the same performance level as a centralized strategy corresponding to a fully connected network, and the network induces an equalization effect across agents.
Distributed learning over peer-to-peer networks addresses challenges of quantized communications, asynchrony, and stochastic gradients, with convergence analysis for the proposed methods.

A distributed ADMM-based algorithm enables agents to perform multiple local training steps between communications and use stochastic gradients, converging to a neighborhood of a stationary or optimal point, with variance reduction achieving exact convergence.

An ADMM-based algorithm achieves joint computation and communication efficiency by using stochastic gradients, multiple training epochs between communication rounds, and compressed transmissions, with exact linear convergence in the strongly convex setting.

LQ-SGD incorporates low-rank approximation and log-quantization to drastically reduce communication overhead in distributed training while ensuring convergence speed and model accuracy, and shows stronger resistance to gradient inversion.

Federated learning can be centralized, decentralized, or semi-decentralized, and choosing the right architecture depends on the application's needs, with trade-offs between different performance indicators.

standard.summary: Attention mechanisms and convolutions represent different approaches to processing visual information. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) use fixed local filters and have been studied for their ability to mimic human attention, often visualized with explainable AI methods such as Grad-CAM (doc_1). CNNs also exhibit variable performance on perceptual tasks like Gestalt closure, with some architectures showing the effect and others not (doc_7). In contrast, attention mechanisms in transformers compute weights over the full input sequence, which is powerful but computationally expensive due to the quadratic attention matrix; however, attention can be made sparse, reducing computation by nearly 80% while maintaining performance (doc_5). Attention weights in transformers can also serve a genuinely explanatory role for model predictions (doc_4), and human-like attention can be integrated into transformer self-attention layers to improve accuracy in tasks like visual question answering (doc_8). Additionally, attention maps extracted from vision transformers can act as saliency signals for downstream tasks, enhancing robotic manipulation policies (doc_10). Thus, while convolutions rely on spatially fixed operations, attention mechanisms dynamically select relevant information across the input, offering different trade-offs in interpretability, flexibility, and computational cost.

citations.claim: CNN attention maps, revealed by Grad-CAM, can be compared to human attention maps, with similarity depending on human tasks and image type.
Different CNNs show variable results for the Gestalt law of closure, with VGG16 and DenseNet-121 exhibiting the closure effect while others do not.
Classical self-attention is quadratic in sequence length, but actual attention is sparse; learning to attend to key features can reduce calculations by close to 80% with similar results.
Attention weights can have a causal explanatory role for transformer model predictions, contradicting claims that they are not explanatorily relevant.
Integrating multimodal human-like attention into transformer self-attention layers achieves state-of-the-art VQA accuracy with about 80% fewer trainable parameters than prior work.
Attention maps from a pre-trained Vision Transformer can be used as pixel-level saliency scores and lifted into voxel representations to improve bimanual robotic manipulation performance.

balanced.summary: Across the provided studies, attention mechanisms in transformer-based models differ from convolution in how they select and weight information: convolutional neural networks (CNNs) process images through learned filters and can exhibit human-like perceptual phenomena such as closure (doc_7), whereas attention mechanisms distribute weights over tokens or image regions, can be sparse for efficiency (doc_5), and can be causally explained through efficient attention (doc_4). Comparisons between CNN attention maps and human gaze are modulated by task and image type (doc_1). In multimodal and VQA models, attention integrates image and text, and human-like attention on text correlates with performance (doc_3); integrating human-like attention into transformer self-attention yields state-of-the-art VQA accuracy with fewer parameters (doc_8). Vision transformer attention maps can also be lifted into voxel representations to improve robotic manipulation (doc_10). Saliency-based explanations of such models have inconsistent effects on human performance (doc_2), and specific attention heads in multimodal LLMs concentrate on visual tokens (doc_6).

citations.claim: The similarity between human attention maps and CNN attention maps (Grad-CAM) strongly depends on image type and the human task used to elicit attention.

A systematic review of 68 user studies found that saliency map explanations can enhance human performance but null effects or costs are common, with benefits depending on task type and AI prediction correctness.
For five VQA models, higher correlation with human attention on text is a significant predictor of VQA performance, pointing to neural text attention mechanisms.
Efficient attention matrices have a causal role for predicting model output in NLP tasks requiring contextual information, contrary to claims that attention weights are not explanatorily relevant.

Classical self attention uses the entire sequence length but actual attention is sparse; a Saccade Attention Network can learn where to attend from a pre-trained model, reducing calculations by close to 80% with similar results.
In multimodal LLMs, a class of attention heads focuses specifically on visual content, with behavior correlated with attention weight distribution over visual tokens.
VGG16 and DenseNet-121 exhibit the Closure effect while other CNNs show variable results, indicating that convolutional networks can demonstrate human-like perceptual organization.
MULAN integrates multimodal human-like attention on image and text into transformer self-attention for VQA, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with about 80% fewer trainable parameters.
Attention maps from DINOv2, a self-supervised ViT, are treated as pixel-level saliency and lifted into voxel grids, improving bimanual robotic manipulation by an average of 8.2%.

standard.summary: Neural search and keyword search differ in how they match queries to documents. Keyword search relies on term-based or lexical matching, which is fast and effective for exact terms but struggles with semantic nuance and vocabulary gaps. Neural search uses embeddings and semantic matching to capture contextual signals and handle paraphrase or concept-level relevance, often improving retrieval quality. However, neural retrievers can introduce biases, such as favoring LLM-generated content, and may require hybrid approaches that combine term-based and neural methods for optimal performance.

citations.claim: IR has evolved from term-based methods to neural models; neural models excel at capturing complex contextual signals and semantic nuances, while term-based sparse retrieval offers rapid response, suggesting a combination of both.

Semantic search modeled as paraphrase span detection outperforms lexical similarity and BERT sentence embedding retrieval baselines, showing a strong advantage of span retrieval over sentence similarity.
Embedding-based neural retrieval (EBR) is an effective search retrieval method in product search for tackling the vocabulary gap between customer search queries and products.

Retrieval methods and user search behaviors are shifting from keyword-based matching to natural language semantic matching; neural crawling policies improve semantic search effectiveness while maintaining keyword query performance.

Neural retrieval models tend to rank LLM-generated documents higher, a source bias, because LLM-generated texts exhibit more focused semantics with less noise, making them easier to match semantically.
Keyword queries on Deep Web sources represented as relational tables with access limitations require a query plan that minimizes accesses to data sources.

balanced.summary: Neural and keyword search are contrasting retrieval paradigms. Keyword/term-based search relies on exact lexical matching, is fast, and remains useful, but it cannot capture deeper semantic relationships or bridge the vocabulary gap. Neural/embedding-based search learns dense representations that capture contextual and semantic signals, improving relevance and handling vocabulary gaps, yet it faces challenges such as data scarcity, interpretability, and biases like ranking LLM-generated text too highly. The most effective systems combine the two, using sparse term-based methods for speed and neural models for language understanding. This shift toward semantic matching is also influencing adjacent areas such as web crawling, where neural policies improve early-stage search effectiveness while remaining comparable on keyword queries.

citations.claim: Neural models excel at capturing complex contextual signals and semantic nuances, but face challenges such as data scarcity and interpretability; the evolution of IR requires a combination of traditional term-based sparse retrieval methods with rapid response and modern neural architectures with powerful language understanding.

Embedding-based neural retrieval (EBR) is an effective method for tackling the vocabulary gap between customer search queries and products, though it initially showed relevance degradation that was addressed with approaches like a Relevance Reward Model and typo-aware training.
Neural retrieval models tend to rank LLM-generated documents higher, a source bias that extends from first-stage retrievers to second-stage re-rankers, showing a specific bias in neural search.

Semantic search framed as extractive paraphrase span detection outperformed a lexical similarity baseline by 31.9pp in exact match and by 22.3pp in token-level F-score, demonstrating an advantage over keyword-style lexical matching.

Retrieval methods and user search behaviors are shifting from keyword-based matching to natural language semantic matching; neural crawling policies significantly improve harvest rate, maxNDCG, and search effectiveness during early crawling while maintaining comparable performance on keyword queries.

standard.summary: Privacy protections in machine learning often come at the cost of model performance, but several methods and analyses show that this trade-off can be mitigated. Differential privacy (DP) noise typically degrades accuracy, but techniques such as model splitting, smooth sensitivity, client grouping, and architecture selection can improve the privacy-utility trade-off. For instance, MS-PAFL reduces noise by injecting it only into the public submodel, improving accuracy under strong privacy guarantees. Similarly, smooth sensitivity for Gini impurity yields higher-accuracy DP rule lists, and GDPFed+ reduces utility loss by grouping clients and optimizing sampling ratios. However, the cost of privacy varies by regime: in differentially private best-arm identification, high-privacy regimes introduce coupled hardness terms, while low-privacy regimes approach non-private bounds. Empirical work on COVID-19 X-ray models shows that stronger DP guarantees only marginally improve practical privacy against membership inference attacks, suggesting that the trade-off may be task-dependent. Additionally, selecting model architectures suited for DP-SGD can reduce fairness disparities without necessarily hurting utility, challenging assumptions that DP always exacerbates unfairness. Overall, the literature indicates that the privacy-performance trade-off is significant but can be managed through careful mechanism design and empirical evaluation.

citations.claim: Federated Learning with DP requires added noise that can substantially degrade model accuracy; MS-PAFL injects calibrated Gaussian noise only into the public submodel to improve the privacy-utility trade-off.

The cost of privacy in best-arm identification has two regimes: in the high-privacy regime hardness depends on a coupled effect of privacy and information-theoretic quantities, while in the low-privacy regime lower bounds reduce to non-private bounds.
Using smooth sensitivity of the Gini impurity instead of global sensitivity yields DP rule lists with higher accuracy for identical privacy budgets.

GDPFed partitions clients by privacy budgets to reduce privacy budget waste and improve utility; GDPFed+ further integrates model sparsification and optimized per-group client sampling ratios to minimize convergence error.

In private COVID-19 detection from X-ray images, increasing DP guarantees only marginally improves empirical privacy against membership inference attacks, indicating a limited practical impact of DP on MIA defense and task-dependent needed privacy levels.

Selecting an optimal model architecture for DP-SGD can cause fairness metric differences across groups to decrease or be negligibly impacted compared to the non-private baseline, challenging the view that DP necessarily exacerbates unfairness.

balanced.summary: The documents collectively cast privacy and model performance as a fundamental trade-off, with differential privacy (DP) noise typically degrading accuracy (doc_1, doc_6, doc_8). Several works propose mechanisms to improve this trade-off: splitting models so noise is confined to public submodels (doc_1), grouping clients and optimizing sampling/sparsification under heterogeneous privacy budgets (doc_8), using smooth sensitivity to scale noise more tightly (doc_6), and deriving sample-complexity lower bounds showing high-privacy regimes are inherently costlier while low-privacy regimes approach non-private performance (doc_3). Empirical work on COVID-19 X-ray classification finds that stronger DP guarantees yield only marginal improvements in practical membership-inference defense, suggesting that task-specific privacy estimation may help tune the trade-off (doc_10). Other studies show that architecture choices for DP-SGD can mitigate negative impacts on fairness (doc_7), and a unified framework for model stealing highlights fundamental utility-privacy tradeoffs in ML models (doc_9). Policy-oriented and measurement-oriented papers further note that deploying DP involves contextual challenges and scalable privacy risk quantification (doc_4, doc_5).

citations.claim: Federated Learning with DP often adds noise that can substantially degrade model accuracy, but model-splitting privacy-amplified federated learning confines calibrated Gaussian noise to a public submodel, significantly reducing noise while preserving utility and achieving a superior privacy-utility trade-off.

For differentially private best-arm identification, lower bounds on sample complexity reveal two privacy regimes: in the high-privacy regime hardness depends on a coupled effect of privacy and information-theoretic quantities, while in the low-privacy regime lower bounds reduce to non-private lower bounds.

Differentially-private mechanisms often cause significant accuracy loss due to added noise, but establishing the smooth sensitivity of the Gini impurity allows DP guarantees with tighter noise, yielding rule lists with higher accuracy than global-sensitivity-based DP for identical privacy budgets.
