Federated Learning with client-level DP suffers utility degradation when enforcing the strictest privacy level across heterogeneous clients; grouping clients by privacy budgets, model sparsification, and optimized per-group client sampling improve model utility while maintaining client-level DP.

In private COVID-19 detection from X-ray images, increasing DP guarantees only marginally improves empirical privacy leakage against membership inference attacks, and DP appears to have limited impact on practical MIA defense, indicating that attack-specific privacy estimation can help achieve better utility-privacy trade-offs.

Selecting a model architecture suited to DP-SGD and optimized for utility can cause fairness metrics across groups to decrease or be negligibly impacted compared to the non-private baseline, challenging the view that differential privacy necessarily exacerbates unfairness.

The Model Privacy framework rigorously formulates model stealing attacks and defenses, quantifies goodness of attack/defense strategies, and analyzes fundamental tradeoffs between utility and privacy in ML models.

Differential privacy is a mathematical definition that can be widely applied when publishing data, but tensions arise when bringing it from theory into practice, so three categories of challenges are identified to help policymakers anticipate deployment impacts.

A systematic refactoring of privacy analyses based on Quantitative Information Flow is flexible, computationally tractable for very large longitudinal datasets, and explainable, as applied to the Brazilian Educational Censuses containing about 50 million individuals.

standard.summary: CNNs and Vision Transformers (ViTs) differ fundamentally in how they process images: CNNs rely on local filters and have an inherent inductive bias, making them efficient and quick to converge with less data, whereas ViTs capture global relationships via self-attention but often overlook fine-grained local details, leading to limited generalization on small datasets (doc_5). Hybrid CNN-ViT architectures have emerged to exploit both local and global image representations, showing exceptional performance across computer vision tasks (doc_1). In direct empirical comparisons, ViTs demonstrate strong performance in general vision tasks, but their alignment with human-like graphical perception is limited compared to CNNs (doc_3). On mobile devices, latency characteristics of ViTs versus CNNs differ substantially; a study measured 190 ViTs and 102 CNNs to identify factors influencing ViT latency (doc_8). Additionally, ViTs are complex and memory-intensive, so compression techniques such as pruning and quantization are needed for resource-constrained environments, with tools like PQV-Mobile achieving significant latency reductions at small accuracy costs (doc_10, doc_9).

citations.claim: ViTs capture global information from the outset but overlook local pixel relationships, lacking inductive bias, while CNNs possess inherent inductive bias from local filters, making them more efficient and quicker to converge than ViT with less data.

Vision transformers can focus on global relationships but may suffer from limited generalization because they do not model local correlation; hybrid CNN-Transformer architectures exploit both local and global image representations and show remarkable results.
ViTs demonstrate strong performance in general vision tasks, but their alignment with human-like graphical perception in the visualization domain is limited compared to CNNs.
A quantitative study of 190 real-world vision transformers on mobile devices compared with 102 CNNs provides insights into factors influencing the latency of ViT architectures on mobile devices.

Vision Transformers are complex and memory-intensive, and combined pruning and quantization tools such as PQV-Mobile can optimize them for mobile applications, e.g., reducing latency by 7.18X with only a 2.24% accuracy loss.

With the adoption of ViT-based architectures and advanced CNNs, model parameters have grown from 62M in AlexNet (2012) to 7B in AIM-7B (2024), creating challenges for embedded systems and necessitating model compression techniques.

balanced.summary: CNNs and vision transformers differ fundamentally in how they process images. CNNs use local filters and possess an inherent inductive bias, making them more efficient and quicker to converge with less data, whereas ViTs capture global context from the outset but overlook local pixel relationships and lack inductive bias, which can hurt generalization on small datasets [doc_5]. ViTs offer large learning capacity by focusing on global relationships, but they may be limited in generalization because they do not model local correlation [doc_1]. Hybrid CNN-transformer architectures aim to combine local and global representations and have demonstrated strong results across vision tasks [doc_1][doc_2]. In controlled graphical perception tasks, ViTs underperform relative to CNNs and humans, indicating limited alignment with human-like perception despite strong general vision performance [doc_3]. A unified comparison of modern image deep networks found that the key difference between attention and convolution lies in their spatial token mixer, and performance differences among token mixers persist even after controlling for network-level and block-level designs [doc_4]. On mobile devices, the inference latency of 190 real-world ViTs was quantitatively compared with 102 CNNs, providing insights into the factors that influence ViT latency and enabling accurate latency prediction [doc_8]. ViTs are complex and memory-intensive, so pruning and quantization tools such as PQV-Mobile can reduce latency by 7.18x with only a 2.24% accuracy loss on a DeiT model [doc_10]. The total parameter count of leading vision backbones has grown from 62M in AlexNet to 7B in AIM-7B, making model compression essential for embedded systems [doc_9]. On the CNN side, spatial transformer networks were designed to help CNNs learn invariance to image transformations, but they generally cannot align feature maps of a transformed image with the original, which is coupled with decreased classification accuracy [doc_6][doc_7].

citations.claim: Vision transformers are a possible substitute to CNNs, offering large learning capacity through global relationships, but they may suffer from limited generalization as they do not model local correlation, prompting hybrid CNN-transformer architectures.
Hybrid CNN-ViT architectures combine vanilla CNN and ViT strengths, exploring synergies that push the boundaries of computer vision.

Although ViTs demonstrate strong performance in general vision tasks, their alignment with human-like graphical perception in the visualization domain is limited compared with CNNs and human participants.

In a unified architecture comparison, the key difference between attention and convolution is their spatial token mixer, and performance differences among token mixers persist even after neutralizing network-level and block-level designs.

CNNs have an inherent inductive bias due to local filters, making them more efficient and quicker to converge than ViTs with less data, while ViTs capture global context but overlook fine-grained local details.

Spatial transformer networks, designed to enable CNNs to learn invariance to image transformations, generally cannot align CNN feature maps of a transformed image with the original, and this inability is coupled with decreased classification accuracy.

STNs do not, in the general case, have the ability to align the feature maps of a transformed image and its original, so parameter sharing between classification and localization networks is advocated.
A quantitative study of 190 real-world ViTs and 102 CNNs on mobile devices provides insights into latency factors and enables accurate prediction of ViT inference latency.
Modern vision backbones including advanced CNNs and ViTs have grown from 62M parameters in AlexNet to 7B parameters in AIM-7B, making model compression essential for embedded systems.
ViTs are replacing CNNs as state-of-the-art but are memory-intensive; a combined pruning and quantization tool reduced latency by 7.18x with only 2.24% accuracy loss on a DeiT model.

standard.summary: Based solely on the provided documents, there is no explicit head-to-head comparison between open source models and proprietary models. The documents address adjacent topics: open-source AI development and licensing, model documentation, and open-vs-proprietary data sources. For instance, one study documents the uncertainties GenAI developers face when documenting models on open-source platforms; another proposes a Contextual Copyleft AI license to extend copyleft from open source training data to generative AI models; a third analyzes the inadequacy of traditional software licenses for ML model publishing and proposes model-specific licenses. The only direct open-vs-proprietary comparison in the documents is in the bibliometrics domain, comparing open metadata with proprietary databases Scopus and Web of Science, not models. Therefore, a direct comparison of open source models versus proprietary models cannot be synthesized from these documents.

citations.claim: GenAI developers on open-source platforms face uncertainties about what content to include in model documentation, how to report key components, and who should take responsibility for documentation.

The Contextual Copyleft AI (CCAI) license extends copyleft requirements from open source training data to resulting generative AI models, enhancing developer control and incentivizing open source AI development, while increasing the risk of direct misuse.

Commonly used software licenses such as GPL and Apache are not clearly defined or bounded for model publishing, and reused ML assets can create license noncompliance risks; the paper introduces ModelGo Licenses as model-specific alternatives.

A large-scale study compared open metadata sources (Crossref, OpenAlex, cOAlition S Journal Checker Tool) with proprietary databases Scopus and Web of Science to estimate hybrid open access impact, finding consistent results despite differences in coverage and metadata quality.

balanced.summary: The documents examine open source models and software from multiple angles, highlighting benefits such as transparency, replicability, and reuse, while also identifying risks and unresolved challenges relative to proprietary alternatives. Open source publishing can be discouraged by demanding good-practice requirements (doc_4), and reuse of open source code increases productivity but also elevates security risks (doc_5). Model-specific licensing remains ambiguous under common software licenses, creating compliance concerns (doc_8), and developers document models under layered uncertainties (doc_1). For generative AI specifically, extended copyleft licensing can incentivize open development and reduce openwashing but requires regulation to mitigate misuse (doc_3). Comparable analyses using open versus proprietary data sources show that combining them yields more robust results than relying on a single source (doc_9). Open source communities are also shaped by shared ideologies and policy-driven licensing choices, which differ from commercial contexts (doc_7, doc_10). Overall, the trade-off between open and proprietary models centers on openness and collaboration versus legal clarity, control, and risk management.

citations.claim: Open source model publication promotes transparency and replicability, but modellers may avoid it because good practices seem demanding.
Reusing open source code improves productivity and quality, but high technical leverage increases vulnerability exposure by 4-7x.
Commonly used licenses like GPL and Apache are software-specific and not clearly defined for model publishing, posing risks of noncompliance and rights infringement.
Developers of GenAI models on open-source platforms face uncertainties about documentation content, how to report components, and who is responsible.

A Contextual Copyleft AI license can extend copyleft from training data to generative AI models, enhancing developer control and mitigating openwashing, but requires complementary regulation due to increased misuse risk.
Open metadata and proprietary databases show strong correlations in measuring hybrid open access, and combining multiple sources provides a more robust understanding than any single source.
Open source development is a social movement in which shared ideologies play critical roles, shaping thoughts, actions, and interactions.
Open data licensing terms reflect policy considerations different from business transactions, and governments should choose licenses according to their IP regimes and policy goals.

standard.summary: The documents frame planning and reactive agent behavior as complementary paradigms with distinct trade-offs. Classical planning and model-based agents require precise, complete models and can fail in novel or uncertain environments, whereas reactive, model-free methods can act without such models but often lack explicit, interpretable abstractions. Rather than viewing them as strictly opposed, several works propose hybrid architectures: HYDRA augments model-based planning with closed-loop execution and novelty detection; Dyna-H incorporates heuristic planning into a model-free online reinforcement learning agent; an open-ended learning system integrates deep reinforcement learning with PPDDL planning; and neuro-symbolic integration combines generative LLMs with symbolic planners. This points toward designs that balance deliberative foresight with reactive responsiveness.

citations.claim: Classical search algorithms such as A* rely on precise and complete models of the search space, whereas model-free methods for sequential decision making under uncertainty are the best choice when such models are not possible.

Model-based reasoning agents are ill-equipped to act in novel situations in which their model of the environment no longer sufficiently represents the world, motivating mechanisms to detect and adapt to environment changes.

Deep reinforcement learning is effective for learning policies in low-level state spaces, but there is still a need for abstraction to understand the knowledge collected by the agent, which classical planning formalisms can provide.

The proposed Dyna-H algorithm incorporates heuristic planning into a model-free online reinforcement learning agent, combining heuristic-search path-finding with the advantages of model-free online learning.
HYDRA augments the PDDL+ planning module with visual reasoning, task selection, and action execution modules for closed-loop interaction with complex environments.

The true potential of LLMs unfolds when they are integrated with traditional symbolic planners, pointing towards a promising neuro-symbolic approach that combines generative aspects with the precision of classical planning methods.

In decentralized scenarios, each agent acts individually relying only on local observations/communications and is free to move in arbitrary direction at any time, choosing actions that balance progressing along paths and avoiding collisions.

balanced.summary: The documents highlight a trade-off between model-based planning and reactive, model-free agents. Planning approaches provide explicit, goal-directed, and verifiable behavior for single- and multi-agent settings, e.g., via epistemic planning or decomposition of LTL specifications, but they often assume accurate or complete models and can struggle in novel or uncertain environments. Reactive or model-free agents act from local observations, learned policies, and online interaction, which makes them suitable when models are unavailable, but they lack the explicit high-level abstraction that planning offers. Several works therefore advocate hybrid architectures that combine planning with learning or language models to leverage both adaptivity and structured knowledge.

citations.claim: Epistemic planning using functional STRIPS delegates reasoning about epistemic formulas to external solvers, avoiding exponential pre-compilation and scaling better than a state-of-the-art planner.

Deep reinforcement learning agents learn policies in low-level state spaces without given goals, while classical planning formalisms are used to explicitly represent acquired knowledge and reach extrinsic goals.

Centralized multi-agent planning under LTL specifications is computationally complex, so the proposed procedure decouples the planning into a decentralized phase and a synchronized phase using compact representations.

In decentralized unlabeled navigation, each agent acts individually relying only on local observations/communications, choosing actions that balance progress along paths and collision avoidance without a centralized planner.

Model-based reasoning agents are ill-equipped to act in novel situations where their model no longer sufficiently represents the world, motivating the HYDRA framework to detect, understand, and adapt to environmental evolution.

The true potential of large language models unfolds when they are integrated with traditional symbolic planners, pointing toward a neuro-symbolic approach that combines generative LLMs with the precision of classical planning.

Classical search algorithms such as A* rely on precise and complete models of the search space, and when such models are unavailable, model-free methods for sequential decision making under uncertainty are the best choice.

standard.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) and pruning are both model compression techniques, but they operate differently: KD transfers knowledge from a larger teacher model to a compact student model (doc_1, doc_3), while pruning reduces network complexity directly. In the provided literature, pruning is often used in conjunction with KD rather than as an alternative. For example, R2KD leverages both correlation distance and network pruning to improve KD performance with data augmentation (doc_2), and ShiftKD analyzes pruning methods as a key factor in the student training process under distribution shift (doc_4). Thus, the comparison highlights that KD focuses on knowledge transfer, whereas pruning targets structural simplification, and they can be combined for better compression and robustness.

citations.claim: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network.
Knowledge Distillation (KD) has emerged as an effective model compression technique in deep learning, enabling the transfer of knowledge from a large teacher model to a compact student model.
We propose a Robustness-Reinforced Knowledge Distillation (R2KD) that leverages correlation distance and network pruning.
We thoroughly analyze key factors in student model training process, including data augmentation, pruning methods, optimizers, and evaluation metrics.

balanced.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) and pruning are both model compression techniques, but they operate differently: KD compresses by training a smaller student to mimic a larger teacher's soft outputs (doc_1), while pruning directly removes parts of a model to reduce its size and computational cost (as used in network pruning within KD methods, doc_2). The two approaches are often complementary: R2KD integrates network pruning to enhance KD (doc_2), and the ShiftKD benchmark treats pruning as a key factor in KD training under distribution shift (doc_4). Progressive knowledge distillation further shows that a teacher can be distilled into a series of smaller students, achieving large FLOP reductions while retaining accuracy (doc_6). However, conventional KD has drawbacks such as dependence on a pre-trained teacher (doc_8), and its success depends on factors like teacher calibration (doc_3) and effective logit utilization (doc_5, doc_10). KD also serves federated learning, where it addresses limitations of parameter averaging (doc_7). Meanwhile, 'pruning' appears in other domains, such as knowledge graphs, where it means extracting relevant subgraphs (doc_9). Overall, KD and pruning are distinct yet synergistic compression strategies.

citations.claim: Knowledge distillation trains a student network using the soft output from a teacher and is a successful method for model compression and knowledge transfer.
The proposed R2KD leverages correlation distance and network pruning to improve knowledge distillation, enabling effective use of data augmentation.
There is a strong correlation between the teacher's calibration error and the student's accuracy, making teacher calibration an important factor for effective KD.
The ShiftKD framework benchmarks KD under distribution shift and analyzes key factors including pruning methods, data augmentation, optimizers, and evaluation metrics.
Swapped logit distillation addresses wrong predictions in logit-based KD by swapping logits and using bi-level teacher alignment.
Progressive knowledge distillation with Mamba blocks distills a large teacher into progressively smaller students, reducing FLOPs while maintaining accuracy.
Federated adaptations of knowledge distillation solve or mitigate weaknesses of parameter-averaging FL algorithms, such as model homogeneity and high communication costs.
Conventional KD relies on pre-trained high-capacity teachers, introducing memory/storage and training costs, while the proposed self-distillation avoids these via intra-class patch swap augmentation.
KGPrune applies analogical pruning to extract subgraphs of interest from Wikidata, showing pruning is also used in knowledge graph contexts.
Dual-head knowledge distillation partitions the linear classifier to exploit logits information without performance degeneration from combining logit-level and probability-level losses.

standard.summary: Cloud computing provides on-demand access to powerful storage and computing, scalability, high availability, and cost effectiveness, but its centralized model introduces latency, network congestion, and rising data-transfer costs as IoT data grows. Edge computing complements cloud by processing data near its source, reducing latency, bandwidth usage, cloud resource requirements, and communication energy while enabling real-time analytics. However, edge platforms face resource constraints, security vulnerabilities, and scalability challenges. Modern systems therefore often distribute workloads across a cloud-to-edge continuum to balance latency, load, and energy.

citations.claim: Cloud computing offers powerful computing and storage, high availability and security, instant accessibility, guaranteed scalability, interoperability, and cost/time effectiveness following a pay-as-you-go method.

Cloud computing offers advantages including mobility, flexibility, and scalability but introduces challenges such as latency; fog and edge computing are complementary solutions that bring services closer to users and bridge the gap.

With rapid data increase, sending all data to the cloud via the Internet becomes more expensive and required cloud computing resources become larger; edge computing processes data before sending it to the cloud, effectively reducing data transmitted and cloud resources required.

Traditional cloud-based ML frameworks face latency and bandwidth constraints, and cloud computing struggles with increased latency and network congestion; strategically distributing ML tasks across Things, Edge, and Cloud layers enables real-time processing at the point of data generation, significantly reducing latency and optimizing network traffic.

Computational resources placed at different points in the edge-cloud continuum affect responsiveness and the energy spent during communications; the edge is favorable in terms of energy consumption compared to more remote locations.

Edge AI processes data in close communication with the location where data is captured, aiming to optimize data processing efficiency and velocity while ensuring data confidentiality and integrity; challenges include constraints on resources, security threats, and scalability problems.

Edge computing brings low-latency and bandwidth-intensive applications close to end-users, but edge computing platforms still face challenges related to resource constraints, connectivity, and security.

balanced.summary: Cloud computing centralizes data storage and processing in remote data centers, offering scalable, flexible, pay-as-you-go services, but it introduces latency, bandwidth, and resource challenges for IoT and real-time applications. Edge computing addresses these issues by moving computation closer to the data source, reducing latency, network traffic, cloud load, and often energy consumption. The two paradigms are largely complementary: many proposed architectures distribute workloads across the cloud-to-edge continuum, with edge handling real-time tasks and cloud providing backend support.

citations.claim: Cloud computing provides powerful computing and storage, high availability, security, scalability, and pay-as-you-go access without needing a physical environment.
Cloud computing offers advantages such as mobility, flexibility, and scalability, but introduces latency; fog and edge computing emerge as complementary solutions that bring services closer to users.

In a cloud environment all data analysis is done in the cloud, which becomes expensive as data volume grows; edge computing processes data before sending it to the cloud, reducing internet transmission and required cloud resources, and lowers latency by more than 50% for two-dimensional data.

Traditional cloud-based ML frameworks face latency and network congestion; the InTec framework distributes ML tasks across the Things, Edge, and Cloud layers, achieving an 81.56% reduction in response time, a 10.92% decrease in network traffic, and a 9.82% improvement in throughput.
In the edge-cloud continuum, edge locations are more favorable in terms of smartphone communication energy consumption compared to more remote cloud locations.

Edge AI processes and analyzes data in close communication with where data is captured, aiming to optimize data processing efficiency and velocity, but faces challenges such as resource constraints, security threats, and scalability.
With rapid cloud adoption and exponential growth of IoT devices, there is a critical need to develop secure and efficient edge-to-cloud architectures that leverage both cloud and edge assets.
Edge computing brings low-latency and bandwidth-intensive applications close to end-users, but edge platforms still face challenges related to resource constraints, connectivity, and security.
Cloud computing, fog computing, and edge computing are emerging paradigms that provide new economic and creative potential for the evolution of computing systems.

standard.summary: Dense retrieval uses learned high-dimensional embeddings and approximate nearest-neighbor search, offering strong effectiveness at higher latency, while sparse retrieval methods (e.g., BM25, learned sparse representations) exploit lexical overlap and inverted indexes for high efficiency. Learned sparse retrieval (LSR) combines pretrained-language-model encoding with sparse bags of words to improve effectiveness over lexical methods while retaining inverted-index efficiency. Sparse and dense approaches capture complementary relevance signals, and techniques such as approximate indexes, inference-free sparse retrieval, and pruning attempt to balance effectiveness and efficiency. Trade-offs between retrieval quality and computational cost are a central theme, with sparse methods generally faster but potentially less effective, and dense methods more effective but slower.

citations.claim: Sparse retrieval methods like BM25 are based on lexical overlap and use inverted indices for high retrieval efficiency, whereas dense retrieval methods use learned dense vectors and are effective but comparatively slow.

Learned Sparse Retrieval (LSR) exploits pre-trained language models for encoding text into a learned bag of words, and sparsity is key to enabling a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness of the query processor.

Sparse retrieval has developed a branch of inference-free retrieval where documents are encoded during indexing time with no model-inference for queries, and there is a trade-off between retrieval effectiveness and computational efficiency.

Learned sparse representations form an effective and interpretable class of embeddings for text retrieval, but exact top-k retrieval over such embeddings faces efficiency challenges, motivating approximate retrieval algorithms.
Learned dense representations encode queries and documents using high-dimensional embeddings, which enable retrieval by performing approximate k nearest-neighbors search (A-kNN).
Late-interaction models such as ColBERT require storing a dense embedding for each document token, leading to a substantial index storage overhead.

balanced.summary: Dense and sparse retrieval represent contrasting approaches: sparse methods rely on lexical overlap and inverted indexes for high efficiency, while dense methods use learned embeddings for effectiveness but incur higher computational cost. Learned sparse retrieval (LSR) combines strengths by producing sparse, interpretable neural representations, with regularization controlling the effectiveness/efficiency balance. Recent work improves sparse retrieval via inference-free encoding, approximate query processing, and hybrid lexical/graph ranking, while dense retrieval research targets efficiency through approximate kNN search and index compression. Both families can also be integrated into shared pipelines, and their performance-efficiency trade-offs are actively studied.

citations.claim: Sparse retrieval models can be inference-free, with documents encoded at indexing time and no model inference for queries; l0-inspired sparsification achieves state-of-the-art BEIR performance among inference-free sparse models and reveals effectiveness/efficiency trade-offs.

Learned Sparse Retrieval (LSR) can be adapted to long documents by aggregating segments, with the first segment consistently dominating retrieval performance; ExactSDM and SoftSDM are re-evaluated across varying document lengths.

In learned sparse retrieval, regularization can be relaxed to produce more effective encoders, and query encoding is the main bottleneck; Li-LSR makes query encoding a table lookup, surpassing Splade-v3-Doc by 1 point of mRR@10 on MS MARCO and 1.8 points of nDCG@10 on BEIR.

Sparse retrieval like BM25 relies on lexical overlap and inverted indices for high efficiency, while dense retrieval uses learned dense vectors and is effective but comparatively slow; LexBoost combines lexical scores with dense-neighbor scores to improve ranking with little overhead.
Dense retrieval uses high-dimensional embeddings and approximate kNN search; early exit strategies based on patience can provide up to 5x speedups in A-kNN with negligible effectiveness losses.

Late-interaction dense models such as ColBERT store a dense embedding for each document token, causing high index storage overhead; Voronoi-cell-based token pruning retains retrieval quality while reducing index size.
Retrieval pipelines can combine sparse, learned-sparse, and dense retrievers within a declarative architecture, demonstrating that both retrieval families remain useful in practical systems.

Learned sparse representations are effective and interpretable but exact top-k retrieval faces efficiency challenges; SeismicWave uses clustered inverted indexes and kNN graphs to reach almost-exact accuracy and is up to 2.2x faster than Seismic.

standard.summary: Graph databases and SQL/relational systems differ fundamentally in schema handling and query capabilities. Relational systems commonly rely on declared schemas and SQL, while NoSQL/graph systems are often schema-on-read, making schema extraction and querying necessary (doc_6). Graph databases optimize connected data with purpose-built engines and languages such as Neo4j/Cypher (doc_1, doc_10) and TigerGraph/GSQL, which can be extended for hybrid vector search (doc_4). Researchers have also sought to bridge the two worlds: U-Schema/SkiQL enables platform-independent schema query across NoSQL and relational models (doc_6), categorical query languages cover multi-model relational-plus-graph data (doc_7), and RDB2RDF views publish legacy SQL data into knowledge graphs (doc_8). Benchmark studies show the choice among graph, document, and multi-model systems depends on graph connectivity, scale, and semantic richness (doc_5). Moreover, relational schemata can be represented in both SQL and graph formats (doc_3).

citations.claim: Most NoSQL systems are schema-on-read: data can be stored without first having to declare a schema, so schemas are implicit in data and code.
VisualNeo is a visual query interface system built upon Neo4j that facilitates efficient subgraph query in large graph databases, performing query processing through the Neo4j driver.
Cypher4BIM is a graph query language tailored for IFC-Graph, built by investigating the graph query language Cypher.
TigerVector extends TigerGraph's graph query language GSQL with vector type expressions to enable query compositions between vector search results and graph query blocks.
SkiQL, designed on the U-Schema unified data model, provides a platform-independent schema query service for querying NoSQL and relational schemas.
Categorical calculus and categorical algebra extend relational calculus and relational algebra to query multi-model databases that store relational, hierarchical, and graph data simultaneously.
To make legacy relational data sources accessible through an enterprise knowledge graph, an RDB2RDF view of the underlying relational data must be created and maintained.

The paper presents a KG-specific benchmarking framework using connectivity density, scale, and Semantic Richness to compare Document-Oriented, Graph, and Multi-Model DBMSs for knowledge graph processing.
SchemaDB contains 2,500 samples of relational schemata in both SQL and graph formats.

balanced.summary: The documents present SQL/relational and graph databases as distinct data models with different query paradigms, but also show increasing convergence. Relational data are standardized in SQL schemas, and can be represented in graph formats (doc_3) or exposed as RDF via RDB2RDF views for enterprise knowledge graphs (doc_8). Graph databases use dedicated query languages such as Cypher (doc_10) and GraphQL (doc_2), and support visual interfaces (doc_1), vector search (doc_4), and graph machine learning (doc_9). Unified schema languages and categorical algebras aim to bridge relational and NoSQL/graph models (doc_6, doc_7). Benchmarking shows that the best NoSQL paradigm, including graph versus document or multi-model, depends on workload characteristics such as connectivity and semantic richness (doc_5).

citations.claim: VisualNeo is a visual query interface built on Neo4j that facilitates efficient subgraph querying in large graph databases, illustrating graph-database-specific tooling.
A native multi-way left-join algorithm allows GraphQL queries to be executed directly over RDF graphs, outperforming a state-of-the-art graph storage solution for GraphQL in runtime and scalability.

SchemaDB contains 2,500 relational database schemata standardized to MySQL syntax and also provides them in graph formats, showing that the same schemas can be represented in both SQL and graph forms.
TigerVector extends TigerGraph's vertex attributes with embeddings and integrates vector search with graph query, outperforming Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, and Milvus in hybrid search.

A KG-specific benchmarking framework reveals performance crossover points across Document-Oriented, Graph, and Multi-Model DBMSs, so paradigm selection should align with graph size, connectivity, and semantic richness.

SkiQL, based on the U-Schema unified model, provides a platform-independent schema query service over NoSQL and relational schemas, making it possible to query and explore schemas across paradigms including graph.

Categorical calculus and categorical algebra extend relational calculus and algebra to multi-model databases, supporting relational, hierarchical, and graph data in a single formal framework with query equivalence.
Legacy relational databases can be made accessible in an enterprise knowledge graph by creating and incrementally maintaining a materialized RDB2RDF view of the relational data.

Graph database and graph machine learning pipelines may rely on incomplete knowledge graphs; incorporating a knowledge completion phase reveals hidden knowledge and changes dataset behavior and metrics.

A tailored graph query language called Cypher4BIM was developed for IFC-Graph and can query individual instances and complex relationships such as spatial structure, space boundary, and space accessibility.

standard.summary: Rule-based systems and machine learning are often contrasted on interpretability versus predictive power. Rule-based models are human-understandable and widely used as surrogate explainers for non-interpretable black-box machine learning models (doc_8), but they can suffer from interpretability issues, e.g., fuzzy rule-based classifiers with complex fuzzy partitions (doc_2), and from inference schemes that may overfit training data in learning fuzzy-classifier systems (doc_4). Machine learning models are frequently black boxes, and their practice is prone to methodological pitfalls unless rigorous evaluation and comparison are followed (doc_9). Hybrid and neurosymbolic approaches attempt to combine the strengths of both, integrating deep learning with rules (doc_1) and modeling human interaction with ML systems (doc_7). Thus, the choice between rule-based systems and machine learning involves trade-offs in transparency, robustness, and adaptability.

citations.claim: Rule-based models offer a human-understandable representation, i.e. they are interpretable, and are used to explain the decisions of non-interpretable black-box models.
Rule-based systems are a popular form of explainable AI, but fuzzy rule-based classifiers can be hard to interpret because fuzzy partitions are not always easy to interpret.

Conventional voting-based and single-winner-based inference schemes in learning fuzzy-classifier systems rely on classification performance on training data and may not perform well on unseen data, risking overfitting.
Mistakes in machine learning practice are commonplace, and a guide is needed to avoid pitfalls across the five stages of the machine learning process.
Neurosymbolic methods cover topics such as the integration of deep learning with rules, the use of embeddings for rule learning, and the application of large language models in rule learning.
Hybrid Decision Making Systems provide a taxonomy and framework for understanding how computer science literature models interaction between humans and machine learning systems.

balanced.summary: Rule-based systems and machine learning are often contrasted in terms of interpretability versus predictive power, but many approaches integrate them. Rule-based systems are a popular form of explainable AI, especially fuzzy rule-based classifiers, though their interpretability can be hindered by fuzzy partitions [doc_2]. They are also used as surrogate models to explain black-box ML models, with methods to ensure decision consistency [doc_8] and to explain differences between models [doc_10]. Conversely, ML methods face pitfalls in practice, requiring rigorous methodology [doc_9], and hybrid decision-making systems model human-ML interaction [doc_7]. Neurosymbolic methods combine deep learning with rules for rule mining [doc_1]. In learning fuzzy-classifier systems, improvements such as Dempster-Shafer-based class inference handle uncertainty better than voting-based schemes [doc_4], and self-adaptive rule representations improve robustness [doc_5]. Conformal prediction and rule-based classifiers can together provide reliability guarantees [doc_3]. Finally, a regulatory analogy distinguishes rule-based and principle-based approaches, recommending a mix for frontier AI [doc_6]. Overall, rather than a strict dichotomy, rule-based and ML approaches complement each other.

citations.claim: Rule mining methodologies include inductive logic programming, path sampling and generalization, and linear programming, and neurosymbolic methods integrate deep learning with rules, use embeddings for rule learning, and apply large language models in rule learning.

Fuzzy rule-based classifiers can be reduced to crisp rule-based classifiers, which helps practitioners understand how fuzzy rule bases partition feature space and how one system can be translated to another.

CONFIDERAI defines a new score function for rule-based classifiers that leverages rules' predictive ability, the geometrical position of points within rule boundaries, and overlaps among rules, adding conformity as a sixth pillar for trustworthy AI.

Learning Fuzzy-Classifier Systems typically use voting-based or single-winner inference schemes that may overfit, whereas a proposed Dempster-Shafer theory-based class inference scheme handles uncertainty well and improves test macro F1 scores across real-world datasets.

Adaptive-UCS introduces a fuzzy indicator as a new rule parameter that sets membership functions to either crisp rectangular or fuzzy triangular shapes, allowing self-adaptation of rule representations and improving classification accuracy and robustness to noise and missing values.

Rule-based regulation provides certainty and enforceability but can quickly become outdated and lead to box-ticking, while principle-based regulation is adaptable but less certain; a mix that starts with principles and becomes more rule-based over time is recommended for frontier AI.

A taxonomy of Hybrid Decision Making Systems provides both a conceptual and technical framework for understanding how current computer science literature models interactions between humans and machine learning systems.

Rule-based surrogate models used to explain black-box models can be fused with XAI-based feature importance to ensure the rule-based model makes decisions consistently with the black box it approximates.

A guide for academic researchers outlines common machine learning pitfalls across five stages: what to do before model building, how to reliably build models, how to robustly evaluate models, how to compare models fairly, and how to report results.

DeltaXplainer is a model-agnostic method for generating rule-based explanations describing the differences between two binary classifiers, which is useful for model selection, monitoring, and lifecycle management.

standard.summary: Documents show that although modern LLMs advertise large context windows, their maximum effective context is often far smaller and varies by task; e.g., models can fail with ~100 tokens and degrade severely by 1000 tokens, while effective context collapses with realistic distractors. Retrieval-augmented generation remains useful, but simple single-stage retrieval can match complex pipelines, and cache-augmented generation can replace retrieval entirely for small, preloadable knowledge bases. Long-context LLMs also show robust performance in NL2SQL with rich context, indicating the choice depends on task, data scale, and complexity.

citations.claim: Maximum Effective Context Window is drastically smaller than reported Maximum Context Window; all models fell far short by as much as 99 percent, with failures at as little as 100 tokens.
Evidence retrieval evaluation shows effective context window is much smaller with realistic distractors, already crumbling at 128 clauses.
A simple retrieve-then-read baseline (DOS RAG) matches or outperforms more intricate multi-stage RAG pipelines on long-context QA benchmarks under matched token budgets.

Cache-augmented generation (CAG) preloads relevant documents into the LLM's extended context and eliminates retrieval latency and retrieval errors for limited, manageable knowledge bases, achieving comparable or superior results.
Google's gemini-1.5-pro long-context LLM is robust to extended contextual information and achieves strong NL2SQL performance without finetuning and expensive self-consistency based techniques.

balanced.summary: Large context windows and retrieval are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Benchmarks show advertised context sizes overstate usable context: [doc_1] found maximum effective context falls far below reported maximum, with severe degradation by 1,000 tokens and variation by problem type. [doc_6] similarly found long-context reasoning collapses when distractors are realistic. In constrained settings, however, long-context approaches can replace retrieval: [doc_2] shows cache-augmented generation preloads all relevant documents and avoids retrieval latency/errors; [doc_5] shows a long-context LLM is robust for NL2SQL with rich context. For larger or dynamic corpora, retrieval remains valuable: [doc_3] shows a simple retrieve-then-read baseline matches or beats complex RAG pipelines, and [doc_8] uses retrieval to handle images exceeding token limits; [doc_9] shows chunking quality determines RAG effectiveness. [doc_4] highlights that retrieval itself is hard for long documents, with early segments dominating scores. [doc_10] suggests model scale reshapes context sensitivity, making larger models more resistant to false claims but more prone to copying irrelevant tokens. Overall, retrieval should be used when context is too large, noisy, or dynamic, while long context is preferable for small curated knowledge bases; simple retrieval baselines should be the default for evaluation.

citations.claim: Models' maximum effective context window is drastically smaller than reported maximum context window, with severe accuracy degradation by 1,000 tokens and variation by problem type.
Cache-augmented generation preloads relevant documents into the LLM's extended context and avoids retrieval latency and retrieval errors, matching or outperforming RAG for limited knowledge bases.
A simple retrieve-then-read baseline (DOS RAG) consistently matches or outperforms more complex multi-stage RAG pipelines under matched token budgets.
Retrieval adaptation for long documents is challenging; the first segment of a document consistently dominates retrieval performance across methods.
Long-context LLMs are robust and do not get lost in extended contextual information, achieving strong NL2SQL performance without fine-tuning or expensive self-consistency techniques.
The effective context window is much smaller when realistic distractors are present, with performance already crumbling at 128 clauses in a long-context reasoning task.
ImageRAG uses retrieval-augmented generation to selectively retrieve relevant portions of ultra-high-resolution images, allowing models to handle inputs that exceed token limits.
Chunking strategy is a key determinant of RAG effectiveness; structure-aware chunking yields higher retrieval effectiveness and lower computational cost on enterprise documents.
Scaling reshapes context sensitivity: larger models become more resistant to counterfactual misinformation but more prone to copying irrelevant tokens from context.

standard.summary: Reasoning-focused LLMs (e.g., OpenAI o3, DeepSeek-R1) are built with techniques such as inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, supervised fine-tuning, and distillation to improve multi-step reasoning [doc_10]. However, controlled comparisons suggest they do not consistently outperform standard LLMs in genuine reasoning: when multiple-choice questions are altered to remove memorization cues, accuracy falls sharply across all models, and the most accurate model (OpenAI-o3-mini) is not the most robust (DeepSeek-R1-70B), implying standard benchmark success does not guarantee reasoning ability [doc_2]. In hierarchical legal reasoning, reasoning LLMs achieve high accuracy on surface-level tasks but degrade on hierarchical reasoning and collapse on integrated analysis (Task 3: 11.46%-33.99%), while spending more computation on incorrect responses, so 'thinking longer' is not always 'thinking smarter' [doc_9]. Likewise, LLMs can match or surpass SOTA in argumentative reasoning under certain I/O abstractions, yet small human-readable alterations reveal they are not actually performing reasoning [doc_4]. This raises broader questions about whether LLMs are becoming formal reasoning mechanisms or simply emulating reasoning, and whether they genuinely represent logical state or rely on memorization [doc_1][doc_3]. Overall, reasoning models push benchmark performance, but robustness, memorization, and genuine reasoning remain open challenges [doc_2][doc_9].

citations.claim: Recent reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI o1 and o3, GPT-4o, Qwen-32B, and various Llama variants enhance reasoning via inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, supervised fine-tuning, and distillation.

When multiple-choice questions are varied to dissociate the correct answer from previously seen tokens, all models experience remarkable accuracy drops (average 57% on MMLU), and the most accurate model (OpenAI-o3-mini) is not the most robust (DeepSeek-R1-70B), suggesting that the best models in standard evaluations may not be the ones with better reasoning capabilities.

Modern reasoning LLMs achieve high accuracy on surface-level reasoning (Task 1), degrade on hierarchical reasoning (Task 2: 64.82%-92.09%), and collapse on integrated analysis (Task 3: 11.46%-33.99%); they also consistently expend more computational resources on incorrect responses than correct ones, suggesting that 'thinking longer' does not always mean 'thinking smarter.'

LLMs match or surpass SOTA in argument mining and argument pair extraction under certain I/O abstractions, but statistical analysis of small, human-readable alterations in I/O representations shows that the models are not performing reasoning.

Syllogistic reasoning is not a uniform emergent property across LLMs; perfect symbolic performances in certain models make us wonder whether LLMs are becoming more and more formal reasoning mechanisms rather than making explicit the nuances of human reasoning.

Despite parallels between programming and proof construction, advances in formalized mathematics have proven significantly more challenging, raising fundamental questions about whether LLMs genuinely represent or merely emulate a notion of evolving logical state.

balanced.summary: The documents collectively compare reasoning-specialized LLMs (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI o1/o3, Qwen) with standard LLMs by testing robustness, memorization, and complex reasoning. When multiple-choice questions are altered to prevent token memorization, all models drop markedly in accuracy, and the most accurate model (OpenAI-o3-mini) is less robust than DeepSeek-R1-70B, indicating standard benchmark accuracy does not equal reasoning ability. In hierarchical legal reasoning, reasoning LLMs excel at surface-level tasks but collapse on integrated analysis and spend more compute on wrong answers, so 'thinking longer' is not 'thinking smarter.' Syllogistic reasoning is not a uniform emergent property across LLMs, some models showing perfect symbolic performance while others fail. LLMs can match SOTA in argumentative reasoning, yet small abstraction changes reveal they are not actually reasoning. Formalized mathematics remains brittle despite coding success, raising questions about genuine deductive state. Recent reasoning models have improved via inference-time scaling, RL, CoT, and distillation, but open problems remain. Current LLM-powered reasoning tools are ad hoc, and a principled neurosymbolic model is proposed to combine neural intuition with symbolic guarantees.

citations.claim: When multiple-choice questions are varied to dissociate correct answers from previously seen tokens, all tested LLMs drop markedly in accuracy (average 57% on MMLU, 50% on UNED-Access 2024), and the most accurate model (OpenAI-o3-mini) was not the most robust (DeepSeek-R1-70B), showing standard evaluation accuracy does not necessarily reflect reasoning ability.

In hierarchical legal reasoning, reasoning LLMs achieve high accuracy on surface-level reasoning but degrade on hierarchical reasoning (64.82%-92.09%) and collapse on integrated analysis (11.46%-33.99%), and they spend more computation on incorrect responses, indicating 'thinking longer' does not mean 'thinking smarter.'

Syllogistic reasoning is not a uniform emergent property across 14 LLMs: some models show perfect symbolic performance while others do not, raising questions about whether LLMs are becoming formal reasoning mechanisms or reproducing human reasoning nuances.

Although LLMs match or surpass SOTA in argument mining and argument pair extraction, small human-readable changes to input/output representations (e.g., BIO tags vs line numbers) reveal via statistical analysis that the models are not performing reasoning, so applications like data labelling must be cautious.

Despite apparent parallels between coding and proof construction, advances in formalized mathematics with LLMs have proven more challenging, raising questions about whether LLMs genuinely represent or merely emulate an evolving logical state.

Recent reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI o1/o3, GPT-4o, Qwen-32B, and Llama variants have enhanced reasoning via inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, supervised fine-tuning, and distillation; open problems include multi-step reasoning without human supervision and robustness in chained task execution.

LLMs can be elicited to produce logic programs such as propositional Horn clauses, Dual Horn clauses, relational triplets, and Definite Clause Grammars, enabling sound reasoning methods and verification of LLM output alignment.

Current practices for building LLM-powered automated reasoning tools are ad hoc and lack strong symbolic guarantees; the proposed Neurosymbolic Transition Systems pair symbolic state with intuition to scale logical reasoning while retaining guarantees.

standard.summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) and transformers are both effective for graph-structured data, with graph transformers integrating graph inductive biases and attention into the transformer architecture [doc_1], while GNNs operate via message passing on node/edge attributes [doc_2]. Comparisons show trade-offs: a custom GNN outperformed a transformer in geometric reasoning and was easier to scale [doc_3], whereas a purely attention-based (transformer-style) encoder outperformed message-passing GNNs and previous transformer methods across many tasks and scaled better [doc_4]. GNNs face issues like over-smoothing, over-squashing, and over-dilution, which transformer-based mechanisms can mitigate [doc_7]; hybrid approaches also combine GNNs and graph transformers for applications such as brain-network classification [doc_10].

citations.claim: Graph transformers integrate graph inductive biases and graph attention mechanisms into the transformer architecture.
Graph neural networks are deep neural networks designed for graphs with attributes attached to nodes or edges.
A Graph Neural Network designed for a geometric reasoning task performed significantly better than a Transformer and was easier to scale.

A purely attention-based approach outperformed message passing baselines and transformer-based methods on more than 70 node and graph-level tasks, and scaled much better than alternatives with similar performance.
Graph neural networks suffer from over-smoothing and over-squashing, and the paper introduces a transformer-based solution that alleviates over-dilution.
A model integrating graph contrastive learning and graph transformers outperforms existing approaches in brain network classification.

balanced.summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) and transformers are both effective for graph-structured data, but they differ in inductive biases and trade-offs. GNNs leverage message passing and graph structure, achieving strong performance across many tasks but struggling with oversmoothing, oversquashing, and over-dilution. Graph transformers integrate attention mechanisms and graph inductive biases, often performing competitively, but face scalability, preprocessing, and interpretability challenges. Empirical results are context-dependent: a purpose-built GNN outperformed a transformer in geometric reasoning, while an attention-based edge-centric approach outperformed message-passing and transformer baselines across numerous benchmarks. Applications span power flow optimization, time series forecasting, and brain network classification, with hybrid GNN-transformer models proving effective. Ongoing research addresses expressive power, robustness to perturbations, and scalability.

citations.claim: Graph transformers integrate graph inductive biases and attention mechanisms, showing strong performance and versatility across graph tasks, while facing challenges such as scalability, interpretability, and dynamic graphs.

Graph neural networks are deep neural networks for graphs with node/edge attributes, achieving impressive performance on a broad range of tasks but exhibiting issues such as oversmoothing and oversquashing.
In a geometric reasoning task, both a GNN and a transformer could predict spatial positions from constraints, but the GNN performed significantly better and was easier to scale.

A purely attention-based edge-centric approach outperformed fine-tuned message passing baselines and transformer-based methods on more than 70 node and graph-level tasks and scaled much better than alternatives with similar performance.

Graph neural networks allow natural use of machine learning on graph-structured power networks, leading to a Proximal Policy Optimization architecture with GNNs for optimal power flow that generalizes to unseen scenarios.

Graph deep learning methods, especially spatiotemporal graph neural networks, leverage pairwise relationships to train global forecasting models on collections of correlated time series while localizing predictions per node.
Message passing neural networks suffer from over-smoothing, over-squashing, and over-dilution; a transformer-based solution was introduced to alleviate over-dilution.
Research on GNN expressive power characterizes limitations via graph isomorphism, subgraph counting, and connectivity, with enhancement categories of feature, topology, and architecture.
Graph convolutional neural networks exhibit a linear relationship between graph shift operator perturbations and output differences, with stability in single-layer GCNNs when GSO errors are bounded.

A hybrid model integrating graph contrastive learning with a dual-domain graph transformer overcame data scarcity and insufficient supervision in brain network classification, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.

standard.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) extend language models (LMs) by adding visual perception, allowing them to process images alongside text. While LMs are initially trained solely on linguistic data, VLMs adapt LM architectures to multimodal tasks; analyses reveal specialized attention heads that focus on visual tokens, helping explain how LMs bridge textual and visual understanding. However, VLMs face challenges such as weak grounding of predictions in visual features, unstable inference, and sycophancy from leading prompts. Domain-specific applications, like radiology report generation, show that language-specific and domain-specific training substantially improve VLM performance, underscoring the importance of adaptation. Overall, VLMs build on LM foundations but require additional considerations for visual grounding, reliability, and domain alignment.

citations.claim: Language models, initially trained solely on linguistic data, can effectively interpret and process visual content, with a unique class of attention heads focusing specifically on visual tokens in multimodal models.

Vision-language models often produce quality predictions that are not fully grounded in generated visual features, and their predicted scores can change unstably during inference, behaviors not aligned with human reasoning.
Large Vision-Language Models exhibit sycophancy, where they are unduly influenced by leading or deceptive prompts, resulting in biased outputs and hallucinations.

For VLM-based radiology report generation, language-specific models substantially outperformed both general and domain-specific models, and models fine-tuned with medical terminology exhibited enhanced performance across all languages compared to models with generic knowledge.

The emergence of large vision models is following in the footsteps of Large Language Models, and domain-specific LVMs are proposed for human-robot interaction due to their superior performance over normal models.

balanced.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) extend language models by adding visual perception through specialized attention heads that focus on visual content, enabling models trained on linguistic data to bridge textual and visual understanding [doc_3]. Relative to text-only LMs, VLMs face additional challenges: they can be sycophantically biased by leading prompts [doc_6], produce unstable and contradictory quality predictions in image assessment [doc_10], and hallucinate on absent objects, requiring visual auditing tools [doc_1]. VLMs also require domain-specific adaptation: instruction-tuning with language-specific and medical data substantially improves radiology report generation [doc_2], while efficient fine-tuning methods like state space modules reduce computational cost [doc_4]. For applications such as human-robot interaction, domain-specific LVMs are selected over normal models to align with context and tasks [doc_5]. Benchmarks further reveal that VLMs do not yet match language-model-level reasoning robustness, with lower accuracy in Hindi and under chain-of-thought constraints [doc_7]. Interestingly, the relative complexity of visual concepts can remain invariant across image and coordinate modalities, suggesting some VLM representations may still be modality-dependent [doc_8].

citations.claim: VLMs adapt language models to multimodal tasks through a unique class of attention heads that focus specifically on visual tokens, bridging textual and visual understanding.
Large vision-language models exhibit sycophancy, being unduly influenced by leading or deceptive prompts, which results in biased outputs and hallucinations.
Vision-language models in blind image quality assessment often produce textual descriptions that contradict their final quality predictions and unstable scores, unlike human reasoning.
IKIWISI uses spy objects and binary heatmaps to help humans evaluate whether vision-language models hallucinate on nonexistent objects when ground truth is unavailable.

For radiology report generation in low-resource languages, language-specific vision-language models substantially outperform general and domain-specific models, and medical fine-tuning improves performance.
State Space Memory Integration enables efficient fine-tuning of large vision-language models by updating only a fraction of parameters while achieving state-of-the-art performance.
A design space for domain-specific large vision models in human-robot interaction emphasizes accurate domain alignment and model selection over normal models.
The GanitBench benchmark shows that vision-language models have lower accuracy on Hindi questions and under double-lock and chain-of-thought settings in mathematical reasoning.

In vision-language models, image-based representations generally require fewer teaching segments and achieve higher accuracy than coordinate-based representations, but concept complexity ranks similarly across modalities.

standard.summary: Multi-agent systems and centralized control differ in how decisions and coordination are organized. Centralized approaches rely on a single central agent or optimizer that gathers information and computes a global solution, as in consensus models where a central agent solicits and combines recommendations (doc1) or in centralized unconstrained optimization for spatial constraints (doc3). In contrast, distributed multi-agent approaches decentralize decision-making: distributed consensus-based optimization approximates the centralized solution through local interactions (doc3), decentralized controllers can be self-organizing and open to agents joining/leaving (doc5), central control nodes can be replaced by distributed coalitional controllers (doc6), and planning can be decomposed into decentralized phases to avoid the extreme computational complexity of centralized planning (doc9). However, consensus (centralized judgment) may not always be appropriate, and models help determine when to use it and how many agents to include (doc1).

citations.claim: Models of consensus for multiple agent systems assume a central agent that solicits recommendations or plans from other agents and then determines the consensus recommendation.
The problem is initially framed as a centralized unconstrained optimization, and a distributed consensus-based optimization scheme is introduced that approximates the centralized solution.

The decentralized multi-agent motion controller is self-organizing, deals with incomplete information and unexpected situations, and has an open structure enabling any agent to join or leave without the remaining agents adjusting how they function.
The role of central control nodes can be undertaken by several controllers in a distributed topology, promoting coalitions of control agents where communication is essential to ensure cooperation.

To fight the extreme computational complexity of centralized multi-agent planning, the proposed procedure systematically decouples the planning procedure for the two types of specifications, first in a fully decentralized way and then using compact representations.

The analysis of the consensus model leads to the conclusion that in some cases consensus judgment is not appropriate, and results allow determining how many agents should be used and under which conditions the consensus model should be used.

balanced.summary: Multi-agent systems distribute control, planning, and decision-making among autonomous agents, whereas centralized agents aggregate information, recommendations, or control at a single node. The documents illustrate this contrast: one model assumes a central agent solicits recommendations and determines consensus (doc_1), while another frames the spatial-constraint problem first as centralized optimization and then approximates it with distributed consensus-based optimization (doc_3). Decentralized multi-agent planning is explicitly proposed to combat the extreme computational complexity of centralized multi-agent planning (doc_9). Central control nodes can be replaced by multiple controllers in a distributed topology, with coalitions formed when beneficial (doc_6). A decentralized, self-organizing potential-field controller scales linearly and lets agents join/leave without global adjustment, contrasting with centralized coordination (doc_5). Multi-sensor systems can also be treated as teams of agents that bargain and aggregate disparate, uncertain information rather than relying on a single integrator (doc_10). Together, these sources indicate that centralized approaches may provide a global optimum but face scalability, complexity, and bottleneck issues, whereas multi-agent/distributed approaches offer scalability, robustness, self-organization, and plug-and-play operation (doc_5, doc_6, doc_7, doc_9). MAS are inherently collaborative and distributed, and their engineering benefits from aligning with distributed-systems patterns (doc_4).

citations.claim: Multiple-agent consensus models assume a central agent solicits recommendations or plans from other agents and determines the consensus; the analysis shows consensus judgment is not appropriate in some cases and can guide how many and which agents to use.

The spatial-constraint problem is initially framed as a centralized unconstrained optimization yielding an optimal configuration, and a distributed consensus-based optimization scheme is introduced that approximates the centralized solution.

A two-phase decentralized planning procedure is proposed to fight the extreme computational complexity of centralized multi-agent planning, decoupling the planning procedure and guaranteeing satisfaction of the overall specification.

Central control nodes can be undertaken by several controllers in a distributed topology that suits the system structure, and coalition formation is promoted whenever it can bring benefit to overall system performance.

A decentralized, self-organizing potential-field controller for a large group of mobile agents has computational effort that increases linearly with the number of agents and an open structure enabling agents to join or leave without the remaining agents adjusting their operation.

In multi-sensor systems, sensors are treated as members/agents of a team able to offer opinions and bargain in group decisions, aggregating disparate and uncertain information rather than relying on a single centralized integrator.
The synthesized heterogeneous multi-agent system under rank-deficient coupling is initialization-free and suitable for plug-and-play operation, supporting distributed design and analysis.

Multi-agent systems are inherently collaborative and distributed, and their engineering can benefit from aligning the architectural characteristics of distributed systems with the distributed nature of MAS.

standard.summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) and large language models (LLMs) are complementary rather than competing: LLMs can support KG construction, query generation, and question answering, while KGs can ground LLMs with factual context, reduce hallucinations, and improve accuracy and explainability. KG embeddings and graph-to-text models exploit KG structure, and benchmarks have been developed to compare LLM capabilities on semantic technology tasks.

citations.claim: The survey investigates the synergistic relationship between LLMs and KGs, including KG question answering, ontology generation, KG validation, and enhancement of KG accuracy and consistency through LLMs, as well as LLMs generating descriptive texts and natural language queries for KGs.
Knowledge graph embedding models are typically applied to KGs for link prediction, but KG structure can be a significant source of bias and partially determinant of overall KGEM performance.

LLM-KG-Bench 3.0 provides an extensible set of tasks for automated evaluation of LLM answers covering different aspects of working with semantic technologies, including capabilities in working with RDF and SPARQL.

LLMs have been studied as neural knowledge bases, and mapping LLM knowledge into a graph representation reveals a knowledge homophily pattern that can improve active labeling and multi-hop path retrieval.

Graph-to-text generation has benefited from pre-trained language models, and a novel tree-level embedding method capturing inter-dependency structures of input knowledge graphs significantly improves text generation metrics.
Incorporating a medical knowledge graph into LLMs via the Dr.Knows model improves accuracy of automated diagnosis generation and offers an explainable diagnostic pathway.

A large language model can generate SPARQL queries on RDF knowledge graphs from natural language questions without fine-tuning, reaching state-of-the-art results on Wikidata benchmarks in a zero-shot setting.
LLMs face challenges such as hallucination and domain-specific issues, and integrating KGs provides factual context that improves performance and delivers more accurate feedback to user queries.

Knowledge-enhanced language models achieve higher factual accuracy and mitigate hallucinations by leveraging knowledge graphs, often combined with adapter modules to reduce computational load and catastrophic forgetting.

balanced.summary: The documents present knowledge graphs (KGs) and large language models (LLMs) not as opposing technologies but as complementary: KGs provide explicit, structured, and verifiable facts, while LLMs offer flexible natural language understanding and generation. Several studies show LLMs supporting KG tasks, such as generating SPARQL queries, constructing or validating KGs, and converting graphs to text. Conversely, KGs are used to ground LLMs, reducing hallucinations and improving factual accuracy in domains like medicine and education, often via adapter modules or auxiliary graph models. Evaluations such as LLM-KG-Bench benchmark LLMs on semantic-technology tasks, while KG-embedding models leverage graph structure for link prediction, and probing LLM knowledge via graph representations reveals implicit knowledge organization. Thus, the literature emphasizes integration and synergy rather than a strict 'versus' dichotomy.

citations.claim: KGs and LLMs have a synergistic relationship; LLMs are applied to tasks like KG question answering, ontology generation, and KG validation, while KGs can improve AI applications.
KG structure can be a significant source of bias and partially determines the performance of knowledge graph embedding models.
LLMs can assist with knowledge graph engineering tasks such as working with RDF and SPARQL, but their capabilities vary and require automated evaluation via frameworks like LLM-KG-Bench.
LLMs store knowledge implicitly, and mapping LLM knowledge into a graph reveals knowledge homophily, enabling efficient knowledge checking and multi-hop retrieval.
Pre-trained language models under-utilize graph structure, and adding tree-level embeddings that capture KG inter-dependencies significantly improves graph-to-text generation.
Combining a medical knowledge graph with LLMs improves automated diagnosis generation and provides explainable diagnostic pathways.
A zero-shot LLM approach can generate SPARQL queries on RDF knowledge graphs from natural language, achieving state-of-the-art results on Wikidata.
Knowledge graph embedding models use graph structure for link prediction, and fully hyperbolic rotation achieves competitive results with fewer parameters.
Constructing a knowledge graph from cross-data sources and integrating it with LLMs helps overcome LLM limitations such as hallucinations in educational question-answering.
Knowledge-enhanced language models combine LLMs with knowledge graphs via adapter modules to achieve higher factual accuracy and mitigate hallucinations.

standard.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are general-purpose systems that can outperform human experts in some prediction tasks, as shown by LLMs surpassing neuroscience experts on BrainBench and by a neuroscience-tuned BrainGPT performing even better [doc_8]. However, compared with specialized or expert-like systems, LLMs show important limitations: for low-resource Maltese NLP, 55 LLMs often performed poorly, especially on generative tasks, while smaller fine-tuned models usually performed better [doc_10]; and LLMs' explicit metalinguistic knowledge is fragmented, failing to beat majority-class baselines even for GPT-4o [doc_6]. LLMs can also be decomposed into task-specific 'experts' via frameworks like DoE, enabling efficient inference without accuracy loss [doc_9], and their synergy with knowledge graphs is a key research direction for improving reasoning and consistency [doc_4]. Overall, LLMs are not simply superior to expert systems; they complement or nest expert-like components, and their advantages depend on data availability and task domain.

citations.claim: LLMs surpass human experts in predicting neuroscience experimental outcomes, and BrainGPT, an LLM tuned on neuroscience literature, performed better yet.

Evaluating 55 publicly available LLMs on low-resource Maltese showed that many models perform poorly, particularly on generative tasks, and smaller fine-tuned models often perform better across all tasks.

GPT-4o performs best but achieves moderate accuracy on metalinguistic knowledge, and all models fail to outperform the majority-class baseline, indicating fragmented knowledge shaped mainly by data availability.

The Decomposition of Experts (DoE) framework dynamically identifies and activates task-specific experts within a language model, achieving up to a x1.73 inference speed-up with a 65% pruning rate without compromising accuracy.
The survey investigates the synergistic relationship between LLMs and Knowledge Graphs, which is crucial for advancing AI's capabilities in understanding, reasoning, and language processing.

balanced.summary: The documents portray LLMs and expert-like systems as complementary rather than strictly opposed. LLMs trained on vast corpora can surpass human experts in predicting domain-specific outcomes, as shown by BrainGPT outperforming experts on neuroscience results (doc_8). However, LLMs have notable limitations: they show only limited metalinguistic knowledge, failing to beat majority-class baselines on linguistic structure tasks (doc_6), and they perform poorly on low-resource languages, where smaller fine-tuned models (a more traditional, expert-like approach) are often more accurate (doc_10). Performance in multilingual LLMs is driven more by data availability than by inherent reasoning (doc_7). Methods such as Decomposition of Experts (DoE) can isolate task-specific parameters inside an LLM to gain efficiency, mimicking expert-system modularity (doc_9). Meanwhile, LLMs and symbolic knowledge graphs can enhance each other, indicating a synergistic relationship rather than a simple contest (doc_4). Overall, the evidence suggests LLMs offer broad, flexible competence, but expert systems and specialized models remain valuable for constrained, low-resource, or precision-critical tasks.

citations.claim: Large language models surpass human experts in predicting neuroscience results, and BrainGPT, an LLM tuned on neuroscience literature, performs better yet.
Many LLMs perform poorly on Maltese, a low-resource language, and smaller fine-tuned models often perform better across all tasks, with prior exposure to Maltese being the most important factor.

LLMs show limited metalinguistic knowledge: even the best model achieves moderate accuracy and all models fail to outperform the majority-class baseline, suggesting they lack fine-grained linguistic distinctions.

For multilingual LLMs, pretraining data size is the most influential factor for SEEN languages, while script type and language family matter for UNSEEN languages, indicating resource-driven performance.

The Decomposition of Experts (DoE) framework dynamically identifies and activates task-specific experts within a language model, achieving up to x1.73 inference speed-up with a 65% pruning rate without sacrificing accuracy.

The survey highlights the synergistic relationship between Large Language Models and Knowledge Graphs, with LLMs used for KG Question Answering, ontology generation, and KG validation, while KGs can enhance LLM reasoning.

standard.summary: Generative models and discriminative models serve complementary, opposing roles in frameworks such as GANs.
