Generative models aim to transform simple distributions into complex target data distributions, while discriminative models are trained to distinguish real from generated samples. In GANs, the generative and discriminative networks engage in a minimax game, and the optimal discriminator relates to differences between score functions. Discriminators also influence generalization; early stopping can improve generalization error, though memorization is inevitable in the long run. Unlike standard discriminative classification, generative models can be trained with alternative criteria such as f-divergences beyond maximum likelihood.

citations.claim: Deep generative models can be viewed as probability transformation functions that map simple predefined distributions into complex target data distributions.
GANs consist of a discriminative network and a generative network engaged in a Minimax game, with the discriminator distinguishing between real and generated data.
In composite-functional-gradient GAN, the optimal discriminator D(x) differentiates the integral of the differences between the score functions of real and synthesized samples.
With early stopping, the generalization error of a simplified GAN measured by Wasserstein metric escapes the curse of dimensionality, despite long-term memorization being inevitable.
Probabilistic models are often trained by maximum likelihood, but alternative non-likelihood training criteria based on f-divergences can also be used for generative models.

balanced.summary: Generative models are presented as distribution learners that transform simple distributions into data distributions (e.g., GANs, flows, diffusion models), whereas discriminative models act as classifiers, typically distinguishing real from generated or between classes. The most direct contrast appears in GANs, where a discriminative network and a generative network engage in a minimax game, and the adversarial objective connects to Jensen-Shannon divergence. The discriminator's role is theoretically important: it affects generalization and can mitigate memorization with early stopping, and its optimal gradient corresponds to differences in score functions between real and synthesized data, which the generator training minimizes. Traditional generative training via maximum likelihood minimizes f-divergences, and GANs offer alternative non-likelihood criteria. Discriminative classifiers are also used for evaluating generative models, as in precision/recall estimation. Other documents focus on generative model families and applications, such as structured generative models and data cleansing for GANs, without framing a full generative-versus-discriminative taxonomy.

citations.claim: GANs consist of a discriminative network and a generative network engaged in a minimax game, and the adversarial principle is connected to Jensen-Shannon divergence.

In a simplified GAN with the generator replaced by a density, the discriminator contributes to generalization; with early stopping, the generalization error measured by Wasserstein metric escapes the curse of dimensionality, although memorization is inevitable in the long term.

In the composite-functional-gradient GAN, the optimal discriminator's gradient differentiates the integral of differences between score functions of real and synthesized samples, while the generator minimizes this difference.

Probabilistic models are often trained by maximum likelihood, which minimizes a specific f-divergence; GANs correspond to alternative non-likelihood criteria that may better match user requirements such as sharp image generation.
Precision and recall curve estimation for generative models is framed as a binary classification problem, yielding statistical guarantees and generalizing landmark PR metrics.

Deep generative models, despite architectural differences such as autoencoders, autoregressive models, GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion models, and flow matching, fundamentally operate by transforming simple predefined distributions into complex target data distributions.

Structured generative models reconstruct 3D scenes by causally explaining images through models of objects, lighting, and camera parameters, and their compositional and generative nature leads to interpretability and editability.

In GAN training, training instances do not directly affect the generator's parameters because they are only fed into the discriminator, so influence estimation uses the Jacobian of the generator's gradient with respect to the discriminator's parameters.

standard.summary: Model compression is a broad field, and quantization is one of its principal techniques. A survey identifies Knowledge Distillation, Model Quantization, and Model Pruning as the three primary approaches to compressing LLMs for resource-constrained environments, with quantization being a core compression method. Quantization itself has multiple variants: quantization-aware training (QAT) involves expensive retraining, while post-training quantization (PTQ) is preferred for LLMs because it avoids retraining costs. However, quantization methods effective on LLMs do not necessarily transfer well to small language models, and PTQ performance depends on calibration data and can degrade at low bit-widths. Thus, quantization is not an alternative to model compression but rather a specific compression strategy with its own trade-offs and sub-methods.

citations.claim: Model compression techniques for LLMs include Knowledge Distillation, Model Quantization, and Model Pruning, aiming to enable efficient inference in resource-constrained environments.
Quantization and pruning form the foundation of compression for neural networks, enabling efficient inference for large language models.

Quantization is an effective technique for compressing models to fit resource-limited devices, with two primary methods: quantization aware training (QAT) and post-training quantization (PTQ); PTQ has become the research hotspot for LLMs.

Quantization has proven effective for LLMs, but its applicability to SLMs is underexplored, and direct transfer of LLM-optimized quantization techniques leads to suboptimal results due to SLMs' unique architectural characteristics and training dynamics.
Post-training quantization (PTQ) techniques have been developed to compress LLMs while avoiding expensive re-training.

balanced.summary: Model compression is a broad umbrella covering techniques that reduce the size, memory footprint, and computational cost of neural networks; quantization is one specific compression technique within that umbrella, not a competing alternative. Doc_6 identifies quantization as one of three primary model-compression approaches alongside knowledge distillation and model pruning. Doc_1 similarly frames quantization as an effective technique for compressing models to fit resource-limited devices, and Doc_10 calls quantization a model compression technique that shrinks large language models. Doc_9 reinforces that quantization and pruning together form the foundation of neural-network compression. At the same time, quantization is not universally transferable: Doc_2 shows that quantization methods optimized for large language models can be suboptimal for small language models, so the choice of compression approach must be tailored to the model. More broadly, Doc_4 illustrates that quantization is also a core step in signal compression, where it converts sampled analog signals into bits. Thus, quantization is best understood as a key subfield of compression, while model compression encompasses additional strategies such as pruning, distillation, and related techniques.

citations.claim: Model compression includes three primary approaches: knowledge distillation, model quantization, and model pruning, making quantization one specific compression technique among several.
Quantization is described as an effective technique for compressing models to fit resource-limited devices while preserving generative quality.
Model compression techniques like quantization can shrink large language models and make them more resource efficient, at the cost of potential performance degradation.
Quantization and pruning form the foundation of compression for neural networks, enabling efficient inference for large language models.

The applicability of quantization as a compression technique differs between small and large language models, so direct transfer of LLM-optimized quantization leads to suboptimal results on smaller models.
In signal processing, quantization is a core step in converting sampled analog signals to digital bits, illustrating quantization as a compression mechanism beyond neural networks.
Compression of LLMs reduces memory footprint, latency, and energy required for inference, and post-training quantization is one developed technique for this compression.

standard.summary: Explainability and accuracy are often in tension: state-of-the-art deep learning models are highly accurate yet opaque, making explanations necessary but difficult (doc_4). In practice, choosing an explainability technique requires balancing comprehensibility with accuracy (doc_8). Recent approaches attempt to reconcile these goals by optimizing explanations for faithfulness and low complexity simultaneously, yielding both accurate and comprehensible explanations (doc_10). Yet highly comprehensible explanations are prone to misinterpretation, so the accuracy of explanations themselves must be scrutinized (doc_3). Formal explainability provides rigorous guarantees but suffers from scalability, which can be mitigated by leveraging robustness queries (doc_9). The appropriate balance between explainability and accuracy is context-dependent; for healthcare AI, a framework defines four classes of explanation necessity to guide when and at what detail explanations are needed (doc_5).

citations.claim: Deep learning algorithms are accurate but notoriously opaque; a necessary criterion for trustworthy explanations is that they should reflect the relevant processes the algorithms' predictions are based on.
In practical business applications, the challenge lies in selecting an explainability method that balances comprehensibility with accuracy.
A framework enhances explainability of deep networks by maximizing both faithfulness and comprehensibility, achieving higher faithfulness and lower complexity in explanations.

Highly comprehensible explanations, such as feature importance and decision surface visualisation, are exceptionally susceptible to misinterpretation since users tend to infer spurious information outside the scope of these explanations.

Formal explainability is rigorous but hampered by poor scalability; novel algorithms compute formal explanations by answering robustness queries, with the number of queries at most linear on the number of features.

The paper proposes four classes of explanation necessity (self-explainable, semi-explainable, non-explainable, and new-patterns discovery) to determine the required level of explanation in healthcare AI applications.

balanced.summary: Across the documents, explainability and accuracy are presented not as a simple either/or but as interdependent concerns requiring deliberate balancing. Deep learning's predictive accuracy comes with opacity, so practical applications require selecting explainability techniques that balance comprehensibility and accuracy (doc8). However, human comprehension can undermine the accuracy of interpretation: highly comprehensible explanations often lead users to infer information outside the explanation's scope and to be overconfident in those inferences (doc3). Trustworthy explanations must therefore reflect the actual processes used by the model, and robustness criteria are needed because different XAI methods can agree yet still produce a wrong explanation (doc4). Without theoretical guarantees, interpretability methods risk being as mysterious as the predictions they explain; analyzing them on simple, interpretable models offers a foundation (doc1). Formal explainability offers rigorous guarantees, though scalability has been a bottleneck; recent algorithms connect formal explanations to robustness queries to improve efficiency (doc9). To evaluate whether explanations are accurate, practitioners use measures such as faithfulness and localization, and the Quality Gap Estimate improves the statistical reliability of such evaluations (doc6). In high-stakes domains like healthcare, the required level of explanation depends on the application, with frameworks distinguishing local, global, or both (doc5). Multi-disciplinary auditing can certify whether systems meet explainability standards (doc2). Finally, work on explanation optimization shows that faithfulness and comprehensibility can be improved simultaneously, with the proposed optimizer outperforming existing XAI methods on faithfulness while reducing complexity (doc10). Collectively, these findings suggest that rather than a fixed trade-off, explainability versus accuracy is managed through method selection, evaluation, and tailoring explanations to context.

citations.claim: In practical business applications, the challenge lies in selecting an appropriate explainability method that balances comprehensibility with accuracy, especially given the opaque nature of deep learning models.

Highly comprehensible explanations are exceptionally susceptible to misinterpretation because users infer spurious information outside the explanation's scope, and they tend to be overconfident when misinterpreting.

A necessary criterion for trustworthy explanations is that they reflect the relevant processes the algorithm's predictions are based on; explanatory robustness and explanation method robustness are required, as all methods can give the same but still wrong explanation.
Interpretability methods frequently lack theoretical guarantees, and analyzing them on simple, already interpretable models can provide a solid foundation for developing new explainability methods.

The paper proposes efficient algorithms for formal explanations by answering robustness queries, establishing a direct relationship between the practical complexity of formal explainability and robustness.

XAI practitioners use quality measures such as faithfulness, localization, and robustness; the proposed Quality Gap Estimate (QGE) offers a direct comparison to the inverse explanation and enhances statistical reliability of quality assessments.

Healthcare AI requires a categorization of explanation necessity (self-explainable, semi-explainable, non-explainable, and new-patterns discovery) to determine whether local, global, or both explanations are needed.

Explainability auditing can ensure the quality of explainability in applied contexts and can be the basis for certification, requiring multi-disciplinary perspectives including technical, psychological, ethical, and legal.

A novel framework enhances explainability through a dual focus on maximizing both accuracy and comprehensibility, with experiments showing faithfulness scores 155% and 63% higher than the best XAI methods in 3D and 2D tasks while also reducing complexity.

standard.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) via adapters or Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) largely matches traditional full fine-tuning performance while updating far fewer parameters: roughly 1–6% versus 40–55% for full fine-tuning in transformer-based instance segmentation models. Using 2–3 adapters per transformer block strikes the best performance/efficiency balance, and LoRA applied to deformable attention is especially parameter-efficient, sometimes outperforming adapters. The effectiveness of PEFT depends on dataset complexity and model architecture. A related study on compression indicates that sequential fine-tuning followed by compression sacrifices performance and creates an unnecessarily large intermediate model, whereas joint fine-tuning and compression into a pruned low-rank structure significantly outperforms that sequential approach.

citations.claim: PEFT methods, specifically adapters and LoRA, achieve competitive performance while fine-tuning only about 1-6% of model parameters, a marked improvement over the 40-55% required in traditional fine-tuning.

Using 2-3 adapters per transformer block offers an optimal balance of performance and efficiency; LoRA exhibits strong parameter efficiency when applied to deformable attention and in certain cases surpasses adapter configurations.
The impact of PEFT techniques varies based on dataset complexity and model architecture, underscoring the importance of context-specific tuning.

Sequential fine-tuning and compression sacrifices performance while creating a larger than necessary model as an intermediate step, whereas joint fine-tuning and compression significantly outperforms other sequential compression methods.

balanced.summary: In the provided literature, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) offers a clear alternative to full fine-tuning: adapters and LoRA achieve competitive instance segmentation performance while updating only about 1–6% of parameters, compared to 40–55% for traditional fine-tuning, and 2–3 adapters per transformer block give an optimal balance. Related work on joint fine-tuning and compression also suggests that building a smaller model during task adaptation can outperform sequential fine-tuning-then-compression pipelines. However, most other supplied documents address auto-tuning and configuration tuning of algorithm hyperparameters rather than model fine-tuning, so they do not directly inform the PEFT-versus-full-fine-tuning comparison.

citations.claim: PEFT methods (adapters and LoRA) achieve competitive performance in instance segmentation while fine-tuning only about 1-6% of model parameters, compared to 40-55% required in traditional fine-tuning; 2-3 adapters per transformer block offer an optimal balance of performance and efficiency.

Sequential fine-tuning followed by compression sacrifices performance and creates a larger-than-necessary intermediate model, whereas jointly fine-tuning and compressing by gradually distilling to a pruned low-rank structure significantly outperforms sequential compression methods.

standard.summary: Vector databases and relational databases serve different core purposes, though they are increasingly converging. Vector databases are specialized for storing and retrieving high-dimensional, often sparse numerical vectors that computationally describe rich data such as texts, images, and video, enabling similarity search and AI workflows like RAG. Relational databases manage structured data using schemas, SQL, and relational algebra, and remain widely adopted. However, vector search is increasingly being integrated into relational database systems: an in-depth study of filter-agnostic vector search in a production PostgreSQL-compatible system shows that the optimal vector search algorithm depends on system-level overheads (e.g., page accesses and filter operations), not just distance computation costs, and that assumptions from specialized vector libraries often do not hold in relational environments.

citations.claim: Vector database management systems have emerged to computationally describe rich data such as texts, images and video, captured as numerical vectors that are computationally inexpensive to store and compare, but with high dimensionality and sparsity demanding specialized solutions.

In a production PostgreSQL-compatible system, filter-agnostic vector search algorithms show that the optimal algorithm is not dictated by distance computation costs alone; system-level overheads from distance computations and filter operations play a significant role.
SchemaDB is a collection of relational database schemata in both SQL and graph formats, standardised to MySQL syntax, providing insight into relational database structures in the wild.

MySQL and PostgreSQL are the most popular DBMSs in a corpus of open-source Java projects, with Redis and MongoDB most frequent among non-relational systems, and projects often combine multiple DBMSs in polyglot persistence.

balanced.summary: Vector databases are optimized for storing and querying high-dimensional embeddings used in similarity search, recommender systems, and RAG workflows, whereas relational databases are built around structured schemas and SQL. However, the boundary is blurring: systems like TigerGraph add vector search to graph databases for hybrid structured/unstructured queries (doc_2), and PostgreSQL-based systems support filtered vector search, though performance depends on system-level costs rather than algorithm alone (doc_4). Adoption studies show relational DBMSs like MySQL and PostgreSQL remain the most popular, while vector-capable systems are often used alongside them in polyglot persistence setups (doc_6). Vector databases play a central role in AI/RAG pipelines and can require adaptive or distributed index strategies to handle large scale (doc_7, doc_8).

citations.claim: Vector database management systems emerged to manage numerically described rich data such as texts, images, and video for use cases like recommender systems, similarity search, and chatbots, where high dimensionality and sparsity demand specialized storage and retrieval solutions.

TigerVector integrates vector search with graph query in TigerGraph, enabling hybrid search that fuses unstructured and structured data and outperforming specialized vector database Milvus in experiments.

In a production PostgreSQL-compatible system, the optimal filtered vector search algorithm is not determined by distance computation cost alone; system-level overheads from filter operations and data access play a significant role, making graph-based approaches sometimes lose to clustering-based indexes like ScaNN.

A historical study of open-source Java projects shows MySQL and PostgreSQL are the most popular DBMSs, while non-relational systems like Redis and MongoDB are also frequently used, with many projects practicing polyglot persistence by combining multiple DBMSs for different data needs.

RAG uses vector databases to expand LLM expertise without retraining, and in embedding data lakes an adaptive partition-based index like CrackIVF can answer queries immediately and scale up as query workload grows, rather than building a full index upfront.

Vector databases have grown in popularity for efficient similarity search over text, images, and video and are central to AI workflows such as retrieval-augmented generation, motivating empirical studies of distributed vector database performance on HPC platforms like Polaris.

standard.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) optimizes policies through environmental interaction and reward signals, while imitation learning (IL) trains policies by mimicking demonstrations. IL can support RL by supplying offline trajectories for pre-training or concurrent training, improving sample efficiency in procedurally generated environments (doc_1). In surgical electrocautery, learning a reward from suboptimal demonstrations and then using RL is more robust than pure imitation learning (doc_4). Inverse RL addresses the inverse problem of inferring rewards from demonstrated behavior, and can simultaneously estimate dynamics (doc_8). IL itself has many variants: hierarchical IL from observations dynamically selects feasible sub-goals (doc_2), state-only distribution matching minimizes divergence between policy and expert transitions non-adversarially (doc_3), and temporal IL with state space models encodes full history to overcome Markov assumptions in long-horizon tasks (doc_7). Surveys of robotic manipulation further position imitation learning as a central paradigm for acquiring skills from human demonstrations (doc_5).

citations.claim: Using IL for pre-training and concurrently during online RL training consistently improves RL sample-efficiency while converging to optimal policies in procedurally generated environments.
A reward function learned from ranked suboptimal demonstrations, followed by RL, yields a more robust policy than pure imitation learning.
Inverse reinforcement learning learns an unknown reward function from observed behavior, and can simultaneously estimate the system's dynamics.
HILONet is a hierarchical imitation learning approach that dynamically chooses feasible sub-goals from demonstrated observations.
A non-adversarial state-only imitation learning method minimizes KL divergence between policy and expert state transition trajectories.
MTIL uses state space models to encode full trajectory history, overcoming the Markov assumption that limits standard IL in long-horizon tasks.
A survey shows imitation learning is a powerful technique for robotic manipulation by mimicking human demonstrations.

balanced.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains policies by interacting with the environment and optimizing a reward signal, typically requiring many environment interactions (doc_1, doc_6, doc_10). Imitation learning (IL) instead learns from expert demonstrations, with methods ranging from direct distribution matching (doc_3) to hierarchical observation-based learning (doc_2) and long-horizon temporal modeling (doc_7), and has been extensively surveyed for robotic manipulation (doc_5). The two paradigms are often complementary: IL can pre-train or be run concurrently with RL to improve sample efficiency (doc_1), and RL can learn policies from rewards inferred from demonstrations, which is more robust than pure IL when demonstrations are suboptimal (doc_4). Other related approaches include inverse RL with simultaneous dynamics estimation (doc_8) and example-based control with auxiliary tasks (doc_9).

citations.claim: RL agents require large numbers of interactions with the environment; using IL from offline data for pre-training or concurrent training consistently improves sample-efficiency in procedurally generated environments.
HILONet is an IL approach that learns from observation-only non-aligned trajectories by dynamically choosing feasible sub-goals, improving performance and learning efficiency.
State-only IL via non-adversarial KLD minimization between policy and expert state transition trajectories yields robust performance and a reliable convergence estimator.
Using a learned reward function from suboptimal demonstrations to obtain a policy via RL is more robust than pure imitation learning.
A survey of imitation learning for robotic manipulation provides a taxonomy, chronological development, and benchmark comparisons of IL techniques.
GPOMDP is an RL algorithm for directly optimizing policy performance in POMDPs via gradient ascent, requiring only a single sample path and no knowledge of the underlying state.
MTIL is a temporal IL method using state space models to encode full trajectory history, overcoming the Markov assumption and achieving superior performance in long-horizon tasks.
Inverse reinforcement learning can simultaneously estimate rewards and dynamics to handle unknown transition models, improving sample efficiency and accuracy.
VPACE improves exploration in example-based control by adding examples of auxiliary tasks and a value penalty, offering an alternative to full-trajectory demonstrations in RL.
A theoretical high-dimensional RL model derives typical policy learning dynamics, including delayed learning under sparse rewards and a speed-accuracy trade-off.

standard.summary: The documents contrast probabilistic approaches and deep learning by highlighting that deep neural networks lack the precise semantics and definitive probabilistic interpretation of probabilistic graphical models, while Bayesian/probabilistic methods offer uncertainty quantification but face scalability challenges in deep models. Several works bridge these fields: DNNs can be viewed as approximate inference in infinite tree-structured PGMs, Monte Carlo dropout approximates Bayesian inference, Bayesian deep learning improves calibration and epistemic uncertainty quantification, and deep learning can model non-Gaussian aleatoric uncertainty. Other applications use deep learning for stochastic control, optimal experimental design, and data augmentation with variational autoencoders combined with Bayesian neural networks. Theoretical limitations of verifying deep learning properties are also discussed.

citations.claim: Deep neural networks lack the precise semantics and definitive probabilistic interpretation of probabilistic graphical models, but can be constructed as infinite tree-structured PGMs that correspond exactly to neural networks.

Bayesian inference provides methodology for parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification in machine learning and deep learning, but MCMC sampling methods face challenges in being adapted to larger models and big data problems.

Monte Carlo Dropout, initially introduced as a regularization technique, has been shown to approximate Bayesian inference by enabling probabilistic modeling through multiple stochastic forward passes.
Bayesian deep learning models are often well calibrated and capable of quantifying and communicating a measure of epistemic uncertainty along with competitive prediction accuracy.
Deep learning offers promising new ways to accurately model aleatoric uncertainty, particularly when uncertainty distributions do not conform to traditional assumptions of being fixed and Gaussian.
This paper proposes two algorithms for solving stochastic control problems with deep learning, focusing on the utility maximisation problem.
A new experimental design methodology uses deep learning, showing that training a network as a Likelihood Free Estimator can simplify the design process and improve parameter estimation.

Data augmentation using variational autoencoder-based deep generative models can improve deep neural network predictive accuracy and reduce prediction uncertainties quantified using Bayesian Neural Networks and conformal prediction.

There is a large family of tasks for which computing and verifying ideal stable and accurate neural networks is extremely challenging, even when ideal solutions exist within the given class of neural architectures.

balanced.summary: Probabilistic programming emphasizes explicit probabilistic models and Bayesian inference for uncertainty quantification, whereas deep learning provides scalable function approximation but often lacks calibrated uncertainty. However, the documents collectively show a convergence: deep neural networks can be given probabilistic interpretations, and Bayesian/probabilistic techniques are increasingly integrated into deep learning to improve uncertainty estimates, sample efficiency, and robustness. Challenges remain in scaling Bayesian inference to large models and in verifying deep learning guarantees.

citations.claim: Deep neural networks can be constructed as infinite tree-structured probabilistic graphical models, and DNN forward propagation performs approximations of exact PGM inference, giving DNNs a precise probabilistic interpretation.

Bayesian inference via MCMC provides parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification, but MCMC has faced challenges scaling to larger deep learning models; gradient-based Langevin proposals help, and the tutorial bridges theory and implementation for Bayesian neural networks.

Traditional neural networks provide deterministic predictions without inherent uncertainty estimates, while Bayesian neural networks offer principled uncertainty quantification but with computational complexity limits; MC Dropout approximates Bayesian inference more efficiently.

Deterministic deep learning models are often poorly calibrated and lack epistemic uncertainty, whereas Bayesian DL models are well calibrated and capable of quantifying and communicating epistemic uncertainty; federated aggregation strategies must be adapted for Bayesian models.

Deep learning offers new ways to accurately model non-Gaussian aleatoric uncertainty, using parametric, discretized, and generative conditional density models that outperform traditional fixed-Gaussian assumptions.

VAE-based deep generative data augmentation improves the predictive accuracy of deep neural networks, and combining it with Bayesian neural networks and conformal prediction reduces prediction uncertainties.

For active sequential hypothesis testing modeled as a POMDP, optimal policies are computationally hard and heuristics are used; deep reinforcement learning provides a heuristic that outperforms existing methods in some scenarios.

Deep learning algorithms solve stochastic control utility maximisation problems via HJB/2BSDE formulations, achieving highly accurate results with low computational cost and handling non-Markovian problems beyond classical stochastic control solvers.

Training a deep network as a likelihood-free estimator simplifies optimal experimental design by circumventing expensive bi-level optimization, improving parameter estimation quality for nonlinear systems.

There is a large family of classification tasks for which computing and verifying ideal stable and accurate neural networks is extremely challenging, if possible at all, highlighting theoretical limits of deep learning guarantees.

standard.summary: Online learning updates models incrementally from streaming data (doc_1), enabling adaptation to distribution changes and avoiding storage of past observations (doc_8). Batch/offline learning trains on accumulated datasets and can offer better convergence and feature selection, but may be less adaptive (doc_2). In delayed-label streaming settings, instance-incremental (online) learning is not necessarily superior to batch learning models such as XGBoost, and batch incremental solutions tend to be favored for interpretability (doc_8). Additionally, batch training can be computationally expensive, though subset pretraining can reduce this cost while achieving similar results (doc_5).

citations.claim: Online learning is a framework that involves incrementally updating a model with streaming data.
Instance incremental algorithms are often favored because they adapt to changes in data distribution and avoid storing observations in memory, but they assume immediate label availability.
Current online learning methods suffer from lower convergence rates and limited capability to select important features compared to their offline counterparts.

In delayed label settings, instance incremental learning is not the superior option compared to batch learning models such as XGBoost; batch incremental solutions tend to be favored for interpretability.
Batch processing is difficult to combine with efficient second-order optimization methods, but even small subsets are representative and computing expense can be reduced to a tenth or less.

balanced.summary: Online learning updates models incrementally from streaming data and is often favored for its adaptability and low memory footprint, whereas batch learning trains on accumulated datasets and is commonly used when labels are delayed or stability is prioritized. However, comparisons are nuanced: online methods can suffer from lower convergence rates and weaker feature selection than offline counterparts, and in delayed-label settings instance-incremental (online) learning is not necessarily superior to batch incremental models such as XGBoost. Offline/batch data can also be leveraged to speed up online reinforcement learning and neural network training, and hybrid approaches—such as federated learning with tuned batch sizes, distributed online optimization, and batch ensembles—further blur the distinction. Overall, the choice between online and batch learning depends on data availability, label delay, computational constraints, and the need for interpretability.

citations.claim: Online learning and continual learning both involve incrementally updating a model with streaming data, and these frameworks are often combined with meta-learning in recent research.
Current online learning methods suffer from lower convergence rates and limited capability to select important features compared to their offline counterparts.

Instance incremental (online) algorithms are favored in evolving data streams because they adapt to distribution changes and avoid storing observations in memory, but batch incremental algorithms are widely used in real-world delayed-label tasks.

In delayed label environments, instance incremental learning is not the superior option compared to state-of-the-art batch learning models such as XGBoost, and batch incremental solutions tend to be favored for interpretability.

Using offline data via imitation learning for pre-training and concurrently during online RL training consistently improves sample-efficiency while converging to optimal policies in procedurally generated environments.
Subset pretraining—optimizing over small subsets of the training set—can reach results equivalent to conventional batch training while reducing computing expense to a tenth or less.

A simple batch ensemble scheme provably achieves near-optimal regret for stochastic multi-armed bandits, showing that batch processing can effectively manage exploration-exploitation trade-offs in online RL.
Online learning over networks with asynchronous computations, unreliable communications, and inexact local computations can be solved robustly using a distributed operator-theoretic ADMM algorithm.

In federated learning with static and streaming datasets, the joint adjustment of mini-batch size and aggregation frequency navigates trade-offs among convergence, cost, and completion time, with offline optimal solutions and online adaptive algorithms both demonstrated.

Federated class incremental learning addresses catastrophic forgetting and non-IID data distribution simultaneously, and the proposed prototypes-injected prompt method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in continual learning benchmarks.

standard.summary: Contrastive learning and classification are related but distinct paradigms: classification typically uses a cross-entropy loss to map inputs directly to labels, whereas contrastive learning builds representations by pulling positive/augmented pairs together and pushing negative pairs apart, often serving as a pretraining or auxiliary objective. A unified contrastive loss can replace all cross-entropy losses in self-training, showing theoretical equivalence to CE while yielding significant improvements with limited labeled data (doc_10). Contrastive-inspired training algorithms also narrow the gap with backpropagation using cross-entropy, even outperforming it under inaccurate supervision (doc_4). However, directly applying contrastive learning is not always beneficial; in domain generalization it can degrade performance unless intra-class connectivity is explicitly addressed (doc_5). In other settings, contrastive pretraining improves downstream classification, e.g., medical image classification, where reducing dataset redundancy boosts AUC and accelerates training (doc_7). Enhanced contrastive losses also improve generalization and convergence on large-scale image classification benchmarks (doc_1). Thus, contrastive learning is best viewed as a representation-learning tool that can complement or, in some cases, outperform classification losses.

citations.claim: Recent advances have shown that the supervised contrastive loss function (SupCon) can be more effective than cross-entropy; replacing all instances of CE losses with a unique contrastive loss shows theoretical equivalence with CE and results in significant performance improvements across three different datasets with a limited number of labeled data.

If Cross Entropy is taken as the baseline loss function in backpropagation, the proposed modifications to the baseline Forward-Forward reduce its performance gap compared to backpropagation on Vision Transformer, and even outperforms it in certain conditions, such as inaccurate supervision.

It is intuitive to conceive the class-separated representations learned in contrastive learning are able to improve domain generalization, while the reality is quite the opposite: users observe directly applying contrastive learning deteriorates the performance.

Self-supervised pre-training of deep learning models with contrastive learning is a widely used technique in image analysis; dataset reduction leads to a considerable performance gain in downstream classification tasks, e.g., AUC improvement from 0.78 to 0.83 for COVID CT classification.

The proposed context-enriched contrastive loss function concurrently improves learning effectiveness and addresses information distortion; experimental results on large-scale image classification benchmarks demonstrate improvements over 16 state-of-the-art contrastive learning methods in terms of generalization performance and learning convergence speed.

Contrastive representation learning is a modern paradigm for learning representations of unlabeled data via augmentations, where models learn to embed semantically similar pairs of samples closer than independently drawn samples.

balanced.summary: Contrastive learning and classification are related but distinct: classification typically trains with cross-entropy to predict labels, whereas contrastive learning learns representations by contrasting positive and negative pairs, often as a pre-training or auxiliary objective to improve downstream classification. The documents collectively show contrastive learning can outperform or augment classification across domains, but its success depends on loss design, data quality, and task setup. For instance, a context-enriched contrastive loss improves image classification accuracy and convergence over existing contrastive methods; dual contrastive branches handle inter-class and intra-class variance in few-shot remote sensing classification; theory provides non-vacuous PAC-Bayesian risk certificates for contrastive loss and downstream classification; contrastive-inspired training matches or beats backpropagation with cross-entropy for Vision Transformers in some conditions; naive contrastive learning can hurt domain generalization, but domain-connecting contrastive learning improves it; contrastive methods can be tailored for clustering as a classification-like downstream task; reducing redundant medical images improves contrastive pre-training for downstream classification; contrastive learning trains neural predictors for architecture search and improves ECG classification; contrastive learning addresses cross-subject sleep staging classification; and a unified contrastive loss can replace cross-entropy in self-training, with theoretical equivalence and improved semi-supervised classification.

citations.claim: A context-enriched contrastive loss improves image classification generalization and convergence speed over 16 state-of-the-art contrastive learning methods on benchmarks including CIFAR and ImageNet.

A Dual Contrastive Network with context-guided and detail-guided contrastive learning branches improves few-shot remote sensing image scene classification by enhancing inter-class discriminability and intra-class invariance.
Non-vacuous PAC-Bayesian risk certificates are derived for contrastive learning, yielding tighter bounds for contrastive loss and downstream classification loss than previous certificates.

Contrastive Forward-Forward, a contrastive-learning-inspired training algorithm for Vision Transformers, improves accuracy and convergence over baseline Forward-Forward and can outperform backpropagation with cross-entropy under inaccurate supervision.

Directly applying contrastive learning deteriorates domain generalization, but the proposed domain-connecting contrastive learning (DCCL) improves generalization across domains and outperforms state-of-the-art DG baselines.

A clustering-friendly contrastive learning method with contrastive analysis enhances features critical for unsupervised image clustering, achieving higher clustering scores than conventional contrastive analysis and deep clustering methods.

Selectively reducing redundant medical image data before contrastive pre-training improves downstream classification performance, e.g., AUC improving from 0.78 to 0.83 on COVID CT classification, and speeds up pre-training.

Dual contrastive learning in evolutionary neural architecture search (DCL-ENAS) trains a high-precision neural predictor and improves classification accuracy on NAS benchmarks and ECG arrhythmia classification.
Contrastive learning based on inter-subject correlation addresses the cross-subject problem in sleep stage classification and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

A unified contrastive loss that replaces cross-entropy in self-training methods is theoretically equivalent to cross-entropy and yields significant performance improvements in semi-supervised classification with limited labeled data.

standard.summary: Symbolic AI and deep learning are often contrasted: symbolic AI works with meaningful, compositional symbols, whereas deep learning is subsymbolic and opaque, with individual units lacking inherent meaning [doc_4]. Deep learning's opacity and difficulty with symbolic/arithmetic tasks motivate extracting symbolic models from networks or augmenting them with symbolic knowledge [doc_5][doc_10][doc_3]. Increasingly, hybrid neuro-symbolic/intersymbolic approaches combine both paradigms, using symbolic knowledge to guide neural learning and neural learning to enhance symbolic reasoning, improving interpretability, generalizability, and effectiveness [doc_9][doc_1][doc_2].

citations.claim: Symbolic AI uses building blocks with inherent meaning, whereas subsymbolic/deep learning creates significance through its entirety even though individual building blocks lack meaning.
Deep learning systems are opaque, and decision trees can be derived from feedforward neural networks to provide interpretable symbolic models.
Even state-of-the-art deep learning models often fall short when probed with relatively simple tasks testing basic numerical and arithmetic knowledge.
Injecting symbolic educational knowledge into deep neural networks (NSAI) yields better generalizability and prioritizes robust causal representations, avoiding spurious correlations.
Neuro-symbolic AI leverages explicit symbolic knowledge representations with data-driven learning to enhance mutual understanding between humans and systems.

Combining gradient descent with evolutionary computation in neural symbolic regression yields equations that are more symbolically and behaviorally accurate than state-of-the-art gradient-based neural symbolic regression.
Symbolic regression was traditionally tackled with genetic programming, but deep learning has recently gained interest as a data-driven method for interpretable model discovery.

balanced.summary: Symbolic AI and deep learning are often contrasted: deep/subsymbolic models are highly effective at learning from large data but are opaque and can lack elementary numerical or symbolic competence, while symbolic approaches operate on meaningful, compositional representations that support reasoning and interpretability. In practice the dichotomy is blurring. Symbolic regression, originally based on genetic programming, is now being tackled with deep learning to make learned equations interpretable. Similarly, neural-symbolic methods inject symbolic knowledge into deep networks to improve generalization, control biases, and extract rules, addressing interpretability in high-risk domains such as education. In robotics, deep learning-based perception is used for symbolic anchoring to connect subsymbolic sensor data to symbolic knowledge. Relational reasoning networks integrate neural architectures with relational/logical structure in the latent space to improve scalability and expressivity. Knowledge-graph-driven neurosymbolic approaches combine top-down symbolic reasoning with bottom-up neural learning for mutual understanding between humans and systems. Symbolic decision models can also be derived from feedforward neural networks to expose their decisions and increase trust. Surveys of neuro-symbolic AI highlight that adding symbolic systems to black-box neural models can enhance explainability and reasoning, though semantic generalization remains challenging. Overall, the literature suggests the most fruitful direction is not a competition but an integration of symbolic and deep learning approaches.

citations.claim: Even state-of-the-art deep learning architectures often fall short on simple tasks testing basic numerical and arithmetic knowledge, highlighting their limitations in symbolic/numerical reasoning.

Symbolic AI uses building blocks with inherent meaning, while subsymbolic AI's individual building blocks escape meaning; Intersymbolic AI combines both to increase effectiveness, like the combination of conscious and subconscious thought.

Symbolic regression is emerging as a promising method for learning interpretable mathematical expressions from data; traditionally tackled with genetic programming, it has recently gained growing interest in deep learning as a data-driven model discovery method.

Integrating symbolic educational knowledge into deep neural networks (NSAI) yields better generalizability and enables extraction of rules, addressing bias and interpretability challenges of ANNs in education.
SAILOR uses deep learning-based sub-symbolic robotic skills such as object recognition and matching to anchor symbolic knowledge to perceptual data in robots.
Relational Reasoning Networks perform relational reasoning in the latent space of a deep learner, overcoming scalability and expressivity limitations of prior neuro-symbolic methods.
Neurosymbolic AI and Knowledge Graphs combine top-down symbolic reasoning with bottom-up neural learning to promote mutual understanding between humans and systems.
Decision trees can be derived from feedforward neural networks, tracing activations to produce transparent symbolic models that capture FNN decision processes and enhance trust.

A task-directed survey of Neuro-Symbolic AI explores how incorporating symbolic systems can enhance explainability and reasoning capabilities of black-box neural models, though semantic generalizability remains a challenge.

standard.summary: Transformers and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have complementary trade-offs. Transformers rely on self-attention to capture causal sequence structure and have outperformed earlier neural methods (including RNN-based approaches) in tasks like sequential recommendation. However, Transformers exhibit a known weakness in length generalization: when trained on shorter sequences, they fail to generalize to longer ones, partly due to vanishing variance in attention outputs. RNNs, on the other hand, can achieve faster inference than Transformers at comparable parameter budgets, though their standard recursive training via backpropagation through time (BPTT) remains a major computational bottleneck; alternative training methods based on state-space feedback can reduce this overhead. Overall, neither architecture is universally superior: Transformers excel at capturing complex context but struggle with length generalization, while RNNs offer inference efficiency but face training-cost challenges.

citations.claim: Self-attention is crucial for encoding the causal structure of sequences.
Transformer-based models, such as SASRec and BERT4Rec, have become common baselines for sequential recommendations, surpassing earlier neural and non-neural methods.
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have recently demonstrated strong performance and faster inference than Transformers at comparable parameter budgets.
The recursive gradient computation with the backpropagation through time (BPTT) algorithm remains the major computational bottleneck.

Transformers, when trained on shorter sequences, fail to generalize robustly to longer ones at test time, and longer sequence length results in a decrease in variance in the output of the multi-head attention modules.
CODE-BiRNN/-BiGRU/-BiLSTM consistently outperform the other architectures on all tasks, demonstrating strong temporal modeling with recurrent architectures.

balanced.summary: Transformers and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) offer different trade-offs in sequence modeling. Transformers rely on self-attention to capture sequence structure; for example, causal Transformers can perform next-token prediction by learning context-dependent functions in-context (doc_1). RNNs, meanwhile, can achieve faster inference than Transformers at comparable parameter budgets, but their recursive backpropagation-through-time training is a major cost; replacing BPTT with fixed state-space-model-style feedback can reduce overhead while retaining long-term dependency capture (doc_7). Transformers have become strong baselines in sequential recommendation (doc_3), PDE surrogate modeling (doc_4), and time-series forecasting, though they can suffer from low-frequency bias and high computational/memory demands (doc_6) and from weak length generalization when trained on short sequences (doc_10). Hybrid RNN/ODE architectures, such as CODE-BiRNN and CODE-BiLSTM, can outperform both pure RNN/ODE models and other baselines on time-series imputation and extrapolation tasks (doc_9). In financial time series, Transformers have also shown encouraging results for volatility prediction (doc_8). Overall, Transformers are versatile and powerful across many domains, but RNNs and their variants remain competitive where inference speed, training efficiency, or temporal dynamics are priorities.

citations.claim: Causal Transformers are trained to predict the next token and can approximate context-dependent next-token mappings through self-attention-based in-context learning.

Recurrent neural networks have demonstrated faster inference than Transformers at comparable parameter budgets, while their recursive BPTT gradient computation is a major training bottleneck; replacing BPTT with a stationary state feedback mechanism reduces training cost.
Transformer-based models such as SASRec and BERT4Rec have become common baselines for sequential recommendation, surpassing earlier neural and non-neural methods.

Transformer architectures can be used to learn the dynamics of physical systems, achieving similar or better results than Fourier Neural Operator and other transformer-based neural operators on Navier-Stokes time-evolution prediction.

Transformer-based models in long time-series forecasting suffer from a bias toward low-frequencies in data and high computational and memory requirements; adding learnable filters improves their performance and allows smaller models.
Transformers trained on shorter sequences fail to generalize robustly to longer ones, with longer sequences causing a decrease in variance in multi-head attention outputs.

Neural Chronos ODE combined with recurrent architectures, especially bidirectional RNN variants, consistently outperforms other ODE-RNN architectures on time-series imputation and forward/backward extrapolation tasks.
Transformer architecture applied to financial time series yields encouraging results for next-move prediction on synthetic data and for quadratic variation and volatility prediction on S&P500 data.

standard.summary: Supervised learning relies heavily on large labeled datasets, while self-supervised learning (SSL) reduces this dependence by learning task-agnostic representations from unlabeled data. In surgical computer vision, SSL pretraining can outperform ImageNet-based supervised initialization, and increasing the diversity of SSL pretraining data further improves performance. However, SSL is not always superior: some self-supervised methods for image reconstruction are suboptimal compared to supervised learning. Conventional supervised learning also tends to underperform in settings with very little labeled data, making SSL a promising alternative for label-scarce scenarios.

citations.claim: Advances in Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) represent a solution, reducing the dependence on large labeled datasets by providing task-agnostic initializations.

In medical image analysis, in-domain SSL pretraining has already been shown to outperform ImageNet-based initialization. Using solely procedure-specific data can lead to substantial improvements of 13.8%, 9.5%, and 36.8% compared to ImageNet pretraining. However, extending this data with more heterogeneous surgical data further increases performance by an additional 5.0%, 5.2%, and 2.5%.
The second class [cross-validation methods] is often suboptimal compared to supervised learning.
Conventional supervised learning methods frequently underperform in scenarios characterised by little labelled data or imbalanced datasets.

balanced.summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is positioned as a label-efficient alternative to supervised learning: it leverages abundant unlabeled data to learn representations, reducing the need for large annotated datasets (doc1, doc2, doc6, doc8). Across medical/surgical imaging, SSL-based pretraining often outperforms supervised transfer from ImageNet, with further gains when pretraining data are diverse (doc4), and it can improve performance in low-label and imbalanced settings where supervised learning struggles (doc5, doc7). SSL also enables learning from noisy data without ground truth, which supervised methods require (doc10), and can work in federated settings with scarce labels (doc9). However, SSL effectiveness depends on pretraining data composition and can suffer from representational collapse/limited nonlinear modeling; kernel-based and other extensions address these issues (doc1, doc2, doc3).

citations.claim: SSL reduces dependence on large labeled datasets by providing task-agnostic initializations, but its downstream value depends on pretraining dataset composition.
SSL addresses scarcity of labeled data, though existing methods often neglect nonlinear dependencies; the proposed CDSSL improves representation quality on diverse benchmarks.
SSL optimizes geometric objectives without labels; Kernel VICReg mitigates representational collapse and improves performance on datasets with nonlinear structure or limited samples.

In surgical computer vision, SSL pretraining outperforms ImageNet-based supervised transfer: procedure-specific SSL improves by up to 36.8%, and adding heterogeneous data increases performance further.
Conventional supervised learning underperforms with little labeled or imbalanced data; self-training with Neurochaos Learning (SSL) yields large performance gains in low-data contexts.
Deep supervised models need large labeled datasets, while semi-supervised/self-supervised methods use unlabeled samples; pseudo-labeling connects these areas.
Combining self-supervised features with semi-supervised learning improves label efficiency with few labeled samples, outperforming baseline by 5.4% on average.

SSL exploits unlabelled data to learn embedding spaces, yet monitoring encoder quality without annotated data remains challenging; label-free metrics correlate with linear probe accuracy only for some methods.
In federated medical imaging, the SelfFed SSL framework overcomes label scarcity and data heterogeneity, outperforming baselines even with only 10% labeled instances.

Self-supervised image reconstruction methods can learn from noisy data alone, bypassing ground-truth references that supervised learning requires; the proposed estimator outperforms existing SSL methods.

standard.summary: Standard deep learning (DL) provides state-of-the-art predictions but typically via deterministic point estimates, leaving models poorly calibrated and unable to reason about epistemic uncertainty [doc_1, doc_3]. Bayesian learning addresses this by treating model parameters as random variables and applying Bayes' theorem, yielding well-calibrated predictions and explicit uncertainty quantification [doc_4, doc_3]. However, full Bayesian inference is computationally demanding, motivating approximations such as variational inference, gradient-based MCMC, MC Dropout, and Laplace approximations [doc_2, doc_5, doc_10]; in some applications, DL surrogates are combined with Bayesian MCMC to balance speed and accuracy [doc_6], while empirical studies caution that deep learning-based uncertainty estimates may not reliably reflect out-of-distribution evidence [doc_8].

citations.claim: Neural networks are often implemented in a frequentist scheme, meaning they are unable to reason about uncertainty in their predictions.

Modern deterministic deep learning models are often poorly calibrated and lack the ability to communicate a measure of epistemic uncertainty in prediction, whereas Bayesian DL models are often well calibrated and capable of quantifying epistemic uncertainty along with competitive prediction accuracy.

Bayesian inference provides a principled probabilistic framework for quantifying uncertainty by updating beliefs based on prior knowledge and observed data through Bayes' theorem; in Bayesian deep learning, neural network weights are treated as random variables with prior distributions.

MCMC sampling methods have faced challenges in being adapted to larger models (such as in deep learning) and big data problems; advanced proposal distributions that incorporate gradients address some limitations of MCMC sampling for Bayesian neural networks.

Bayesian Neural Networks offer a principled approach to uncertainty quantification, but their computational complexity limits scalability; Monte Carlo Dropout approximates Bayesian inference through multiple stochastic forward passes.
The Laplace approximation can compute model evidence analytically, enabling efficient hyperparameter tuning and model comparison without posterior sampling.

DL-based surrogate models can accelerate Bayesian inverse problems, but generally cannot match the accuracy of high-fidelity numerical models; a hybrid two-level MCMC method combines DL surrogates and high-fidelity solvers to achieve the same accuracy at a fraction of the cost.

All tested algorithms showed reasonably good calibration on synthetic test sets, but none of the deep learning based algorithms provided uncertainties that consistently reflect lack of experimental evidence for out-of-distribution data points.

balanced.summary: Bayesian learning and deep learning are often contrasted: standard deep neural networks are usually trained in a frequentist manner and lack principled uncertainty quantification, whereas Bayesian learning treats parameters as distributions and updates beliefs via Bayes' theorem, enabling uncertainty reasoning. Bayesian deep learning combines these ideas, but faces scalability challenges: MCMC sampling has difficulty with large modern models, and variational approximations are computationally demanding. Approximate techniques such as Monte Carlo Dropout, Laplace approximations, and PAC-Bayesian analysis help bridge the gap, while hybrid methods can combine deep learning surrogates with Bayesian/MCMC correction for efficiency. Empirical studies show deterministic deep learning models are often poorly calibrated, and deep learning-based uncertainty estimates do not always reflect out-of-distribution evidence, whereas Bayesian approaches generally provide better-calibrated epistemic uncertainty. Overall, the choice is not strictly either/or: Bayesian principles can be integrated into deep learning for uncertainty quantification, sparsification, federated learning, and physics-informed modeling, although computational cost and generalization guarantees remain active research areas.

citations.claim: Neural networks are typically implemented in a frequentist scheme and are unable to reason about uncertainty in their predictions; Bayesian Neural Networks are introduced to address this limitation.
Bayesian inference provides parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification, but MCMC sampling methods have faced challenges adapting to larger deep learning models and big data problems.

Modern deterministic deep learning models are often poorly calibrated and lack epistemic uncertainty, while Bayesian deep learning models are often well calibrated and can quantify epistemic uncertainty with competitive prediction accuracy.
Bayesian methods lack theoretical generalization guarantees for unseen data, and PAC-Bayesian analysis provides a frequentist framework to derive generalization bounds for randomized predictors.

Monte Carlo Dropout approximates Bayesian inference by enabling probabilistic modeling through multiple stochastic forward passes, maintaining computational efficiency while improving uncertainty estimates.

A hybrid two-level MCMC method combines deep learning surrogate speed with high-fidelity numerical solver corrections, achieving the same accuracy as pure numerical MCMC at a small fraction of the computational cost.

Bayesian model reduction (BMR) provides a more efficient alternative for pruning deep neural network weights than hierarchical horseshoe prior approaches, reducing computational demands of full Bayesian sparsification.

In empirical tests, none of the deep learning based algorithms provided uncertainties that consistently reflect lack of experimental evidence for out-of-distribution data points, although calibration on synthetic test sets was reasonably good.
Deep learning methods can accurately model non-Gaussian aleatoric uncertainty in robotic state estimation, capturing complex uncertainty patterns beyond traditional fixed Gaussian assumptions.

An evidence-driven Bayesian formulation of physics-informed neural networks uses Laplace approximation to compute model evidence analytically, enabling efficient hyperparameter tuning and predictive uncertainties without posterior sampling.

standard.summary: Federated optimization and pure local training are two baseline strategies in federated learning, and their relative merit depends on data heterogeneity: minimax analysis shows an approximate alternative where FedAvg is rate-optimal when heterogeneity is small, while local training (empirical risk minimization without communication) is rate-optimal when heterogeneity is large, with a sharp threshold up to a constant. Local training alone can suffer from non-IID data, which negatively affects convergence and motivates strategies for selecting or guiding local gradients; federated optimization with local training can still converge to near-optimal solutions in heterogeneous environments, but the convergence gap is controlled by the level of heterogeneity. Additional federated optimization techniques address communication and heterogeneity trade-offs, such as clustering client selections to reduce communication cost or projecting local gradients to improve efficiency.

citations.claim: The excess risks of personalized federated learning using FedAvg and pure local training reveal an approximate alternative: FedAvg is minimax rate optimal when data heterogeneity is small, whereas local training is minimax rate optimal when data heterogeneity is large, with a sharp threshold.
Non-IID data in federated learning negatively affect the convergence efficiency of the global model, and the BHerd strategy selects a beneficial herd of local gradients to accelerate convergence.

Federated learning faces significant hurdles in non-IID data scenarios, and FedLEx optimizes learning behavior for non-IID settings by using a global guidance matrix to guide clients' gradient updates.
Federated softmax policy gradient with local training converges to a near-optimal policy in terms of average agent value, with a gap controlled by the level of heterogeneity.
A dynamic clustering scheme for client selection reduces communication and transmission costs by almost 50% compared with traditional federated learning without affecting model accuracy.
Heterogeneous federated learning faces challenges from diversity in data, model, task, device, and communication, increasing the complexity of model training.

balanced.summary: The documents collectively examine the trade-off between federated optimization (e.g., FedAvg) and pure local training. One key result shows a minimax alternative: FedAvg is rate-optimal when data heterogeneity is small, whereas local training is rate-optimal when heterogeneity is large, with a sharp threshold; combining the two baselines is also rate-optimal (doc_1). Another document derives convergence rates for federated softmax policy gradient with local training, showing the convergence gap is controlled by heterogeneity and that federated objectives may inherently require stochastic policies (doc_7). Several works address challenges posed by heterogeneity and communication in federated optimization (doc_2, doc_8), and propose communication-efficient methods such as adaptive client clustering (doc_4), selecting beneficial local gradients (doc_5), projecting gradients onto historical descent directions (doc_9), and second-order FL with over-the-air aggregation (doc_10). Federated customization of large models is also explored, with prefix-tuning shown to be feasible and close to centralized performance (doc_3). Finally, a loss-exploration approach is introduced to improve convergence under non-IID data (doc_6).

citations.claim: FedAvg is minimax rate optimal when data heterogeneity is small, while pure local training is minimax rate optimal when heterogeneity is large, with a sharp threshold up to a constant.
A dichotomous strategy choosing between FedAvg and local training is rate-optimal from a worst-case perspective.
Federated softmax policy gradient with local training converges to a near-optimal policy in terms of average agent value, with a gap controlled by the level of heterogeneity.
Federated objectives may inherently require stochastic policies, unlike single-agent settings where optimal policies can be deterministic.

Federated learning training is inherently decentralized and poses unique challenges distinct from data-center settings, including heterogeneity of data and devices, communication issues, and privacy concerns.

Heterogeneous federated learning involves challenges from data, model, task, device, and communication heterogeneity, and approaches are categorized at data-level, model-level, and architecture-level.
Dynamically adjusting the number of clusters for client selection can reduce communication and transmission costs by almost 50% without affecting model accuracy.
The BHerd strategy selects a beneficial herd of local gradients to mitigate non-IID effects and accelerate federated model convergence.
ProjFL and ProjFL+EF project local gradients onto a shared subspace spanned by historical descent directions, achieving comparable accuracy while substantially reducing communication costs.
A scalable second-order FL algorithm using a sparse Hessian estimate and over-the-air aggregation achieves more than 67% communication and energy savings compared to first and second-order baselines.

Federated prefix-tuning is feasible in the federated learning framework, with performance close to centralized approaches and competitive efficiency and robustness compared with other federated customization methods.
FedLEx uses a global guidance matrix from client gradient deviations to guide updates and improve convergence under non-IID data without additional data sharing or distribution statistics.

standard.summary: The documents address gradient descent and evolutionary algorithms largely as different optimization paradigms, with some empirical and theoretical comparisons and some hybrid approaches. Experimentally, the gradient-based quasi-Newton BFGS algorithm is compared with derivative-free evolutionary methods (CMA-ES, DE, PSO), with performance depending on problem conditioning and rotational invariance (doc_1). Evolutionary algorithms are also characterized as black-box and derivative-free: the (1+1)-evolution strategy achieves linear convergence on locally strongly convex functions without needing gradient or Lipschitz knowledge, unlike existing derivative-free analyses (doc_5). Hybrid methods can combine gradient information with evolutionary/swarm mechanisms: a consensus-based optimization variant using memory and gradient information provably converges to global minimizers and shows numerical advantages in machine learning and compressed sensing (doc_9), and a method combining gradient descent with evolutionary computation improves neural symbolic regression accuracy over gradient-only training (doc_10). Additionally, evolutionary algorithms often struggle with exploitation in hyperparameter optimization, and adding a linear surrogate model improves their performance (doc_3).

citations.claim: The gradient-based quasi-Newton BFGS algorithm is experimentally compared with derivative-free evolutionary algorithms CMA-ES, DE, and PSO on benchmark functions, investigating dependence on conditioning and rotational invariance.

The (1+1)-evolution strategy converges linearly on locally strongly convex functions with Lipschitz continuous gradient without prior gradient or Lipschitz knowledge, whereas existing analyses of derivative-free algorithms typically require such knowledge.

A consensus-based optimization variant incorporating memory effects and gradient information provably converges to a global minimizer in mean-field law and demonstrates numerical superiority in applications such as machine learning and compressed sensing.

A method combining gradient descent and evolutionary computation yields neural networks that generate more symbolically and behaviorally accurate equations than state-of-the-art gradient-based neural symbolic regression methods.

Evolutionary algorithms often struggle with effective exploitation in hyperparameter optimization; integrating a linear surrogate model into a genetic algorithm improves exploitation, achieving an average improvement of 1.89% over existing HPO methods.

balanced.summary: Gradient descent is a local search method that exploits derivative information, whereas evolutionary algorithms are population-based metaheuristics offering broader exploration but often weaker exploitation. Empirical and theoretical works in the provided documents show that hybridizing evolutionary or swarm search with gradient/surrogate information can improve exploitation and global convergence, and that rigorous benchmarking is essential for fair comparisons between these algorithm families.

citations.claim: An experimental comparison of BFGS, NEWUOA, CMA-ES, DE, and PSO investigates how performance depends on problem conditioning and rotational invariance.

Evolutionary algorithms show promise in hyperparameter optimization but often struggle with effective exploitation, and integrating a linear surrogate model improved their average performance by 1.89% over existing HPO methods.
Hybrid evolutionary-swarm metaheuristics combining PSO and GA achieve superior convergence and consistency, especially in higher-dimensional search spaces, compared with their standard basic forms.

The (1+1)-evolution strategy converges linearly on locally strongly convex functions with Lipschitz continuous gradient, and unlike existing derivative-free optimization analyses, it does not require prior knowledge of the objective's Lipschitz constant.

Methodological guidelines for comparing bio-inspired optimization algorithms emphasize using appropriate benchmarks, reference algorithms, and principled validation to guarantee significance of reported results.
SEvoBench provides a modular C++ framework with efficient PSO and DE implementations, parallel benchmarking, and SIMD vectorization for comparing evolutionary single-objective optimizers.

A consensus-based optimization variant using memory effects and gradient information provably converges to a global minimizer in mean-field law, showing gradient information can be leveraged in multi-particle metaheuristics while preserving global convergence.

A method combining gradient descent and evolutionary computation for neural symbolic regression produces equations that are more symbolically and behaviorally accurate than those from state-of-the-art gradient-based neural symbolic regression methods.

standard.summary: Embedding search (dense retrieval) captures semantic similarity and can outperform lexical methods on tasks like paraphrase detection, where a span-detection model beat a lexical-similarity baseline by 31.9pp exact match (doc_1). However, dense retrieval via ANN lacks a natural cutoff and produces cosine similarity scores that are hard to interpret, making relevance filtering difficult, whereas lexical retrieval inherently limits the retrieved set through keyword matching (doc_2). Lexical knowledge also remains important for tasks like question answering, where explicit lexicalization can significantly boost performance (doc_8). Overall, the choice between embedding and lexical search depends on the task: embeddings excel at semantic matching but require additional relevance filtering, while lexical search provides interpretable, keyword-based matching with a natural cutoff.

citations.claim: A paraphrase span detection model outperformed lexical similarity and BERT sentence embedding retrieval baselines by 31.9pp and 22.4pp respectively in exact match, showing a strong advantage of span retrieval over sentence similarity.

Unlike lexical retrieval, which inherently limits the size of the retrieved set through keyword matching, dense retrieval via ANN search has no natural cutoff, and cosine similarity scores are often difficult to interpret.

Explicit lexical knowledge, or lexicalization, significantly eases the lexical gap in question answering and can increase performance by up to 35.8% in micro F1 score compared to the best QA system on QALD-9.

balanced.summary: Embedding search (dense retrieval) matches by semantic similarity and can be accelerated with ANN indexes, but it lacks a natural result cutoff, can be biased and domain-sensitive, and needs careful model/pooling selection; lexical search relies on explicit keyword/lexical matching, which provides natural cutoffs and interpretable lexical knowledge but misses paraphrase-style semantic matches. The documents illustrate these tradeoffs: semantic/paraphrase models outperform both lexical and embedding baselines for semantic search; dense retrieval requires extra relevance filtering because cosine scores are hard to interpret and have no natural cutoff; embedding model and pooling choices substantially affect retrieval; efficiency techniques (early exit, topical locality, graph indexes) make dense search faster; neural retrievers exhibit source bias; and lexicalization remains important for compositional QA even in the LLM era. Overall, the choice between embedding and lexical search depends on the task, domain, latency, and the need for interpretability or semantic generalization.

citations.claim: A paraphrase span detection model outperformed both lexical similarity and BERT sentence embedding baselines for semantic search by 31.9pp and 22.4pp exact match respectively.

Unlike lexical retrieval, which inherently limits retrieved set size through keyword matching, dense retrieval via ANN search has no natural cutoff and cosine similarity scores are difficult to interpret, motivating a relevance filtering component.

The choice of embedding model significantly impacts retrieval performance, with the general-domain BGE model consistently outperforming all others including medical-specific models, and performance varying across datasets and query formulations.

Learned dense representations enable retrieval via approximate k-nearest-neighbor search, and an unsupervised early-exit patience method can improve A-kNN efficiency with up to 5x speedups while achieving negligible effectiveness losses.

By leveraging query embedding similarities in conversational dense retrieval, restricting the search space to semantically relevant document clusters achieved up to 10.4X speedup with little loss in performance.

Neural retrieval models tend to rank LLM-generated documents higher than human-written ones, showing source bias that extends from first-stage retrievers to second-stage neural re-rankers, partly because LLM-generated texts have more focused semantics.

Cross-modal embedding queries become out-of-distribution relative to base data, causing state-of-the-art ANNS approaches to suffer poor performance; a projected bipartite graph index achieves up to 3.56x faster search at 90% recall for such queries.

Explicit lexical knowledge in a compositional QA system increased micro F1 by up to 35.8% over the best QA system on QALD-9, whereas LLMs showed limited ability to exploit lexical knowledge compositionally.
Despite the emergence of generative AI, the continued need for search systems remains essential because users have concerns about authoritativeness, timeliness, and contextualization of search.

Generalist text embedding models pre-trained on large-scale corpora can provide strong zero-shot performance without specialized adaptation, outperforming traditional and fine-tuned models in sequential recommendation and product search.
